[Container] [Composite<CompositeReceiptChannel, IReceiptChannel>] [Composite<BackupReceiptChannel, IReceiptChannel>] // two composites for one service public static partial class CoffeeShop; Fix: Keep one [Composite] per service and remove the others; only the first one is used.

Error A [Composite]'s collection parameter is of a base type of the composed service, not the composed service itself. // IReceiptChannel : IChannel public sealed class CompositeReceiptChannel(IEnumerable<IChannel> channels) : IReceiptChannel; // IChannel is a base type [Container] [Transient<PrinterChannel, IReceiptChannel>] [Composite<CompositeReceiptChannel, IReceiptChannel>] public static partial class CoffeeShop; Fix: Make the element type exactly the composed service: IEnumerable<IReceiptChannel> channels.

Error A key in a [Decorate]'s Keys matches no registration of the decorated service, so that key has nothing to wrap. A null entry names the unkeyed registrations. For the open generic typeof form, no closing of the service is registered under the key. [Container] [Singleton<CardTerminal, IPaymentTerminal>] [Decorate<LoggingTerminal, IPaymentTerminal>(Keys = new object?[] { "backup" })] // nothing is registered under "backup" public static partial class CoffeeShop; Fix: Register the decorated service under that key, or remove the key from Keys.

Error A [Decorate] sets both Keys and AllKeys. AllKeys already selects every key, so set one or the other. The decorator is skipped. [Container] [Singleton<CardTerminal, IPaymentTerminal>] [Decorate<LoggingTerminal, IPaymentTerminal>(Keys = new object?[] { null }, AllKeys = true)] public static partial class CoffeeShop; Fix: Set Keys to decorate selected keys, or AllKeys = true to decorate every key, not both.

Error A [Composite]'s Key matches no registration of the composed service, so the composite has nothing to front. For the open generic typeof form, no closing of the service is registered under the key. [Container] [Transient<PrinterChannel, IReceiptChannel>] [Composite<CompositeReceiptChannel, IReceiptChannel>(Key = "kitchen")] // nothing is registered under "kitchen" public static partial class CoffeeShop; Fix: Register the members under that key ([Transient<PrinterChannel, IReceiptChannel>(Key = "kitchen")]), or change the composite's Key.

Error An open generic registration's implementation and service have different arity. The open [Decorate]/[Composite] typeof forms are held to the same rule (decorator/composite arity must match the service). [Container] [Transient(typeof(Repository<>), typeof(IRepository<,>))] // one type parameter vs two public static partial class CoffeeShop; Fix: Pair an implementation and a service with the same number of type parameters: [Transient(typeof(Repository<>), typeof(IRepository<>))].

Error A required closed type violates the open generic implementation's type-parameter constraints, so the dependency cannot be satisfied. (For the open [Decorate]/[Composite] case, where the base service still resolves, see the warning AWT171.) public sealed class Repository<T> : IRepository<T> where T : class; public sealed class Ledger(IRepository<int> repo); // int is not a class [Container] [Transient(typeof(Repository<>), typeof(IRepository<>))] [Singleton<Ledger>] public static partial class CoffeeShop; Fix: Depend on a closing that satisfies the constraints (here a reference type, such as IRepository<Order>), or relax the implementation's constraint.

Warning The decorator/composite counterpart to AWT126: a closing of an open generic [Decorate]/[Composite] cannot be constructed because its type arguments violate the decorator's or composite's type-parameter constraints. A warning, not an error, because the base service still resolves. That one closing is left as-is (undecorated/unfronted), and the remaining closings are decorated/composed as usual. public interface IHandler<T> { } public sealed class Handler<T> : IHandler<T> { } public sealed class Logging<T>(IHandler<T> inner) : IHandler<T> where T : class; // reference types only public sealed class Counter(IHandler<int> handler); // needs the closing IHandler<int> [Container] [Transient(typeof(Handler<>), typeof(IHandler<>))] [Transient<Counter>] [Decorate(typeof(Logging<>), typeof(IHandler<>))] // IHandler<int> can't take Logging<int>: warned and skipped public static partial class CoffeeShop; Fix: Relax the decorator's or composite's constraint so it covers every closing (here drop where T : class). If the closing should stay undecorated, the warning says exactly that and can be left as is.

Error The typeof-argument form of [Decorate] or [Composite] must receive unbound open generic types. A lifetime attribute's typeof form accepts a closed pair, but when one of its two types is an unbound generic, both must be. [Container] [Transient(typeof(Repository<>), typeof(IRepository<Order>))] // open implementation, closed service public static partial class CoffeeShop; Fix: Pass unbound generics on both sides, typeof(Repository<>), typeof(IRepository<>), or register the closed pair with the generic form: [Transient<Repository<Order>, IRepository<Order>>].

Error An open generic implementation does not expose its service with type parameters in declaration order. The open [Decorate]/[Composite] typeof forms are held to the same rule. public sealed class Map<TKey, TValue> : IMap<TValue, TKey>; // parameters swapped [Container] [Transient(typeof(Map<,>), typeof(IMap<,>))] public static partial class CoffeeShop; Fix: Expose the service with the implementation's type parameters in declaration order: Map<TKey, TValue> : IMap<TKey, TValue>.

Error Open generic expansion nested too deep, indicating an unbounded generic recursion. public sealed class Box<T>(Box<Box<T>> inner); // Box<Order> needs Box<Box<Order>> needs ... public sealed class Consumer(Box<Order> box); [Container] [Transient(typeof(Box<>))] [Singleton<Consumer>] public static partial class CoffeeShop; Fix: Break the recursion: an implementation must not depend on an ever-larger closing of its own open registration, as Box<T> does with Box<Box<T>>.

Error A closed typeof registration's implementation is not a class or interface assignable to its service. The generic form [Singleton<Clock, IClock>] rejects such a pair through its type constraints; the typeof form has none, so Awaiten reports it. public sealed class Clock; // does not implement IClock [Container] [Singleton(typeof(Clock), typeof(IClock))] public static partial class CoffeeShop; Fix: Let the implementation implement the service (public sealed class Clock : IClock;), or use the generic form [Singleton<Clock, IClock>], whose constraints check the pair.

Error Eager or Instance is set on an open generic typeof registration. Both describe one concrete instance, but the closings of an open generic are whatever the graph asks for, so eagerly building "every closing" would start services because some other consumer happens to close the generic, and one pre-built instance cannot be every closing. Register the closings you want eager or pre-built with a closed type. The option is ignored. [Container] [Singleton(typeof(Cache<>), typeof(ICache<>), Eager = true)] // which closings? [Singleton(typeof(Cache<Order>), typeof(ICache<Order>), Eager = true)] // fine: one closed type public static partial class CoffeeShop; Fix: Remove Eager or Instance from the open generic registration and register each closing you want eager or pre-built with a closed type, as the second line does.

Error The Factory of an open generic typeof registration is not a generic method with exactly the service's type parameters. Awaiten closes the factory per closing with the closed service's type arguments, in declaration order, so the method needs one type parameter for each of the service's. The registration is dropped. [Container] [Transient(typeof(IRepository<>), Factory = nameof(Create))] public static partial class CoffeeShop { private static IRepository<Order> Create() => new Repository<Order>(); // needs Create<T>() } Fix: Make the factory a generic method with exactly the service's type parameters: private static IRepository<T> Create<T>() => new Repository<T>();.

Error A closing of an open generic typeof registration violates the type-parameter constraints of its generic Factory, so the factory cannot be called for it. Like AWT126, the closing is skipped and the dependency that asked for it is unsatisfied. public sealed class Ledger(IRepository<int> numbers); // int is not a class [Container] [Transient(typeof(IRepository<>), Factory = nameof(Create))] [Singleton<Ledger>] public static partial class CoffeeShop { private static IRepository<T> Create<T>() where T : class => new Repository<T>(); } Fix: Relax the factory's constraint so it covers the closing, or depend on a closing that satisfies it (here a reference type, such as IRepository<Order>).

Error An [Inject] property has no set or init accessor the container can assign through. public sealed class Barista { [Inject] public ITimeSystem? Time { get; } // get-only, nothing to assign } [Container] [Transient<Barista>] [Singleton<RealTimeSystem, ITimeSystem>] public static partial class CoffeeShop; Fix: Give the property an accessible set or init accessor ({ get; set; }), or remove [Inject].

Error An [Inject(Deferred = true)] property is init-only or required rather than assignable after construction. public sealed class Node { [Inject(Deferred = true)] public Node? Peer { get; init; } // deferred needs a plain set } [Container] [Singleton<Node>] public static partial class CoffeeShop; Fix: Give the property a plain set accessor and do not mark it required: public Node? Peer { get; set; }.

Error A deferred property cycle consists entirely of transients and cannot terminate. public sealed class A { [Inject(Deferred = true)] public B? B { get; set; } } public sealed class B { [Inject(Deferred = true)] public A? A { get; set; } } [Container] [Transient<A>] // all transient: a fresh instance every step, so the cycle never closes [Transient<B>] public static partial class CoffeeShop; Fix: Make at least one participant a singleton or scoped ([Singleton<A>]), so the cycle closes on a cached instance, or break the cycle.

Error A deferred property cycle includes an async-initialized service and cannot terminate. public sealed class A : IAsyncInitializable { [Inject(Deferred = true)] public B? B { get; set; } public Task InitializeAsync(CancellationToken ct) => Task.CompletedTask; } public sealed class B { [Inject(Deferred = true)] public A? A { get; set; } } [Container] [Singleton<A>] [Singleton<B>] public static partial class CoffeeShop; Fix: Break the cycle, or make every participant synchronous: neither IAsyncInitializable nor dependent on an async service.

Error A deferred property cycle still traverses a construction-time edge that duplicates a cached participant or recurses forever. public sealed class A(B b); // construction-time edge into the cycle public sealed class B { [Inject(Deferred = true)] public A? A { get; set; } } [Container] [Transient<A>] [Transient<B>] public static partial class CoffeeShop; Fix: Turn the remaining constructor parameter into an [Inject(Deferred = true)] property too, and register one participant as a singleton or scoped, since a cycle of transients never terminates (AWT145). Or remove one of the dependencies.

Error An [Inject(Optional = true)] property is required and cannot be omitted from the object initializer. public sealed class Barista { [Inject(Optional = true)] public required ITimeSystem Time { get; set; } // required cannot be omitted } [Container] [Transient<Barista>] public static partial class CoffeeShop; Fix: Drop required, or drop Optional = true so that a missing dependency is reported as AWT101 instead.

Warning An [Inject(Optional = true)] property is init-only, so an unregistered dependency leaves it permanently at its default. public sealed class Barista { [Inject(Optional = true)] public ITimeSystem? Time { get; init; } // init-only stays default forever } [Container] [Transient<Barista>] public static partial class CoffeeShop; Fix: Give the property a plain set accessor, so a value can still be assigned after construction when the dependency is not registered.

Error An [InjectProperty<T>] names a member that is not a settable property on the implementation: an unknown name, a field or method, or a read-only property. For an open-generic target such as [InjectProperty(typeof(OrderBook<>), ...)] the generic definition is checked, once. public sealed class Barista { public ITimeSystem? Time { get; set; } } [Container] [Singleton<RealTimeSystem, ITimeSystem>] [Singleton<Barista>] [InjectProperty<Barista>("Tim")] // no such property (typo); use nameof(Barista.Time) public static partial class CoffeeShop; Fix: Name the property with nameof(Barista.Time), and make sure it is a property with a set or init accessor rather than a field, method or read-only member.

Error An [InjectProperty<T>] targets an implementation produced by a Factory or Instance registration. Such an instance is built whole by its source, so there is no object initializer for the container to fill. public sealed class Barista { public ITimeSystem? Time { get; set; } } [Container] [Singleton<RealTimeSystem, ITimeSystem>] [Singleton<Barista>(Factory = nameof(MakeBarista))] [InjectProperty<Barista>(nameof(Barista.Time))] // Barista is factory-produced, not container-constructed public static partial class CoffeeShop { private static Barista MakeBarista() => new(); } Fix: Remove the [InjectProperty] entry and set the property in the factory, which can take the dependency as a parameter (MakeBarista(ITimeSystem time) => new() { Time = time }), or let the container construct the type.

Warning Two [InjectProperty] entries name the same property of the same implementation, both closed or both open-generic. The property is filled once; the duplicate is ignored. A closed entry and an open-generic typeof entry that meet on one closing are reported only when the closed entry repeats the open entry's Key, Optional and Deferred: the closed entry wins on its closing either way, so one that changes an option is a deliberate specialization of that closing and is not reported. This is an analyzer diagnostic, so a deliberate duplicate can be suppressed in source with #pragma warning disable AWT179 or [SuppressMessage]. public sealed class Barista { public ITimeSystem? Time { get; set; } } [Container] [Singleton<RealTimeSystem, ITimeSystem>] [Singleton<Barista>] [InjectProperty<Barista>(nameof(Barista.Time))] [InjectProperty<Barista>(nameof(Barista.Time))] // filled once; the second entry is redundant public static partial class CoffeeShop; Fix: Remove the duplicate entry, or suppress the warning where the duplicate is deliberate.

Warning An [InjectProperty<T>] names an implementation that has no container-constructed registration, so the entry is never applied: the type is unregistered, or it is an open generic no consumer closed. public sealed class Barista { public ITimeSystem? Time { get; set; } } [Container] [Singleton<RealTimeSystem, ITimeSystem>] [InjectProperty<Barista>(nameof(Barista.Time))] // Barista itself is never registered public static partial class CoffeeShop; Fix: Register the implementation as a constructed service ([Singleton<Barista>]), or remove the entry. For a generic definition, make sure a consumer requires one of its closings.

Warning A property carries both [Inject] and a container-side [InjectProperty<T>] entry. The property is filled once, from [Inject], so the entry's Optional/Deferred/Key are ignored. public sealed class Barista { [Inject] public ITimeSystem? Time { get; set; } } [Container] [Singleton<RealTimeSystem, ITimeSystem>] [Singleton<Barista>] [InjectProperty<Barista>(nameof(Barista.Time))] // [Inject] already fills it: remove one public static partial class CoffeeShop; Fix: Remove one of the two: the [Inject] attribute on the property or the [InjectProperty] entry on the container.

Warning A [Scan] matched no concrete type assignable to its marker. public interface IPlugin; // no implementations exist [Container] [Scan<IPlugin>] public static partial class CoffeeShop; Fix: Check the marker for a typo and that its implementations live in the scanned assembly (use InAssembliesOf for another one), or remove the scan.

Warning A [Scan(As = ScanAs.Marker)] matched a type with no assignable interface. public abstract class Report; public sealed class QuarterlyReport : Report; // a Report, but implements no interface [Container] [Scan(typeof(Report), As = ScanAs.Marker)] public static partial class CoffeeShop; Fix: Scan a marker interface, or add the Self flag to keep the self registration: As = ScanAs.Self | ScanAs.Marker.

Warning A [Scan(InAssembliesOf = …)] named an assembly with no candidate types. [Container] [Scan(typeof(IPlugin), InAssembliesOf = new[] { typeof(string) })] // that assembly has no IPlugin types public static partial class CoffeeShop; Fix: Name a type from the assembly that holds the implementations, and check that its project is referenced and the marker is the right one.

Warning A [Scan(SkipUnconstructable = true)] match the container cannot construct is skipped. public sealed class LegacyPlugin : IPlugin { private LegacyPlugin() { } // no usable constructor, so it is skipped } [Container] [Scan(typeof(IPlugin), SkipUnconstructable = true)] public static partial class CoffeeShop; Fix: Make the match constructable (an accessible constructor, registered dependencies) so it registers, or exclude it from the scan to state that the skip is intended.

Warning Scans register one implementation with conflicting lifetimes. public sealed class Widget : IPlugin, IHandler; // matched by both scans [Container] [Scan(typeof(IPlugin), Lifetime = Lifetime.Singleton)] [Scan(typeof(IHandler), Lifetime = Lifetime.Transient)] // two lifetimes for Widget public static partial class CoffeeShop; Fix: Give the overlapping scans the same Lifetime, exclude the type from one of them, or register it explicitly, which the scans yield to.

Error A [Scan(InAssembliesOf = …)] resolved to no assembly at all. [Container] [Scan(typeof(IPlugin), InAssembliesOf = new Type[0])] // no assemblies to scan public static partial class CoffeeShop; Fix: List one type from each assembly to scan, or remove InAssembliesOf to scan the container's own assembly.

Warning A [Scan]'s name, namespace or exclude filters removed every marker-assignable match. public sealed class GrinderPlugin : IPlugin; // assignable, but filtered out by the pattern below [Container] [Scan<IPlugin>(NamePatterns = ["*Handler"])] // no IPlugin ends in "Handler", so nothing registers public static partial class CoffeeShop; Fix: Loosen the NamePatterns, NamespacePatterns or Exclude filters so they keep the types you mean, here NamePatterns = ["*Plugin"].

Warning A [Scan] exclusion (an Exclude type or a !-prefixed pattern) matched no candidate. public sealed class GrinderPlugin : IPlugin; [Container] [Scan<IPlugin>(Exclude = [typeof(RenamedPlugin)])] // RenamedPlugin is no longer a candidate: stale public static partial class CoffeeShop; Fix: Remove the stale exclusion, or update it to the type's new name.

Warning A [Scan] include pattern matches every candidate, so it does not narrow the scan. public sealed class GrinderPlugin : IPlugin; [Container] [Scan<IPlugin>(NamePatterns = ["*"])] // "*" matches every name; drop it public static partial class CoffeeShop; Fix: Remove the pattern; it does not narrow anything.

Warning A [Scan(As = ScanAs.MatchingInterface)] matched a type that implements no interface named I + its own name. public interface IEspresso; public sealed class Espresso : IEspresso; public sealed class Ristretto : IEspresso; // no IRistretto, so it is not registered [Container] [Scan<IEspresso>(As = ScanAs.MatchingInterface)] public static partial class CoffeeShop; Fix: Implement the convention interface (IRistretto), or add the Self flag to keep the self registration: As = ScanAs.Self | ScanAs.MatchingInterface.

Error A markerless [Scan] includes the Marker exposure, or declares no scoping filter. [Container] [Scan(As = ScanAs.MatchingInterface)] // markerless, but no NamePatterns/NamespacePatterns/InAssembliesOf public static partial class CoffeeShop; Fix: Give a markerless scan at least one NamePatterns, NamespacePatterns or InAssembliesOf filter, and leave ScanAs.Marker out of its As, since there is no marker.

Warning A markerless [Scan] matched candidate types but registered none of them. [Container] // Nothing under CoffeeShop.Legacy follows the I + name convention, so nothing registers. [Scan(As = ScanAs.MatchingInterface, NamespacePatterns = ["CoffeeShop.Legacy.**"])] public static partial class CoffeeShop; Fix: Widen the filters until they match the types you mean, and with ScanAs.MatchingInterface check that the matches follow the I + name convention.

Error A [Scan]'s As resolved to no ScanAs flag, so it would register nothing (usually & written for |). [Container] [Scan<IDrink>(As = ScanAs.Self & ScanAs.Marker)] // & is empty; use | to combine flags public static partial class CoffeeShop; Fix: Combine flags with | (ScanAs.Self | ScanAs.Marker), or omit As for the Self default.

Warning A [Scan(As = ScanAs.MatchingInterface)] matched a type implementing several same-named convention interfaces, so it registers under each of them. namespace CoffeeShop.Old { public interface IMenu; } namespace CoffeeShop.New { public interface IMenu; } namespace CoffeeShop { public interface IShopService; // No CoffeeShop.IMenu exists to win the own-namespace tiebreak, so Menu registers under both. public sealed class Menu : IShopService, Old.IMenu, New.IMenu; [Container] [Scan<IShopService>(As = ScanAs.MatchingInterface)] public static partial class Shop; } Reported only when several interfaces actually register (an inaccessible candidate is dropped, which AWT188 covers when the match registers nothing) and only for a marker scan: a markerless [Scan] registers the ambiguous match silently, like the other per-match scan warnings. Fix: Keep a single convention interface, declare the one you want in the type's own namespace so it wins the tiebreak, or exclude the type from the scan.

Warning A scan match's only exposure interface is inaccessible to the generated container, so the match is not registered. // In a referenced assembly: the convention interface is internal. internal interface IRoaster; public sealed class Roaster : IRoaster, IEquipment; // Registering Roaster under IRoaster would not compile in the container's assembly. [Container] [Scan<IEquipment>(As = ScanAs.MatchingInterface, InAssembliesOf = [typeof(IEquipment)])] public static partial class CoffeeShop; Fix: Make the interface accessible to the container's assembly (public, or InternalsVisibleTo), or add the Self flag to register the type under itself.

Warning A [Scan] matched a type that is inaccessible to the generated container, so it is not registered. // In a referenced assembly: the implementation itself is internal. public interface IEquipment; internal sealed class Roaster : IEquipment; // Roaster is assignable to the marker, but the container cannot name it to construct it. [Container] [Scan<IEquipment>(InAssembliesOf = [typeof(IEquipment)])] public static partial class CoffeeShop; Where AWT188 is about an interface the match cannot be exposed under, this one is about the match itself, so no ScanAs flag rescues it: every registration has to name the implementation. Make the type public, grant the container's assembly InternalsVisibleTo, or exclude it with a NamePatterns/NamespacePatterns entry (the Exclude type list cannot name an inaccessible type). Reported only for a type the marker matched and the scan's filters kept, so an unrelated internal type in a scanned assembly stays silent, as does one you already excluded. Fix: Make the type public, grant the container's assembly InternalsVisibleTo, or exclude it with a NamePatterns or NamespacePatterns entry.

Error A generic lifecycle hook on an open-generic [Scan] marker could bind a match through more than one closed marker form, so its type arguments are ambiguous. public interface IView<TViewModel>; public sealed class DualView : IView<Orders>, IView<Payments>; // closes IView<> twice [Container] [Scan(typeof(IView<>), As = ScanAs.Marker, OnActivated = nameof(Wire))] public static partial class CoffeeShop { private static void Wire<TViewModel>(IView<TViewModel> view) { } // TViewModel would be Orders or Payments? } A generic scan hook binds its type argument from a closed marker form, so it needs exactly one it can bind. DualView, which closes IView<> at both Orders and Payments, offers two; the same happens when two scans bind the same generic hook through differently-closed markers of one type. Register the type explicitly with the intended hook, or split the family so only one closed form binds it. Which closed forms count Only forms the hook could actually bind count: matching arity, type arguments the generated container can access, satisfied constraints, and a first parameter that accepts the match. If exactly one form remains after those checks the hook binds it, so a where TViewModel : class constraint can settle a family that closes the marker at one class and one struct, and a closing at another assembly's internal type yields to an accessible sibling. Reported only when the ambiguous generic method is the sole usable overload of the hook name: if another overload also accepts the match, the collision is between overloads rather than closings (settling the closings would still leave two usable overloads), so it is AWT190 instead. Only a generic hook is affected: a non-generic hook (its parameter typed as the marker or object) takes no type argument, so a match with several closings is fine for it, as is a match closing the marker several times without any hook (each closed form registers as its own collection member). Fix: Register the type explicitly with the hook you intend, or split the family so only one closed marker form binds the hook.

Warning Two [Scan] attributes match one implementation with conflicting lifecycle hooks; the first scan's hook is used. public sealed class Widget : IPlugin, IHandler; // matched by both scans [Container] [Scan(typeof(IPlugin), OnActivated = nameof(PluginStarted))] [Scan(typeof(IHandler), OnActivated = nameof(HandlerStarted))] // two OnActivated hooks for Widget public static partial class CoffeeShop { private static void PluginStarted(object instance) { } private static void HandlerStarted(object instance) { } } Which method ran for Widget would depend on attribute order, so the contradiction is surfaced instead, mirroring AWT142 for lifetimes. Overlapping scans that agree are fine: two scans naming the same method merge, and so do scans hooking different slots (one scan's OnActivated combines with another's OnRelease). A hook name is owner-relative, though: a module [Scan] resolves its hooks against the module and a container [Scan] against the container, so a module scan and a container scan naming the same method name still conflict, because each means its own method. An explicit registration of the type is not reported either: a scan yields to it wholesale, hooks included, so the explicit registration's hooks (or its deliberate lack of them) replace the scan's. Fix: Name the same hook method in both scans, or register the type explicitly with the hook it should get; a scan yields to an explicit registration, hooks included.

Error An [Import] names a type that is not marked [Module]. public static class PaymentHelpers; // not marked [Module] [Container] [Import(typeof(PaymentHelpers))] public static partial class CoffeeShop; Fix: Import the intended [Module], or mark the imported type [Module] and give it registrations.

Error An imported module has its own [Import], which is not followed. [Module] [Import(typeof(BaseModule))] // a nested import is not followed [Singleton<CardTerminal, IPaymentTerminal>] public static class PaymentModule; [Container] [Import(typeof(PaymentModule))] public static partial class CoffeeShop; Fix: Import the nested module on the container directly ([Import(typeof(BaseModule))]) and remove the [Import] from the module; imports are followed one level deep.

Warning An imported module declares no registrations. [Module] public static class EmptyModule; // nothing to contribute [Container] [Import(typeof(EmptyModule))] public static partial class CoffeeShop; Fix: Add the registrations the module is meant to contribute, or remove the [Import].

Error An imported [Module] class is not declared static. [Module] [Singleton<CardTerminal, IPaymentTerminal>] public class PaymentModule; // must be static [Container] [Import(typeof(PaymentModule))] public static partial class CoffeeShop; Fix: Declare the module static: public static class PaymentModule;.

Error A module Factory/Instance member is not accessible from the generated container. [Module] [Singleton<Grinder>(Factory = nameof(MakeGrinder))] public static class EquipmentModule { private static Grinder MakeGrinder() => new(); // private, so the container cannot call it } [Container] [Import(typeof(EquipmentModule))] public static partial class CoffeeShop; Fix: Make the member public, or internal when the container is in the same assembly (or one the module's assembly grants InternalsVisibleTo).

Error An imported module declares a [Scan], but its assembly carries no generated expansion. // In a referenced library that was compiled WITHOUT the Awaiten source generator: [Module] [Scan<IDrink>] // never expanded, so it would contribute nothing public static partial class MenuModule; [Container] [Import(typeof(MenuModule))] public static partial class CoffeeShop; Repurposed id This id previously rejected any [Scan] on a module. A [Scan] on a [Module] is self-compiled in the module's own build, which stamps the module with a generated marker even when the scan matched nothing. A module whose metadata carries a [Scan] but no marker was compiled without the Awaiten generator, or with a version predating self-compiled scans, so its scan would silently contribute nothing. Rebuild the library with the Awaiten generator referenced. Reported at the consumer's [Import]. The self-compilation constraints themselves are reported as AWT194 to AWT197 and AWT200 to AWT202. Fix: Rebuild the module's assembly with the Awaiten package referenced, so its generator expands the scan.

Warning Two imported modules strongly register the same service with different implementations. [Module] [Singleton<RealTimeSystem, ITimeSystem>] public static class ModuleA; [Module] [Singleton<MockTimeSystem, ITimeSystem>] public static class ModuleB; [Container] [Import(typeof(ModuleA))] [Import(typeof(ModuleB))] // both strongly register ITimeSystem public static partial class CoffeeShop; Fix: Override the service on the container with a registration of its own, or make one module's registration an overridable default with Fallback = Fallback.Warn or Fallback = Fallback.Silent.

Error A [Module] that declares a [Scan] is not partial (or is nested in a type that is not), so its scan cannot be self-compiled. [Module] [Scan<IPlugin>(As = ScanAs.MatchingInterface)] public static class PluginModule; // must be partial to receive the generated factories A self-compiled module scan emits a factory method and a registration attribute into the module's partial, re-opening the whole nesting chain of a nested module. Add the partial modifier to the module class and every type containing it. Reported in the module's own build. Fix: Add partial to the module and every type that contains it: public static partial class PluginModule;.

Error A self-compiled module [Scan] match has a constructor parameter of a type inaccessible outside the module's assembly. internal sealed class Secret; internal sealed class Roaster(Secret secret) : IRoaster; // Secret is internal [Module] [Scan<IRoaster>(As = ScanAs.MatchingInterface)] public static partial class PluginModule; The generated factory is a public method whose parameters are resolved from the consuming container's graph, so each parameter type has to be nameable by the consumer. Widen the parameter type's accessibility, or exclude the match. (A v1 limitation: a self-compiled scan cannot construct a match through an inaccessible parameter.) Fix: Make the parameter type public, or exclude the match from the scan.

Warning A self-compiled module [Scan] match has no exposure interface accessible outside the module's assembly, so it is skipped. internal sealed class Roaster : IPlugin; [Module] [Scan<IPlugin>(As = ScanAs.Self)] // Self exposes the internal type, which a consumer cannot name public static partial class PluginModule; A consumer resolves a self-compiled match only through an accessible interface. ScanAs.Self over an internal implementation exposes nothing nameable, so the match registers nothing and is skipped, mirroring the warning severity a container scan gives a match it cannot register (AWT182/AWT188/AWT193). The skip holds even when the importing container lives in the module's own assembly, so a module scan registers the same matches wherever the module is imported from. Expose it through a public interface (ScanAs.MatchingInterface or ScanAs.Marker), or exclude the match. Fix: Expose the match through a public interface with ScanAs.MatchingInterface or ScanAs.Marker, or exclude it from the scan.

Error A self-compiled module [Scan] match would be exposed under more than one interface. internal sealed class Roaster : IPlugin, IRoaster; [Module] [Scan<IPlugin>(As = ScanAs.Marker | ScanAs.MatchingInterface)] // IPlugin and IRoaster both apply public static partial class PluginModule; A self-compiled match is reached through a generated factory that returns a single accessible interface, so a shared instance across several interfaces cannot be expressed (unlike a container [Scan], whose matches coalesce on the concrete type). The same applies across scans: two [Scan]s on one module that expose the same type under two different interfaces would emit two factories and silently split the instance, so that overlap is also rejected. Narrow the exposure to a single interface (typically ScanAs.MatchingInterface), or exclude the match. This is a v1 limitation. Fix: Narrow As to a single interface, typically As = ScanAs.MatchingInterface, or exclude the match.

Error A self-compiled module [Scan] match carries injection metadata the generated factory cannot mirror. internal sealed class Roaster : IRoaster { public Roaster(IClock clock) { } [Inject] // keys, optionality and deferral live on this attribute public IGrinder Grinder { get; set; } } [Module] [Scan<IRoaster>(As = ScanAs.MatchingInterface)] public static partial class PluginModule; The generated factory reduces a match to a plain parameter list resolved from the consuming container's graph. An [Inject] property, or a constructor parameter marked [Inject] or [Arg], carries per-dependency semantics that plain parameters cannot express, so the consumer would silently construct the match differently than a container [Scan] would. Remove the attribute, exclude the match, or register the type through a hand-written module factory. Fix: Remove the [Inject] or [Arg] attribute, exclude the match from the scan, or register the type through a hand-written module factory.

Error A generic [Module] (or one nested in a generic type) declares a [Scan]. [Module] [Scan<IPlugin>(As = ScanAs.MatchingInterface)] public static partial class PluginModule<T>; // no closed PluginModule<T> exists to [Import] A consumer imports a module by typeof, so there is no single closed module type to import from a generic declaration, and the generated partial could not re-open it by its bare name. Move the [Scan] onto a non-generic module. Fix: Move the [Scan] onto a non-generic module.

Error A module [Scan] declares InAssembliesOf, but a self-compiled scan sweeps only the module's own assembly. [Module] [Scan<IPlugin>(As = ScanAs.Marker, InAssembliesOf = new[] { typeof(OtherLibMarker) })] public static partial class PluginModule; A self-compiled scan exists to reach the module's own internal types. Sweeping another assembly from a module would see only that assembly's public types, which a container [Scan] with InAssembliesOf already covers, so the module form would silently do less than the container form. Remove InAssembliesOf to scan the module's own assembly, or move the [Scan] onto the container. Fix: Remove InAssembliesOf to scan the module's own assembly, or move the [Scan] onto the container.

Error A self-compiled module [Scan] hook has a parameter, after the instance, whose type is not accessible outside the module's assembly. internal sealed class Secret; internal sealed class Roaster : IPlugin, IRoaster; [Module] [Scan<IPlugin>(As = ScanAs.MatchingInterface, OnActivated = nameof(Wire))] public static partial class PluginModule { internal static void Wire(Roaster roaster, Secret secret) { } // Secret is internal to the module } The module emits a public wrapper for the hook, and that wrapper's parameters after the instance are resolved from the consuming container's graph, so each type has to be nameable by the consumer, the same rule a self-compiled factory parameter gets (AWT195). The instance parameter itself is exempt: it is the accessible exposure interface, cast back to the internal implementation inside the module. Widen the parameter type's accessibility, resolve a different dependency, or drop the hook. Fix: Make the parameter type public, take a different dependency, or drop the hook.

Error A self-compiled module [Scan] hook has a parameter, after the instance, marked [FromKey] or [Inject]. internal sealed class Roaster : IPlugin, IRoaster; [Module] [Scan<IPlugin>(As = ScanAs.MatchingInterface, OnActivated = nameof(Wire))] public static partial class PluginModule { internal static void Wire(Roaster roaster, [FromKey("main")] IClock clock) { } } The hook's parameters after the instance mirror onto the generated public wrapper as a bare type-and-name signature, so the attribute's per-dependency semantics (a key, optionality, deferral) would be silently dropped: a cross-assembly consumer would resolve the plain type while a same-compilation container, binding the module's own hook directly, honored the attribute, so the same source would inject different instances depending on which side of the assembly boundary the consumer sits. This is the hook-parameter twin of the factory's AWT200, rejected rather than silently degraded. Remove the attribute, resolve the dependency plainly, or drop the hook. Fix: Remove the [FromKey] or [Inject] attribute and resolve the dependency plainly, or drop the hook.

Error A keyed dictionary (IReadOnlyDictionary<TKey, TService>) has a key type that is neither string nor an enum, or one whose keyed registrations do not all match it. public sealed class Router(IReadOnlyDictionary<int, IMilk> milks); // the key must be string or an enum [Container] [Singleton<OatMilk, IMilk>(Key = "Oat")] [Singleton<Router>] public static partial class CoffeeShop; Fix: Use a key type that every keyed registration of the service carries, a string or an enum: IReadOnlyDictionary<string, IMilk>.

Error A [FromKey] is applied to a synthesized keyed collection (IReadOnlyDictionary<string, TService>), which resolves every key. public sealed class Router([FromKey("Oat")] IReadOnlyDictionary<string, IMilk> milks); // the map already holds every key [Container] [Singleton<OatMilk, IMilk>(Key = "Oat")] [Singleton<Router>] public static partial class CoffeeShop; Fix: Remove the [FromKey] and pick the key from the dictionary (milks["Oat"]), take the single service with [FromKey("Oat")] IMilk milk, or register a dictionary service under that key, which takes precedence over the synthesized one.

Error A runtime-type dispatch dictionary (IReadOnlyDictionary<Type, Func<TBase>>) cannot be built: its value is not Func<TBase> over a non-generic interface, it carries a [FromKey], a closing that implements TBase has more than one type argument, or the closings come from more than one generic interface, so a type argument does not identify one entry. See Dispatch by runtime type. public interface IOrderHandler; public interface IOrderHandler<T> : IOrderHandler; public interface IRefundHandler<T> : IOrderHandler; // a second family under the same base public sealed class OrderPlacedHandler : IOrderHandler<OrderPlaced>; public sealed class OrderPlacedRefund : IRefundHandler<OrderPlaced>; public sealed class Counter(IReadOnlyDictionary<Type, Func<IOrderHandler>> handlers); // typeof(OrderPlaced) is ambiguous [Container] [Singleton<OrderPlacedHandler, IOrderHandler<OrderPlaced>>] [Singleton<OrderPlacedRefund, IRefundHandler<OrderPlaced>>] [Singleton<Counter>] public static partial class CoffeeShop; Fix: Request IReadOnlyDictionary<Type, Func<TBase>> over a non-generic base interface, without [FromKey], and let only one generic family with one type argument implement that base (here, do not derive IRefundHandler<T> from IOrderHandler).

Warning A WhenInjectedInto contextual binding never applies because the named consumer has no unkeyed direct constructor parameter to redirect. public sealed class KitchenDisplay; // has no IReceiptPrinter parameter to redirect [Container] [Singleton<ThermalPrinter, IReceiptPrinter>] [Singleton<WidePrinter, IReceiptPrinter>(WhenInjectedInto = typeof(KitchenDisplay))] [Singleton<KitchenDisplay>] public static partial class CoffeeShop; Fix: Let the consumer take the service as an unkeyed constructor parameter or [Inject] property (KitchenDisplay(IReceiptPrinter printer)), or remove the binding.

Error A registration sets both WhenInjectedInto and Key. A contextual binding is reached only through its consumer, so the Key could never be selected by a [FromKey] and is silently dropped. Remove one of the two. [Container] [Singleton<ThermalPrinter, IReceiptPrinter>] [Singleton<WidePrinter, IReceiptPrinter>(WhenInjectedInto = typeof(DriveThroughRegister), Key = "wide")] // Key is dropped [Singleton<DriveThroughRegister>] public static partial class CoffeeShop; Fix: Remove either WhenInjectedInto or Key.

Error Two different implementations set WhenInjectedInto for the same service and consumer, so both claim the one contextual slot for that consumer. [Container] [Singleton<WidePrinter, IReceiptPrinter>(WhenInjectedInto = typeof(DriveThroughRegister))] [Singleton<ThermalPrinter, IReceiptPrinter>(WhenInjectedInto = typeof(DriveThroughRegister))] // two bindings for one consumer [Singleton<DriveThroughRegister>] public static partial class CoffeeShop; Fix: Keep one contextual binding per service and consumer, and remove the other.

Error A Key property or [FromKey] uses a constant whose type is not a supported key type. A resolution key must be a string, an enum value, or a typeof(...). public sealed class LatteRecipe([FromKey(5)] IMilk milk); // int is not a supported key type [Container] [Singleton<OatMilk, IMilk>(Key = "Oat")] [Singleton<LatteRecipe>] public static partial class CoffeeShop; Fix: Use a string, an enum value or a typeof(...) as the key: [FromKey("Oat")].

Error A type is declared [ImportService] (drawn from the host provider) but is also registered on the container. A type is either host-owned or Awaiten-owned, not both. For an open generic import such as [ImportService(typeof(ILogger<>))], this is reported for each closing that a dependency routes to the host while the container also registers it. [Container] [ImportService<IPaymentGateway>] // declared external [Singleton<StripeGateway, IPaymentGateway>] // …but is also registered, a contradiction public static partial class CoffeeShop; Fix: Remove the registration to keep the service host-owned, or remove the [ImportService] to build it in the graph.

Warning A type declared [ImportService] is never consumed by any dependency in the graph, so the declaration is dead. For an open generic import, no closing of it is consumed. This is most often a stale or mistyped [ImportService]. [Container] [ImportService<IPaymentGateway>] // nothing in the graph depends on IPaymentGateway [Singleton<Menu>] public static partial class CoffeeShop; Fix: Remove the declaration, or add the dependency that should consume it.

Error The typeof argument of [ImportService(typeof(...))] or [InjectProperty(typeof(...), name)] is neither a closed type nor an unbound generic definition, so it names neither one type nor every closing of one generic type. That is a type nested in an unbound generic, such as typeof(Recipe<>.Step), which C# accepts, or a partially open type, such as typeof(Shelf<Order>.Slot<>), which C# rejects as well (CS7003). Pass a closed type such as typeof(Recipe<Espresso>.Step), or an unbound generic definition with every type argument omitted such as typeof(ILogger<>) or typeof(Shelf<>.Slot<>). public sealed class Recipe<T> { public sealed class Step { public ITimeSystem? Time { get; set; } } } [Container] [ImportService(typeof(Recipe<>.Step))] // a type nested in an unbound generic is neither [InjectProperty(typeof(Recipe<>.Step), "Time")] // the same for [InjectProperty] [Singleton<Menu>] public static partial class CoffeeShop; Fix: Pass a closed type such as typeof(Recipe<Espresso>.Step), or an unbound generic definition with every type argument omitted.
These guard the line between your domain and the container. They are suppressible warnings, reported by the analyzer rather than the generator, so a deliberate exception can opt out in source.

Warning A container-side composition attribute (a lifetime registration, [Scan], [Decorate], [Composite], [Import], [ImportService], or [InjectProperty]) is applied to a class in an assembly that declares no [Container]. Composition belongs on the [Container] (or an imported [Module]); domain code should stay free of it. This is a best-effort guard: it stays silent in an assembly that also declares the [Container], where the cross-assembly boundary is better enforced by an architecture test. // A domain library that declares no [Container]: [Singleton<EspressoMachine>] // registration belongs on the [Container], not here public sealed class EspressoMachine; Fix: Move the attribute onto the [Container] or an imported [Module]. Where the attribute is deliberate, suppress the warning in source.

Warning A resolver seam (IAwaitenResolver, IAwaitenScope, IAwaitenRoot, and the like) is injected into a type that is not the [Container] composition root. Resolving from the container at run time is the Service Locator anti-pattern: it hides the type's real dependencies and defeats the compile-time graph check. Inject the dependency you actually need instead, or, if the type is a host-integration adapter, suppress this on it with a justification. The typed fast paths IAwaitenResolver<T> and IAwaitenAsyncResolver<T> are single-service seams and are not reported. public sealed class Barista(IAwaitenResolver resolver) // locates dependencies at run time { public Cup Serve() => resolver.Resolve<Cup>(); } Fix: Inject what the type actually needs: Barista(Func<Cup> cups) for a fresh cup per call, or Barista(Cup cup) for one. Suppress the warning only on a host-integration adapter, as described below. Dispatching by a type known only at run time, like a mediator looking up the handler for message.GetType(), needs no resolver either: inject a dispatch dictionary. One kind of type is meant to hold a resolver: an adapter that bridges the container to a host's own dependency-injection surface, where holding it is the adaptation rather than a hidden run-time dependency. AwaitenServiceProvider is one, and anything you write against a framework's own registrar is another. This is an analyzer diagnostic, so suppress it in source, with the justification saying which adapter it is. Below, IServiceLocator stands for whatever single-method resolution interface your framework declares, where returning null is how an adapter says "not mine". Both answers that are not a plain instance carry their weight: the collection convention every framework expects, and the withheld reason that keeps a container's own failure from being reported as absence. using System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis; [SuppressMessage("Awaiten", "AWT135:Service locator: a resolver interface is injected into a service", Justification = "This is a custom bridge adapter: holding the scope is the adaptation itself, not a hidden run-time dependency.")] internal sealed class AwaitenServiceLocator(IAwaitenRoot container, IAwaitenScope scope) : IServiceLocator { public object? Resolve(Type? type) { if (type is null) { return null; } if (scope.TryResolve(type, out object? instance)) { return instance; } // Reported as absent, the framework would bind it from elsewhere and fail far from the cause. if (container.GetResolvability(type, null).Reason is { } reason) { throw new InvalidOperationException(reason); } return EmptyCollectionElement(type) is { } elementType ? Array.CreateInstance(elementType, 0) : null; } /// <summary> /// The element type to answer with an empty sequence rather than <see langword="null" />, because a /// framework uses a collection as an extension point and "no handlers" still has to enumerate. A value /// element would need an array type native AOT does not generate; a resolvable one has members an empty /// sequence would drop. /// </summary> private Type? EmptyCollectionElement(Type type) { if (!type.IsConstructedGenericType || type.GetGenericTypeDefinition() != typeof(IEnumerable<>)) { return null; } Type elementType = type.GenericTypeArguments[0]; return elementType.IsValueType || container.GetResolvability(elementType, null).Status != AwaitenResolvabilityStatus.NotRegistered ? null : elementType; } } AwaitenServiceProvider is the same shape against MS.DI's IServiceProvider, so read it alongside this if your framework's surface is keyed or asks resolvability questions. Suppress it on the adapter, never project-wide: the diagnostic is right about every other type.

Warning User code constructs an Owned<T> with new. The handle disposes the scope it is given, so one built over the container root disposes the root, and one built over any other scope ends that scope behind its owner's back. Only the container creates Owned<T>, over the throwaway scope it built the value in: resolve Owned<T> or inject Func<Owned<T>> instead. The generated container's own handles are not reported, and a deliberate construction, such as a test double, can suppress the warning in source. Owned<Cup> cup = new Owned<Cup>(root, new Cup()); // disposing it disposes the root Owned<Cup> owned = root.Resolve<Owned<Cup>>(); // the container builds the handle Fix: Resolve Owned<T>, as the second line does, or inject Func<Owned<T>>. Suppress the warning in source only for a deliberate construction, such as a test double.

This page opens a coffee shop from scratch. By the end you have a working container, you know how to resolve services, and you have seen the compiler catch a mistake. note Where an example checks a result in a test, it uses aweXpect in the form await That(...). aweXpect is optional; Awaiten works with any test framework and assertion library.

.NET 10.0.300 SDK and C# 11 Build with the .NET SDK 10.0.300 or later. The source generator needs the C# compiler that ships with it. Write C# 11 or later. The registration attributes in these docs, such as [Singleton<T>], are generic attributes. Target net10.0, net8.0 or any framework that supports netstandard2.0, including .NET Framework 4.8. The package has no third-party dependencies; on netstandard2.0 it references only Microsoft.Bcl.AsyncInterfaces, for async disposal.

.NET CLI PackageReference Central Package Management dotnet add package Awaiten <PackageReference Include="Awaiten" Version="0.8.0" /> Directory.Packages.props <PackageVersion Include="Awaiten" Version="0.8.0" /> Project file <PackageReference Include="Awaiten" /> Latest version: 0.8.0 Package Description Awaiten The core: attributes, the source generator, and the runtime seams. No third-party dependencies; on netstandard2.0 only Microsoft.Bcl.AsyncInterfaces. Awaiten.Extensions.DependencyInjection Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection interop for ASP.NET Core, the generic host, and other containers. See the MS.DI bridge.

In short: declare a [Container], register your services on it, then create its Root and start resolving. A container is a static partial class marked with [Container]. You register services with lifetime attributes on that class. Nothing else is needed. The source generator does the rest at build time. Program.cs using Awaiten; using CoffeeShop.Root shop = new(); Cup cup = shop.Resolve<Cup>(); public sealed class EspressoMachine; public sealed class Grinder; public sealed class Cup(EspressoMachine machine, Grinder grinder); [Container] [Singleton<EspressoMachine>] [Singleton<Grinder>] [Transient<Cup>] public static partial class CoffeeShop; The generator emits a nested Root type for you. The Root is your composition root. It owns the singletons and it is the outermost scope. You create it, then ask it for services with Resolve<T>(). Awaiten built the Cup for you and passed in the shared EspressoMachine and Grinder. You wrote no factory code. Dispose the Root when you are done. It disposes everything it owns. Use await using if any of your services are async-disposable.

Most services hide behind an interface. Pass the implementation first, then the service type: public interface IBrewer; public sealed class EspressoBrewer : IBrewer; [Container] [Singleton<EspressoBrewer, IBrewer>] public static partial class CoffeeShop; // resolve by the interface: IBrewer brewer = shop.Resolve<IBrewer>();

Some things belong to a single order, like the running tab. Register them as [Scoped] and open a scope for each order: [Container] [Scoped<Order>] public static partial class CoffeeShop; using CoffeeShop.Root shop = new(); using (IAwaitenScope order = shop.CreateScope()) { Order o = order.Resolve<Order>(); } // the order and everything it owns is disposed here Inside one scope you get the same Order every time. A different scope gets a different one. See Scopes for the full picture.

Forget to register a dependency and you do not find out at runtime. You find out when you build. public sealed class Cup(Grinder grinder); [Container] [Transient<Cup>] // Grinder is never registered public static partial class CoffeeShop; Build error error AWT101: 'Cup' cannot be resolved: 'Cup' requires 'Grinder', which is not registered on the container Cyclic graphs, captive dependencies, and async services touched synchronously are caught the same way. The full list is on the Diagnostics page.
documents.s: Let the compiler check your wiring

documents.t: Complete example for a full container that uses the main features together. Lifetimes for singleton, scoped, and transient in depth. Resolving services for the full resolve surface. Async initialization once a service needs async setup.

Not everything comes from Awaiten. When you run under ASP.NET Core or the generic host, some services live in the host's provider. The payment gateway, the framework logger, and the configuration are wired there. External services let an Awaiten graph pull those in.

Declare a service type external with [ImportService<T>] on the container, or with its typeof form [ImportService(typeof(T))]; the two behave the same. Every unregistered dependency of that type is satisfied from the external provider instead of the graph, whether it is keyed or not, and whether it arrives as a constructor parameter, a factory parameter, or an [Inject] property. No Awaiten registration is needed for it. Every other unresolved dependency still gets the missing-dependency check (AWT101), so this is safer than the blanket fall-through below. Generic typeof [Container] [ImportService<IPaymentGateway>] [Singleton<Till>] [Singleton<Register>] public static partial class CoffeeShop; public sealed class Register(Till till, IPaymentGateway gateway); // IPaymentGateway comes from the host [Container] [ImportService(typeof(IPaymentGateway))] // same as [ImportService<IPaymentGateway>] [Singleton<Till>] [Singleton<Register>] public static partial class CoffeeShop; For a keyed external service, select the key on a container factory method so the consumer stays a plain class; the [FromKey] is forwarded to the resolver. public sealed class Report(ITimeSystem timeSystem); // a plain class, no attributes [Container] [ImportService<ITimeSystem>] [Singleton<Report>(Factory = nameof(MakeReport))] public static partial class CoffeeShop { private static Report MakeReport([FromKey("utc")] ITimeSystem timeSystem) => new(timeSystem); } [ImportService] works on an imported [Module] too, exactly as it does on the container. Keeping DI out of your domain Because external-ness is declared on the container, a service that consumes a host type just asks for it as an ordinary parameter, with no Awaiten reference in the domain class. [ImportService] is the clean-domain form. The only per-parameter attribute involved is [FromKey], and only when you need a keyed external service. Only the direct dependency of type T is routed. A relationship or collection over it (Func<T>, Lazy<T>, Task<T>, IEnumerable<T>, and the like) is not, because the resolver hands back an instance, not a deferred or fanned-out shape. Such a dependency still resolves from the Awaiten graph, so with no registration it surfaces as AWT101 (or an empty collection). Declaring a type external that nothing in the graph consumes is a dead declaration and is reported as AWT176.

Some host services are generic, and every consumer asks for its own closing: under the generic host each class wants an ILogger<ThatClass>. Pass the unbound generic definition to the typeof form, and every closing that a dependency asks for comes from the external provider. The generic form cannot express this, because C# does not allow an unbound generic such as ILogger<> as a type argument. Generic typeof using Microsoft.Extensions.Logging; public sealed class OrderDesk(ILogger<OrderDesk> logger); public sealed class Roaster(ILogger<Roaster> logger); [Container] [ImportService<ILogger<OrderDesk>>] // one declaration per consumer [ImportService<ILogger<Roaster>>] [Singleton<OrderDesk>] [Singleton<Roaster>] public static partial class CoffeeShop; using Microsoft.Extensions.Logging; public sealed class OrderDesk(ILogger<OrderDesk> logger); public sealed class Roaster(ILogger<Roaster> logger); [Container] [ImportService(typeof(ILogger<>))] // ILogger<OrderDesk>, ILogger<Roaster>, and any later consumer [Singleton<OrderDesk>] [Singleton<Roaster>] public static partial class CoffeeShop; Each closing is routed exactly as if it were imported on its own: a [FromKey] key is forwarded, a relationship or collection over a closing is not routed, and the closing is listed as an external dependency of the container, so startup verification checks every closing the graph consumes. A closing that is routed to the host but also registered on the container is reported as AWT175, and an open import none of whose closings is consumed as AWT176. The argument must be a closed type or an unbound generic definition; anything in between, such as typeof(Outer<>.Inner), is reported as AWT215.
documents.s: Pull every closing of a generic type

documents.t: Put [ImportServices] on the container and any unregistered direct dependency falls through to the external provider automatically. You trade some compile-time safety for less annotation. [Container] [ImportServices] [Singleton<Register>] public static partial class CoffeeShop; // Register's IPaymentGateway is resolved from the host, unannotated

Awaiten does not create the external provider. It asks an external resolver for these dependencies, and you supply that resolver once, up front. Under the MS.DI bridge this is automatic. AddAwaitenContainer and the startup initialization wire the container to the host's IServiceProvider, so [ImportService] and [ImportServices] dependencies resolve from the host with nothing extra to do. Standing alone, you set it yourself. Implement IExternalResolver and pass it to the generated Root constructor, so it is in place before anything resolves, eager singletons included. using System.Diagnostics.CodeAnalysis; public sealed class HostResolver : IExternalResolver { public bool TryResolve(Type serviceType, object? key, [NotNullWhen(true)] out object? instance) { if (serviceType == typeof(IPaymentGateway)) { instance = new StripeGateway(); return true; } instance = null; return false; // not found: Awaiten reports a missing external dependency } } using CoffeeShop.Root shop = new(new HostResolver()); Register register = shop.Resolve<Register>(); // its IPaymentGateway comes from HostResolver The key argument carries the [FromKey] value for a keyed external dependency. A child scope, and the throwaway scope behind an Owned<T>, inherit the resolver from the scope that created them, so passing it once to the root is enough. A scope's resolver is set once. Hosts that wire a resolver later, as the MS.DI bridge does for each scope, call IAwaitenExternalResolverHost.SetExternalResolver. Setting the resolver a scope already holds again does nothing; setting a different one throws an InvalidOperationException, because the scope would then mix instances from two providers.
Awaiten advertises its external dependencies so you can check them at startup. If one is missing from the provider, verification throws and names it. See MS.DI bridge for VerifyAwaitenContainers.
An externally supplied instance belongs to the external provider. Awaiten never disposes it.
MS.DI bridge for host integration and verification. Keyed services for [FromKey].

This page is for apps that register their services on an IServiceCollection today, under ASP.NET Core, the generic host or a plain ServiceProvider, and want those registrations checked by the compiler instead. It maps each Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection (MS.DI) concept to its Awaiten counterpart, migrates a small coffee shop step by step, and lists what has no direct equivalent. You do not have to move everything at once. The MS.DI bridge projects an Awaiten container into a service collection, so the host keeps running on MS.DI while you move one group of services after another. .NET CLI PackageReference Central Package Management dotnet add package Awaiten dotnet add package Awaiten.Extensions.DependencyInjection <PackageReference Include="Awaiten" Version="0.8.0" /> <PackageReference Include="Awaiten.Extensions.DependencyInjection" Version="0.8.0" /> Directory.Packages.props <PackageVersion Include="Awaiten" Version="0.8.0" /> <PackageVersion Include="Awaiten.Extensions.DependencyInjection" Version="0.8.0" /> Project file <PackageReference Include="Awaiten" /> <PackageReference Include="Awaiten.Extensions.DependencyInjection" /> Latest version: Awaiten 0.8.0, Awaiten.Extensions.DependencyInjection 0.8.0

In MS.DI you call methods on a service collection at startup, and the provider wires the graph at run time. In Awaiten you declare the same registrations as attributes on a static partial class marked [Container], and a source generator wires the graph at build time. Two consequences shape the whole migration: The registrations are fixed when the project compiles. There is no collection to add to, replace in or remove from at run time. What ValidateOnBuild and ValidateScopes find at startup, and what MS.DI reports only on the first resolve, is a build error: a missing dependency is AWT101, a cycle AWT102, a singleton capturing a scoped service AWT105.

MS.DI Awaiten services.AddSingleton<IBrewer, EspressoBrewer>() [Singleton<EspressoBrewer, IBrewer>]: the implementation comes first, then the service. See Lifetimes. services.AddScoped<Order>() [Scoped<Order>] services.AddTransient<Cup>() [Transient<Cup>] services.AddSingleton<IBrewer>(sp => ...) [Singleton<IBrewer>(Factory = nameof(MakeBrewer))] with a static method on the container. Its parameters resolve from the graph, so there is no sp.GetRequiredService inside it. See Factories and instances. services.AddSingleton(menuBoard) [Singleton<MenuBoard>(Instance = nameof(Menu))] with a static field or property. As in MS.DI, the container never disposes it. services.TryAddSingleton<ITimeSystem, RealTimeSystem>() [Singleton<RealTimeSystem, ITimeSystem>(Fallback = Fallback.Silent)], typically in a module: it contributes only when nothing else provides the service. See overridable defaults. An AddPayments() extension method on IServiceCollection A static class marked [Module], pulled in with [Import(typeof(PaymentModule))]. See Modules. Several AddSingleton<ISyrup, ...>() calls and an IEnumerable<ISyrup> parameter Several [Singleton<..., ISyrup>] registrations and the same IEnumerable<ISyrup> parameter; arrays, IReadOnlyList<T> and the other collection shapes work too. A single ISyrup resolves to the first registration, not the last. services.AddKeyedSingleton<IMilk, OatMilk>("Oat") [Singleton<OatMilk, IMilk>(Key = "Oat")] [FromKeyedServices("Oat")] IMilk milk [FromKey("Oat")] IMilk milk, or keep the consumer free of attributes with WhenInjectedInto or a factory. See Keyed services. services.AddTransient(typeof(IRepository<>), typeof(Repository<>)) [Transient(typeof(Repository<>), typeof(IRepository<>))]. Awaiten generates the closings the graph asks for. See Open generics. ActivatorUtilities.CreateInstance<Cup>(sp, "Large") An [Arg] parameter and a Func<string, Cup> dependency. See Runtime arguments. provider.GetRequiredService<Cup>() shop.Resolve<Cup>() provider.GetService<Cup>() shop.TryResolve<Cup>(out Cup? cup) provider.GetServices<ISyrup>() shop.Resolve<IEnumerable<ISyrup>>() provider.GetRequiredKeyedService<IMilk>("Oat") shop.Resolve<IMilk>("Oat"). See Resolving services. provider.CreateScope(), provider.CreateAsyncScope() shop.CreateScope(), disposed with using or await using. CreateScopeAsync also initializes the scope's async services up front. See Scopes. IServiceScopeFactory injected into a service Func<Owned<T>>: each call builds T in its own scope, which the handle disposes. See Owned. IDisposable and IAsyncDisposable services Disposed by the scope or root that built them, in reverse creation order. A service that is only IAsyncDisposable needs await using, as in MS.DI (AWT156). See Disposal. services.Configure<Settings>(...) and IOptions<Settings> Configuration stays in MS.DI. The container consumes it with [ImportService(typeof(IOptions<>))]. See External services. services.AddHostedService<Roaster>() Stays in MS.DI. The hosted service's constructor can take services the bridge projects from the container.

The shop below runs on MS.DI. It validates its graph when the provider is built and opens a scope per order. using Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection; ServiceCollection services = new(); services.AddSingleton<EspressoMachine>(); services.AddSingleton<IBrewer, EspressoBrewer>(); services.AddScoped<Order>(); services.AddTransient<Cup>(); services.AddKeyedSingleton<IMilk, OatMilk>("Oat"); services.AddKeyedSingleton<IMilk, WholeMilk>("Whole"); services.AddSingleton<ISyrup, VanillaSyrup>(); services.AddSingleton<ISyrup, CaramelSyrup>(); services.AddSingleton(MenuBoard.Load()); await using ServiceProvider provider = services.BuildServiceProvider( new ServiceProviderOptions { ValidateOnBuild = true, ValidateScopes = true }); await using (AsyncServiceScope order = provider.CreateAsyncScope()) { Order current = order.ServiceProvider.GetRequiredService<Order>(); IMilk milk = order.ServiceProvider.GetRequiredKeyedService<IMilk>("Oat"); IEnumerable<ISyrup> syrups = order.ServiceProvider.GetServices<ISyrup>(); }

Translate each call into an attribute on a container class. Swap the type arguments where a service type is named: Awaiten takes the implementation first. The pre-built menu board becomes a static property that Instance points at. [Container] [Singleton<EspressoMachine>] [Singleton<EspressoBrewer, IBrewer>] [Scoped<Order>] [Transient<Cup>] [Singleton<OatMilk, IMilk>(Key = "Oat")] [Singleton<WholeMilk, IMilk>(Key = "Whole")] [Singleton<VanillaSyrup, ISyrup>] [Singleton<CaramelSyrup, ISyrup>] [Singleton<MenuBoard>(Instance = nameof(Menu))] public static partial class CoffeeShop { private static MenuBoard Menu { get; } = MenuBoard.Load(); }

There is no ValidateOnBuild to set: the build is the validation. If Cup needed a Grinder that nothing registers, the build fails with AWT101 instead of the provider throwing at startup. Each entry on the Diagnostics page ends with the fix.

The generated CoffeeShop.Root takes the place of the ServiceProvider, and its scopes take the place of the MS.DI scopes. await using CoffeeShop.Root shop = new(); await using (IAwaitenScope order = shop.CreateScope()) { Order current = order.Resolve<Order>(); IMilk milk = order.Resolve<IMilk>("Oat"); IEnumerable<ISyrup> syrups = order.Resolve<IEnumerable<ISyrup>>(); }
documents.s: 3. Replace the provider with the root

documents.t: Under ASP.NET Core or the generic host, the host still needs an IServiceCollection. Project the container into it, and warm any async services on startup: using Awaiten.Extensions.DependencyInjection; using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Builder; WebApplicationBuilder builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(); builder.Services.AddAwaitenContainer<CoffeeShop.Root>() .WithInitialization(); Controllers, minimal API handlers and hosted services now receive the container's services from MS.DI. See the MS.DI bridge for the details, including how scopes and disposal line up.

A large app rarely moves in one step. With the bridge, both containers serve the same host while you migrate: Pick a group of services that belong together, such as everything behind the counter, and move their registrations into a [Container]. Project the container with AddAwaitenContainer<CoffeeShop.Root>(). The services that stay in MS.DI keep their registrations and can take the projected services as constructor parameters. Where a moved service still depends on a service MS.DI registers, declare it with [ImportService<T>] on the container. Every other missing dependency remains a build error. Call VerifyAwaitenContainers() on the provider at startup, which throws and names any imported service the host does not register. Remove the moved registrations from the service collection, and repeat with the next group. using Awaiten.Extensions.DependencyInjection; using Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection; [Container] [ImportService<IPaymentGateway>] // still registered in MS.DI [Singleton<EspressoMachine>] [Scoped<Order>] [Transient<Barista>] public static partial class CoffeeShop; ServiceCollection services = new(); services.AddSingleton<IPaymentGateway, StripeGateway>(); // not migrated yet services.AddAwaitenContainer<CoffeeShop.Root>(); await using ServiceProvider provider = services.BuildServiceProvider(); provider.VerifyAwaitenContainers(); While a group is half moved, [ImportServices] lets every unregistered dependency fall through to the host instead of naming each one. It trades away the missing-dependency check, so replace it with [ImportService<T>] declarations once the group is done. See External services. tip LifetimeSafety.Loose on the container lets a disposable transient resolve from the root, as MS.DI allows. It can help while code still relies on that, but the strict default with Owned<T> is the leak-free target. See Lifetime safety.

Changing registrations at run time. Replace, RemoveAll, or registering only if (configuration["UseFilter"] == "true") have no counterpart, because the graph is built at compile time. Make the choice in a factory method that takes the setting as a parameter, or keep that registration in MS.DI. Last registration wins. In MS.DI a later registration overrides an earlier one for single resolution. In Awaiten the first one wins, and an override is declared explicitly: a module offers an overridable default with Fallback, and the container's own registration replaces it. Lambda factories. A factory is a named static method on the container or a module, not a closure. Values it needs come from its parameters or from an Instance member. KeyedService.AnyKey. A key selects exactly one registration; there is no wildcard key. To get every keyed implementation at once, take an IReadOnlyDictionary<string, IMilk>. Injecting IServiceProvider or IServiceScopeFactory into a service. Resolving from the container inside a service is the service locator pattern, which Awaiten reports when its own resolver interfaces are injected (AWT135). Take the dependency itself, a Func<T>, a Func<Owned<T>>, or a dispatch dictionary for a type known only at run time. Disposable transients on the root. MS.DI keeps every disposable transient resolved from the root provider until the provider is disposed. Awaiten's strict default withholds them from the root and points you to Owned<T> or a scope; LifetimeSafety.Loose restores the MS.DI behavior. Collections across the bridge. The bridge projects each registration, not Awaiten's synthesized collections, so consume IEnumerable<T> of container services inside the container. Open generic closings only the host asks for. The container generates the closings its own graph uses. A closing that only a framework requests, for example as a minimal API parameter, is not available through the bridge. See Feature detection. Options, logging and hosted services. They stay registered in MS.DI. The container imports what it needs, such as [ImportService(typeof(ILogger<>))]. MS.DI has no counterpart to async initialization either: a service that needs asynchronous setup implements IAsyncInitializable, and the bridge exposes it to MS.DI as Task<T>.
MS.DI bridge for the projection, scopes and disposal under a host. External services for services that stay in MS.DI. Diagnostics for every build error and its fix.

Most .NET apps run on Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection. ASP.NET Core, the generic host, and worker services all speak it. The Awaiten.Extensions.DependencyInjection package bridges your generated container into that world, so you keep Awaiten's compile-time safety and still fit the host. Install it alongside the core package: .NET CLI PackageReference Central Package Management dotnet add package Awaiten.Extensions.DependencyInjection <PackageReference Include="Awaiten.Extensions.DependencyInjection" Version="0.8.0" /> Directory.Packages.props <PackageVersion Include="Awaiten.Extensions.DependencyInjection" Version="0.8.0" /> Project file <PackageReference Include="Awaiten.Extensions.DependencyInjection" /> Latest version: 0.8.0

AddAwaitenContainer<TRoot> registers the container and projects its registrations into the IServiceCollection. Awaiten lifetimes align to ServiceLifetime, and one Awaiten scope aligns to each MS.DI scope. using Awaiten.Extensions.DependencyInjection; using Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection; ServiceCollection services = new(); services.AddAwaitenContainer<CoffeeShop.Root>(); using ServiceProvider provider = services.BuildServiceProvider(); IBrewer brewer = provider.GetRequiredService<IBrewer>(); It returns an AwaitenContainerBuilder<TRoot> for the container's hosting options, such as startup initialization. Its Services property is the collection, for chaining further registrations. To configure the root before the host sees it, for example to construct it with your own external resolver, build it yourself and pass it in. The root is projected as-is and stays yours, as with any instance you register in MS.DI: the provider never disposes it, so dispose it after the provider. using CoffeeShop.Root shop = new(myResolver); services.AddAwaitenContainer(shop); An async-only service has no synchronous path, so this projection does not register its bare type. It is available as Task<T>, which routes through ResolveAsync. (Under the replacement path the bare type does resolve, into the container's guidance naming this projection, because there the container answers every request rather than contributing descriptors.) Task<EspressoMachine> machine = provider.GetRequiredService<Task<EspressoMachine>>(); A keyed registration is projected under its key, so [FromKeyedServices] and GetKeyedService reach it. An async-only keyed service is projected as a keyed Task<T>, the same way its unkeyed counterpart is. public sealed class Router([FromKeyedServices("fast")] IChannel channel);

For the generic host or WebApplicationBuilder, plug in AwaitenServiceProviderFactory<TRoot>. Host registrations and Awaiten services coexist, so a host component can inject an Awaiten service and the other way round. builder.Host.UseServiceProviderFactory( new AwaitenServiceProviderFactory<CoffeeShop.Root>()); The factory takes an optional callback that receives the same AwaitenContainerBuilder<TRoot>, so its options read the same on both paths: builder.Host.UseServiceProviderFactory( new AwaitenServiceProviderFactory<CoffeeShop.Root>(c => c.WithInitialization()));
documents.s: Use it as the host's provider factory

documents.t: On both paths above, Awaiten disposes everything it built exactly once, with the scope that owns it. The Awaiten scope aligned to an MS.DI scope is disposed with that scope, and the container root with the root provider. (After a plain AddAwaitenContainer<TRoot>(), the root provider takes over the root on the first bridged resolution or when WithInitialization() warms it, so dispose a root you only use directly yourself. A root you passed to AddAwaitenContainer(root) is always yours to dispose.) That includes disposables reached only as nested dependencies, which MS.DI never sees, and instances awaited through Task<T>. Disposing the provider or a scope with DisposeAsync drains them asynchronously, so IAsyncDisposable-only services are supported there. A pre-built Instance member stays yours and is never disposed. MS.DI additionally calls Dispose on every instance a projected registration hands out, once per service type it was resolved as, before the Awaiten scope or root that built it. That is how MS.DI treats any factory registration, for example AddSingleton<IWriter>(sp => sp.GetRequiredService<Ledger>()), and it relies on Dispose being idempotent, as the IDisposable contract requires. A singleton Ledger resolved as both IReader and IWriter therefore sees three Dispose calls: one per service type from MS.DI, then one from Awaiten. That is also why a service built with SuppressDisposal = true cannot be projected when it is or may be disposable: MS.DI would dispose it no matter what the container promised. Both paths above throw at startup instead, naming the service, and AWT214 reports the projection at build time. Remove SuppressDisposal, register a pre-built Instance you own, or let Awaiten own everything as described next. A service that needs asynchronous initialization is unaffected, because MS.DI only receives its Task<T>.

AwaitenServiceProvider adapts an Awaiten scope directly to IServiceProvider, IKeyedServiceProvider, and IServiceScopeFactory. Awaiten is then the single owner of construction and disposal. GetService maps to TryResolve, so a missing service returns null, and GetKeyedService/GetRequiredKeyedService reach a keyed registration by its key. using CoffeeShop.Root shop = new(); using AwaitenServiceProvider provider = new(shop); using IServiceScope scope = provider.CreateScope(); Pass ownsContainer: false if you want to keep ownership of the container yourself.
