If no parameter is provided, it matches any CancellationToken: CancellationTokenSource cts = new CancellationTokenSource(); httpClient.Mock.Setup .GetAsync(It.IsAny<string>(), It.Is(cts.Token)) .ReturnsAsync(new HttpResponseMessage(HttpStatusCode.OK)); await httpClient.GetAsync("https://example.com", cts.Token);
Use It.IsUri(string?) to match URIs using a wildcard pattern against the string representation of the URI. The pattern supports * to match zero or more characters and ? to match a single character.

Filter requests by URI scheme using .ForHttps() or .ForHttp(): // Match only HTTPS requests httpClient.Mock.Verify .GetAsync(It.IsUri("*testably.org*").ForHttps()) .Once(); // Match only HTTP requests httpClient.Mock.Verify .GetAsync(It.IsUri("*testably.org*").ForHttp()) .Never();
Filter requests by host using .WithHost(string). You can provide a wildcard pattern to match against the host name: httpClient.Mock.Verify .GetAsync(It.IsUri().WithHost("*testably.org*")) .Once();
Filter requests on a specific port using .WithPort(int): httpClient.Mock.Verify .GetAsync(It.IsUri().WithPort(443)) .Once();
Filter requests by path using .WithPath(string). You can provide a wildcard pattern to match against the path: httpClient.Mock.Verify .GetAsync(It.IsUri().WithPath("/foo/*")) .Once();

Filter requests by query parameters using .WithQuery(...). You can provide one or many key-value pairs or a raw query string to match against the query parameters. The order of the key-value pairs does not matter: // Match query string containing "x=42" httpClient.Mock.Verify .GetAsync(It.IsUri().WithQuery("x", "42")) .Once(); // Match query string containing "x=42" and "y=foo" (in any order) httpClient.Mock.Verify .GetAsync(It.IsUri().WithQuery(("x", "42"), ("y", "foo"))) .Once(); // Match query string containing "x=42" and "y=foo" (in any order) httpClient.Mock.Verify .GetAsync(It.IsUri().WithQuery("x=42&y=foo")) .Once();

Use It.IsHttpContent(string?) to match the HTTP content, optionally providing an expected media type header value: httpClient.Mock.Setup .PostAsync( It.IsAny<string>(), It.IsHttpContent("application/json")) .ReturnsAsync(new HttpResponseMessage(HttpStatusCode.OK));

To verify against the string content, use the following methods: .WithString(Func<string, bool>): to match the string content against the given predicate .WithString(string): to match the content exactly as provided .WithStringMatching(string): to match the content using wildcard patterns .WithStringMatching(string).AsRegex(): to match the content using regular expressions httpClient.Mock.Setup .PostAsync( It.IsAny<string>(), It.IsHttpContent("application/json").WithStringMatching("*\"type\": \"Dark\"*")) .ReturnsAsync(new HttpResponseMessage(HttpStatusCode.OK)); Add the .IgnoringCase() modifier to make the string matching case-insensitive.

To verify against the binary content, use the following methods: .WithBytes(Func<byte[], bool>): to match the binary content against the given predicate .WithBytes(byte[]): to match the content exactly as provided httpClient.Mock.Setup .PostAsync( It.IsAny<string>(), It.IsHttpContent("application/octet-stream").WithBytes([0x01, 0x02, 0x03, ])) .ReturnsAsync(new HttpResponseMessage(HttpStatusCode.OK));

To verify against the URL-encoded form data content, use the following methods: .WithFormData(string, string): checks that the form-data content contains the provided key-value pair .WithFormData(IEnumerable<(string, string)>): checks that the form-data content contains the provided key-value pairs .WithFormData(string): checks that the form-data content contains the provided raw form data string httpClient.Mock.Setup .PostAsync( It.IsAny<string>(), It.IsHttpContent("application/x-www-form-urlencoded").WithFormData("my-key", "my-value")) .ReturnsAsync(new HttpResponseMessage(HttpStatusCode.OK)); As with query parameters, the order of the form-data key-value pairs does not matter. Add the .Exactly() modifier to also check that no other form data is present.

To verify against the HTTP content headers, use the following methods: .WithHeaders(string, HttpHeaderValue): checks that the content headers contain the provided key-value pair .WithHeaders(IEnumerable<(string, HttpHeaderValue)>): checks that the content headers contain all key-value pairs .WithHeaders(string): checks that the content headers contain the provided raw headers httpClient.Mock.Setup .PostAsync( It.IsAny<string>(), It.IsHttpContent().WithHeaders(("Content-Type", "application/json"), ("X-My-Header", "my-value"))) .ReturnsAsync(new HttpResponseMessage(HttpStatusCode.OK)); httpClient.Mock.Setup .PostAsync( It.IsAny<string>(), It.IsHttpContent().WithHeaders(""" Content-Type: application/json X-My-Header: my-value """)) .ReturnsAsync(new HttpResponseMessage(HttpStatusCode.OK)); By default, only the content headers are checked, not the headers of the HttpRequestMessage. To check both, add the .IncludingRequestHeaders() modifier.

Overloads of .ReturnsAsync simplify specifying the return value for HTTP method setups. httpClient.Mock.Setup.GetAsync(It.IsAny<Uri>()) // Returns a response with status code 200 OK and no content .ReturnsAsync(HttpStatusCode.OK); httpClient.Mock.Setup.GetAsync(It.IsAny<Uri>()) // Returns a response with status code 200 OK and a string content "some string content" .ReturnsAsync(HttpStatusCode.OK, "some string content"); httpClient.Mock.Setup.GetAsync(It.IsAny<Uri>()) // Returns a response with status code 200 OK and a JSON content {"foo":"bar"} .ReturnsAsync(HttpStatusCode.OK, "{\"foo\":\"bar\"}", "application/json"); byte[] bytes = new byte[] { /* ... */ }; httpClient.Mock.Setup.GetAsync(It.IsAny<Uri>()) // Returns a response with status code 200 OK and a binary content with the provided bytes .ReturnsAsync(HttpStatusCode.OK, bytes); httpClient.Mock.Setup.GetAsync(It.IsAny<Uri>()) // Returns a response with status code 200 OK and a PNG image content with the provided bytes .ReturnsAsync(HttpStatusCode.OK, bytes, "image/png");

Use It.IsHttpRequestMessage(HttpMethod?) together with Setup.SendAsync(...) to match against the entire HttpRequestMessage, optionally restricted to a specific HTTP method. This is the catch-all entry point that the verb-specific overloads (GetAsync, PostAsync, …) route through internally; reach for it when you need the full request (e.g. to inspect headers, or to handle non-standard verbs like HEAD or OPTIONS). Chain builders to add constraints: .WhoseUriIs(string) / .WhoseUriIs(Action<IUriParameter>): same surface as It.IsUri(...). .WhoseContentIs(Action<IHttpContentParameter>) / .WhoseContentIs(string mediaType, …): same surface as It.IsHttpContent(...). .WithHeaders(...): require specific request headers. // Match any POST to /api/chocolate/dispense with a JSON body containing "Dark" httpClient.Mock.Setup .SendAsync(It.IsHttpRequestMessage(HttpMethod.Post) .WhoseUriIs(uri => uri.WithPath("/api/chocolate/dispense")) .WhoseContentIs("application/json", c => c.WithStringMatching("*\"type\": \"Dark\"*"))) .ReturnsAsync(HttpStatusCode.OK);

When the code under test pulls clients from IHttpClientFactory and wraps them in using blocks (using HttpClient client = _factory.CreateClient("chocolate-api");), two naive mocking patterns both break: Returning the same mocked HttpClient instance from every CreateClient call throws ObjectDisposedException on the second call, because the first using block already disposed it. Returning a freshly created mocked HttpClient from a Returns(() => ...) factory avoids the disposal exception but spreads invocation history across many short-lived mocks, so verifications can no longer see the full call sequence. The fix is to mock the underlying HttpMessageHandler once and hand out fresh HttpClient wrappers that all share it. Because Mockolate intercepts on the handler, the registry (and therefore the invocation history) lives on the handler and survives any number of wrapper disposals. Pass disposeHandler: false when constructing each wrapper so that disposing the wrapper does not also dispose the shared handler. // One mocked handler shared by every HttpClient the factory hands out. HttpMessageHandler handler = HttpMessageHandler.CreateMock(); // Setup goes on any HttpClient wrapping the handler; the shared registry routes the // configuration to every wrapper that uses the same handler. HttpClient setupClient = HttpClient.CreateMock(handler, disposeHandler: false); setupClient.Mock.Setup .GetAsync(It.IsUri("*testably.org/api/chocolate/inventory/*").ForHttps()) .ReturnsAsync(() => new HttpResponseMessage(HttpStatusCode.OK)); // The factory returns a fresh HttpClient each call, all sharing the handler. // `disposeHandler: false` keeps the shared handler alive when consumers `using` the client. IHttpClientFactory factory = IHttpClientFactory.CreateMock(); factory.Mock.Setup.CreateClient(It.IsAny<string>()) .Returns(() => HttpClient.CreateMock(handler, disposeHandler: false)); // The code under test can now safely use `using` blocks. Each call goes through the same // handler, so the invocation history is preserved across every disposed wrapper. foreach (string type in new[] { "Dark", "Milk", "White" }) { using HttpClient client = factory.CreateClient("chocolate-api"); _ = await client.GetAsync($"https://testably.org/api/chocolate/inventory/{type}"); } setupClient.Mock.Verify .GetAsync(It.IsUri("*testably.org/api/chocolate/inventory/*").ForHttps()) .Exactly(3); warning disposeHandler: false is the critical bit. HttpClient.Dispose() disposes its handler by default, which would tear down the shared mock after the first using block. Setup and verification can target any HttpClient wrapping the same handler. The setupClient above is just one convenient handle; the clients handed out by the factory work equally well.
Each section starts with a symptom and gives a short answer with a link to the detailed page. The limitations at the end list what Mockolate cannot mock and why.

CreateMock() and the Mock property are C# 14 extension members that the source generator emits into the Mockolate namespace. When the compiler does not find them, check: The using directive: add using Mockolate; (or a global using) to the test file. The SDK and the language version: the generator needs the compiler of the .NET 10 SDK. If your test project pins <LangVersion>, it must be 14 or later (or latest). An older compiler cannot load the generator, so it emits no mocks. The package reference: the generator and the analyzers are in the analyzers folder of the Mockolate package. A PackageReference that excludes the analyzers asset (with ExcludeAssets, or an IncludeAssets without it) also excludes the generator. The project language: the generator is packaged for C# projects only. If the IDE keeps showing outdated generated members after you fixed the cause, run dotnet clean and build again.
documents.s: CreateMock() or the Mock property does not exist

documents.t: Besides the mocks, the generator emits a fallback CreateMock() that accepts any type. The compiler picks it when the generator emitted no mock for your type, usually because the type cannot be mocked. Assigning its result to your type does not compile, and calling it throws a MockException: public class LockedChocolateDispenser { private LockedChocolateDispenser() { } } _ = LockedChocolateDispenser.CreateMock(); Failure message This method should not be called directly. Either 'MyNamespace.LockedChocolateDispenser' is not mockable or the source generator did not run correctly. Check the type against the limitations. For most of them, the Mockolate0002 analyzer already fails the build with the reason: public sealed class SealedChocolateDispenser { } // Mockolate0002: Type 'MyNamespace.SealedChocolateDispenser' cannot be mocked: type is sealed SealedChocolateDispenser dispenser = SealedChocolateDispenser.CreateMock();

When the mocked type already has a member named Mock, the generator names the accessor Mockolate_Mock instead, so that your member stays reachable. If that name is taken as well, it appends a number (Mockolate_Mock__1, Mockolate_Mock__2, …). public interface IChocolateMachine { int Mock { get; } } IChocolateMachine machine = IChocolateMachine.CreateMock(); machine.Mockolate_Mock.Setup.Mock.Returns(4); await That(machine.Mock).IsEqualTo(4);
documents.s: The mock has Mockolate_Mock instead of Mock

documents.t: .Implementing<T>() returns a new mock and leaves the original one unchanged. Keep the returned reference, and reach the setups of the additional interface with Mock.As<T>(). See Implementing additional interfaces.
documents.s: .Implementing<T>() has no effect on my mock

documents.t: By default, a mock never fails for a missing setup. Methods return a default value (false, 0, an empty string, an empty collection, a completed task, or null for other reference types), and properties and indexers store the values written to them. A method that returns an interface or a class therefore returns null until you set it up. To fail on every call without a matching setup, create the mock with ThrowingWhenNotSetup(). To change the default value of a type, use WithDefaultValueFor<T>(…).
documents.s: A member without setup returns a value instead of failing

documents.t: A mock created with ThrowingWhenNotSetup() throws a MockNotSetupException for every call that no setup matches, also when other setups of the same member exist: IChocolateDispenser dispenser = IChocolateDispenser.CreateMock(MockBehavior.Default.ThrowingWhenNotSetup()); dispenser.Mock.Setup.Dispense("Dark", It.IsAny<int>()).Returns(true); dispenser.Dispense("Milk", 1); Failure message The method 'global::MyNamespace.IChocolateDispenser.Dispense(string, int)' was invoked without prior setup. For a property, the message reads The property '…' was accessed without prior setup. Add a setup for the reported member, or use a matcher such as It.IsAny<string>() so that the existing setup covers the call.

When several setups match a call, the one defined last wins. A general setup defined after a specific one therefore hides it. Every dispenser.Mock.Setup.X statement also starts a new setup, so chain everything that belongs to one setup. See What happens when the mock is called.

A class mock can only override virtual and abstract members. Other members always run the real implementation (see members that are not mocked). A virtual member also calls the base class implementation when a setup matches; the setup's return value takes precedence. Use SkippingBaseClass() to turn the base class calls off.
documents.s: My class mock runs the real implementation

documents.t: The count methods are extension methods in the Mockolate.Verify namespace. Add using Mockolate.Verify; to the test file. See Verify interactions.
documents.s: .Once() and the other count methods do not exist

documents.t: A verification without a count method checks nothing. Add a count such as .Once() or .AtLeastOnce(); the code fix adds .AtLeastOnce() for you. See Mockolate0001.

The MockVerificationException states the expected call with its arguments and how often it actually happened: dispenser.Dispense("Dark", 1); dispenser.Dispense("Milk", 2); dispenser.Mock.Verify.Dispense(It.IsAny<string>(), It.IsAny<int>()).AtLeast(3); Failure message Expected that mock invoked method Dispense(It.IsAny<string>(), It.IsAny<int>()) at least 3 times, but it did twice. When the count is lower than you expect, check: The arguments: a plain value matches with EqualityComparer<T>.Default, so a class without its own Equals only matches the same instance. Use It.Satisfies<T>(…) or a custom equality comparer instead. Background threads: if the code under test calls the mock asynchronously, the call may not have happened yet. Use Within(…). A monitor or a reset: interactions outside a monitor scope, or before ClearAllInteractions(), are not counted. A mock created with SkippingInteractionRecording() records nothing, so every verification on it throws a MockException.
documents.s: A verification fails although the method was called

documents.t: Mockolate generates mocks at compile time, so it can only override what C# lets a derived class override, and only what your test assembly can access. The generator skips what it cannot mock; the analyzers report most of these cases.

Type Reported by A struct, an enum, a record or a sealed class (delegates are supported) Mockolate0002 A type declared in the global namespace Mockolate0002 Any other kind of type, such as an array Mockolate0002 A type with an abstract member that your assembly cannot access, or whose signature uses a type your assembly cannot access Mockolate0002 A class in .Implementing<T>(): additional types must be interfaces Mockolate0002 A class without a public, protected or protected internal constructor whose parameter types your assembly can access no diagnostic; the fallback CreateMock() throws a MockException A nested type declared private or private protected no diagnostic; the fallback CreateMock() throws a MockException

These members keep their real behavior, or throw, and get no Setup or Verify members: Non-virtual members of a class cannot be overridden and always run the real implementation. If the class implements them for an interface, .Implementing<T>() makes the calls through the interface mockable. Sealed members (sealed override) cannot be overridden either. Static members of a class cannot be virtual. static abstract and static virtual interface members are supported on .NET 8 or later; see Static interface members. internal and private protected virtual members declared in another assembly are only overridden when that assembly grants your test assembly InternalsVisibleTo. Virtual members whose signature uses an inaccessible type: when the return type, a parameter type or a generic constraint names a type your test assembly cannot access (including a protected nested type), the member is not overridden, because the setup and verification members would have to name that type. Members with ref structs other than Span<T> and ReadOnlySpan<T> in an unsupported position, such as a returned ref struct, have no setup; calling them throws a NotSupportedException, unless a virtual class member can forward to the base class. The Mockolate0003 warning lists the cases and the requirements for ref struct parameters. Generic methods with an allows ref struct type parameter that is used in the return type or in a parameter type throw a NotSupportedException when called. No analyzer reports them. For the abstract counterparts of the inaccessible members above, the mock cannot be created at all, and Mockolate0002 reports the type. Members with more than four parameters For members with more than four parameters, a setup or verification takes either values for all parameters or matchers for all of them. See Mixing values and matchers.

Every interaction with a mock is recorded. Use dispenser.Mock.Verify to check that methods, properties, indexers or events were used with specific arguments, and how many times: dispenser.Mock.Verify.Dispense("Dark", 5).AtLeastOnce(); A verification fails with a MockVerificationException that describes the expected and the actual calls. Arguments are matched with the same values and matchers as in setups. note The count methods are extension methods in the Mockolate.Verify namespace, so add using Mockolate.Verify; to your test files.

Method The interaction occurred … .Never() never .Once() exactly once .Twice() exactly twice .Exactly(n) exactly n times .AtLeastOnce() at least once .AtLeastTwice() at least twice .AtLeast(n) at least n times .AtMostOnce() at most once .AtMostTwice() at most twice .AtMost(n) at most n times .Between(min, max) between min and max times (inclusive) .Times(predicate) a number of times that satisfies the predicate

// Dispense("Dark", 5) was called at least once dispenser.Mock.Verify.Dispense("Dark", 5).AtLeastOnce(); // Dispense was never called with "White" and any amount dispenser.Mock.Verify.Dispense("White", It.IsAny<int>()).Never(); // Dispense was called exactly twice, with any arguments dispenser.Mock.Verify.Dispense(Match.AnyParameters()).Exactly(2); // Dispense was called an even number of times dispenser.Mock.Verify.Dispense(It.IsAny<string>(), It.IsAny<int>()).Times(count => count % 2 == 0); You can also verify how often a specific setup was used: IMethodSetup setup = dispenser.Mock.Setup.Dispense("Dark", 5).Returns(true); // Act dispenser.Mock.VerifySetup(setup).AtLeastOnce();

// The property 'TotalDispensed' was read at least once dispenser.Mock.Verify.TotalDispensed.Got().AtLeastOnce(); // The property 'TotalDispensed' was set to 42 exactly once dispenser.Mock.Verify.TotalDispensed.Set(42).Once(); // The property 'TotalDispensed' was set to a value greater than 10 dispenser.Mock.Verify.TotalDispensed.Set(It.Satisfies<int>(v => v > 10)).AtLeastOnce();

// The indexer was read with the key "Dark" exactly once dispenser.Mock.Verify["Dark"].Got().Once(); // The indexer was set for the key "Milk" to 7 at least once dispenser.Mock.Verify["Milk"].Set(7).AtLeastOnce(); Both the keys and the value accept matchers.

// A handler was subscribed to 'ChocolateDispensed' at least once dispenser.Mock.Verify.ChocolateDispensed.Subscribed().AtLeastOnce(); // A handler was unsubscribed from 'ChocolateDispensed' exactly once dispenser.Mock.Verify.ChocolateDispensed.Unsubscribed().Once();

Use Then to verify that calls occurred in a specific order: dispenser.Mock.Verify.Dispense("Dark", 1).Then( m => m.Dispense("Milk", 2), m => m.Dispense("White", 3)); If the order is different or a call is missing, a MockVerificationException is thrown.

If the code under test calls the mock from a background thread, use Within(TimeSpan) to wait until the expected interactions occurred: // Wait up to 1 second for Dispense("Dark", 5) to be called dispenser.Mock.Verify.Dispense("Dark", 5) .Within(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(1)) .AtLeastOnce(); Use WithCancellation(CancellationToken) to wait until the token is canceled instead. If you combine it with Within, both the timeout and the token are respected. Both block the test until the expected interactions occurred, or throw a MockVerificationException when the time is up. tip aweXpect.Mockolate offers awaitable verifications, including an asynchronous Within(TimeSpan) that does not block the test thread: await That(dispenser.Mock.Verify.Dispense("Dark", 5)).AtLeastOnce().Within(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(1));
Monitor interactions to only count the interactions within a scope. Check for unexpected interactions to check that all interactions were verified or all setups were used.

aweXpect is a fluent assertion library for .NET. It turns test verifications into readable sentences and produces failure messages that explain in plain English what was expected and what actually happened. await That(message).IsEqualTo("It's a compliment"); Failure message Expected that message is equal to "It's a compliment", but it was "It's a complement", which differs at index 12: ↓ (actual) "…a complement" "…a compliment" ↑ (expected) aweXpect v4 pre-release This documentation describes aweXpect v4, which is available as a pre-release; Getting started shows how to install it. If you are upgrading from v3, read From aweXpect 3.x.

Async-first Extensible Performant Any runner Native AOT Every expectation is awaited. The same fluent chain works for sync values, Task, IAsyncEnumerable, exceptions and HTTP responses (with the separate aweXpect.Web package): there is no parallel …Async() API to remember. // Plain value await That(result).IsEqualTo(42); // Task<T> await That(_artists.GetAsync(id)) .Satisfies(a => a.IsActive); // IAsyncEnumerable<T> - the cancellation token flows through the stream await That(_radio.StreamAsync()) .Contains(s => s.IsLive) .WithCancellation(cancellationToken); // Delegate that throws await That(() => _player.SetVolumeAsync(-1)) .ThrowsExactly<ArgumentOutOfRangeException>(); Because the chain is awaited, Because(...) and WithCancellation(...) attach once at the end instead of being threaded through every method. Multiple expectations compose directly via Expect.ThatAll(...), without a thread-static assertion scope. The aweXpect.Core package is intentionally kept stable so extensions don't fight over versions. Ready-made extension packages cover JSON (aweXpect.Json), HTTP (aweXpect.Web), architecture tests (aweXpect.Reflection), file and time systems (aweXpect.Testably) and mocks (aweXpect.Mockolate). Add expectations for any other type as extension methods on IThat<T>. For a simple condition, a source generator writes the expectation, its negation and the failure messages for you: public static partial class ThatTrack { [GenerateExpectation("Is{Not}RadioFriendly", "is {not} radio friendly")] private static bool IsRadioFriendly(Track track) => track.Duration < TimeSpan.FromMinutes(4); } // usage await That(track).IsRadioFriendly(); The full walkthrough is at Extending aweXpect. The happy path (passing assertions, the common case in a healthy test suite) is the path that has been optimized. Comparing strings, ignoring case Time aweXpect109.0 ns FluentAssertions266.6 nsFluentAssertions compared to aweXpect over the last 16 runs (dashed line: equal)+145% TUnit173.8 nsTUnit compared to aweXpect over the last 16 runs (dashed line: equal)+59% Memory aweXpect344 B FluentAssertions2.25 KiBFluentAssertions compared to aweXpect over the last 16 runs (dashed line: equal)+570% TUnit912 BTUnit compared to aweXpect over the last 16 runs (dashed line: equal)+165% Captured on commit 99f75dcf (2026-10-31) on ubuntu-latest. See the benchmarks for the full set. [Fact] // xUnit [Test] // NUnit / TUnit [TestMethod] // MSTest public async Task IsActive() => await That(artist.IsActive).IsTrue(); xUnit, NUnit, MSTest and TUnit are detected automatically, see the supported versions: a failure usually throws the assertion exception of the test framework, see failed expectations for the exact types. Fail and Skip fail or skip a test without an expectation. aweXpect and aweXpect.Core are trimmable and AOT compatible on .NET 8 and later, see Native AOT and trimming.

Getting started: install the package and write your first test. Find the expectation you need: the page that lists the expectations for your subject, from values and collections to delegates, events and the extension packages. Migration: the aweXpect.Migration analyzer ships code fixes that rewrite most FluentAssertions and xunit.Assert call sites for you; the guide also covers upgrading from aweXpect 2 or 3. How it works: awaiting, negation, combining, null, options, time and cancellation, and the configuration of the defaults. Setup and integration: test frameworks, target frameworks and Native AOT. Extending aweXpect: add expectations for your own types using aweXpect.Core.

The aweXpect package includes analyzers that report common mistakes while you write the test. Errors stop the build, warnings point at code that compiles but probably does not do what you meant. Most rules come with a code fix. The analyzers and the source generators need Roslyn 4.8 or later, which ships with the .NET 8 SDK and Visual Studio 2022 17.8. An older compiler skips them with warning CS8032. Rule Severity Reported when aweXpect0001 Error an expectation is neither awaited nor verified aweXpect0002 Error Equals is called on an expectation aweXpect0003 Warning a Has… expectation directly follows Throws aweXpect0004 Error an expectation for an object is applied to a delegate aweXpect0005 Warning an expectation is awaited in an async void method or lambda aweXpect0006 Warning a collection without a defined order is compared by position aweXpect0007 Error a delegate returns a ValueTask on a target without its overload aweXpect0008 Warning the value of an .Or combination is used aweXpect0009 Warning the result of an option method is discarded aweXpect1001 to aweXpect1004 Suppression nullability warnings after e.g. IsNotNull() aweXpect2001 Warning a type in [assembly: GenerateMetadata(…)] gets no registration aweXpect2002 Warning a test project on .NET 8 or later sets <LangVersion> below 9 aweXpect4001 to aweXpect4004 Error a method cannot be turned into a generated expectation aweXpect4005 Error a module initializer of an extension cannot be called

Error An expectation is neither awaited nor verified, so it is never evaluated and never fails. A code fix is available. bool value = false; That(value).IsTrue(); // reported: never evaluated await That(value).IsTrue(); // fixed: awaited, so it fails The code fix awaits the expectation and makes the enclosing method, local function or lambda async where needed. It is not offered where that would not compile or would change a signature that other code depends on. Where the code fix is not offered in a lambda that is not async, such as one converted to an Action in a constructor, a property, an iterator, a lock statement or unsafe code in a function with ref locals or ref struct locals in a method with ref, out, in, pointer or ref struct parameters, or one that returns by reference in a partial or [Conditional] method in a method or local function whose return type would have to change while other code depends on it: an override, a virtual method, an interface implementation (also one that only a derived class declares), or one that is called or used as a method group elsewhere For a ref struct that cannot be used in an async method, verify the expectation synchronously instead, see When you cannot await.

Error Equals is called on an expectation. It compares the expectation object itself and does not verify anything. int subject = 1; bool isEqual = That(subject).Equals(2); // reported: verifies nothing await That(subject).IsEqualTo(2); // fixed

Warning A Has… expectation is used directly after Throws, where the sentence "throws a …" needs the With… vocabulary. Two code fixes are available: switch to the With… twin, or insert .Which. void Act() => throw new InvalidOperationException("Yesterday"); await That(Act).Throws<InvalidOperationException>().HasMessage("Yesterday"); // reported await That(Act).Throws<InvalidOperationException>().WithMessage("Yesterday"); // fixed The Has… vocabulary belongs after .Which. See Delegates.

Error An expectation for an object is applied to a delegate subject, so it checks the delegate instead of what it returns. A code fix is available for a delegate that returns a value. int Act() => 3; await That(Act).IsEqualTo(3); // reported: checks the delegate await That(Act).DoesNotThrow().WhoseResult.IsEqualTo(3); // fixed: checks the returned value See Delegates.

Warning An expectation is awaited in an async void method or lambda, so its failure is thrown after the test has completed and is not observed by the test. List<int> values = [1, 2, 3]; values.ForEach(async x => await That(x).IsGreaterThan(0)); // reported: async void lambda foreach (int x in values) { await That(x).IsGreaterThan(0); // fixed: awaited by the test } Return a Task instead, or await the expectation in the test method itself.

Warning A collection without a defined order, such as a set or a dictionary, is compared by position. A code fix is available. HashSet<int> values = [1, 2, 3]; await That(values).IsEqualTo([1, 2, 3]); // reported: depends on the enumeration order await That(values).IsEqualTo([1, 2, 3]).InAnyOrder(); // fixed IsEqualTo, Contains and IsContainedIn compare by position unless .InAnyOrder() is appended, which the code fix does. StartsWith, EndsWith and IgnoringInterspersedItems() are about the order itself and have no meaning for such a collection, so .InAnyOrder() does not help there. Sorted collections are not reported. See Collections.

Error A delegate subject returns a ValueTask on a target without ValueTask delegate overloads, so the ValueTask is never awaited. A code fix is available. async ValueTask Act() => await Task.Yield(); await That(() => Act()).DoesNotThrow(); // reported on targets before .NET 8 await That(() => Act().AsTask()).DoesNotThrow(); // fixed On any target, the rule also reports a delegate whose ValueTask is given explicitly as the type argument, as in That<ValueTask>(() => Act()). An explicit Task type argument has the same effect and is reported as well, as in That<Task>(() => ActAsync()): remove the type argument, so that the task is awaited. See Delegates. Why targets before .NET 8 are affected These older targets use the .NET Standard 2.0 build of aweXpect, which has no ValueTask delegate overloads.

Warning The value of an expectation is used although an .Or combines it with an alternative that has no value of this type, so the value can be the default. object subject = "Yesterday"; int count = await That(subject).Is<string>().Or.Is<int>(); // reported: 0 for a string subject await That(subject).Is<string>().Or.Is<int>(); // fixed: the value is not used The value is default (also null for a reference type that is not annotated as nullable) when another alternative was met. Do not use it, or check it first and suppress the warning there. The rule is not reported when the value has the type of the subject, or a base type or an interface of it, because then every alternative returns the subject. See Combining expectations.

Warning The value returned by an option method of an immutable option, such as a Quantifier or the StringEqualityOptions, is discarded, so the call has no effect. using aweXpect.Core; using aweXpect.Options; OptionsHolder<Quantifier> quantifier = new(Quantifier.Default); quantifier.Value.AtLeast(2); // reported: the quantifier stays unchanged quantifier.Value = quantifier.Value.AtLeast(2); // fixed: the holder gets the new quantifier quantifier.AtLeast(2); // fixed: the option method of the holder replaces its value The options are immutable values, so an option method returns new options and leaves the ones it is called on unchanged. The rule covers every options type marked with [ImmutableOptions]: those of aweXpect, those of the extension packages, e.g. the JsonOptions, also in a lambda with a block body like o => { o.IgnoringMember("id"); return o; }, and those of other extensions that mark their own. A call that is the whole body of a lambda or local function written with => is not reported, as it is usually there to check that the option throws. Authors of extensions find more in Options.

After an expectation that a null subject can never satisfy, such as IsNotNull(), the aweXpect package suppresses the nullability warnings CS8600, CS8602, CS8604 and CS8629 for that subject, with the suppression IDs aweXpect1001 to aweXpect1004. Expectations of extension packages take part when they are marked with [GuaranteesNotNull], see nullability warnings. string? title = new Track().Title; await That(title).IsNotNull(); int length = title.Length; // no CS8602 When the suppression applies The subject has to be a local variable or a parameter that is neither a ref nor a parameter of a primary constructor, which any member can write to, and the expectation has to be awaited or verified in a preceding statement in the same method, local function or lambda, without a branch, a label or a write to the subject in that statement or in between. Assigning the result of an expectation to its own subject, as in subject = await That(subject).IsNotNull();, does not count as a write, because the result is the subject. A ref alias of the subject prevents the suppression, as it can change the subject unnoticed. Only the warnings are suppressed; the null state of the compiler is unchanged.
The source generator warns with aweXpect2001 when a type named in [assembly: GenerateMetadata(typeof(…))] yields no registration and stays on the reflection path. See Native AOT and trimming.

The source generator warns with aweXpect2002 when a test project on .NET 8 or later sets <LangVersion> below 9. The generated test framework adapter registers itself with a module initializer, which needs C# 9, and on .NET 8 or later the loaded assemblies are not scanned for it. Without the adapter, aweXpect throws its own exceptions, so a skipped or inconclusive test is reported as failed. Set <LangVersion> to 9 or later, or register the adapter before the first expectation, see test framework adapter. TestFrameworkRegistry.Register(new aweXpect.Frameworks.NunitAdapter());
These rules are reported while you build an extension package on aweXpect.Core.

The source generator in aweXpect.Core reports an error for a method marked with [GenerateExpectation] or [GenerateCollectionExpectation] that it cannot turn into an expectation, see generated expectations: Rule Reported when aweXpect4001 the class of the method is not a top-level, non-generic, static partial class or is file-local aweXpect4002 the method, its parameters, the name or the expectation text are not supported, with the reason aweXpect4003 the Result names no static method that returns a string and takes the subject aweXpect4004 the FormattedItem names no static method that returns a value and takes the item

The source generator in aweXpect.Core reports the error aweXpect4005 when a name in the MSBuild property AweXpectModuleInitializers names no accessible static method without parameters, and leaves the call out of the module initializer. The build targets of an extension set this property, see registration from the test project.

Describes the possible expectations for code that runs: delegates, tasks, events and callbacks. Page Expectations Delegates Throws, ThrowsExactly, DoesNotThrow, the thrown exception, Eventually, ExecutesIn, Allocates, IsCollectedAfter Tasks the delegate expectations for a running Task or ValueTask, the result of a Task<T> Events Triggered, DidNotTrigger, TriggeredPropertyChanged, TriggeredPropertyChangedFor Callbacks Signaled, DidNotSignal on a Signaler Many of these expectations wait: for a delegate or a task to complete, for callbacks to be signaled, or with Within(…) for events to be triggered. Time and cancellation describes how long they wait, how WithTimeout(…) and WithCancellation(…) limit it, and how a timeout or a cancellation is reported.

Describes the possible expectations for working with callbacks. Expectation Negated Summary Signaled DidNotSignal the callback was signaled (a number of times) Wait, WaitAsync, IsSignaled waits for or checks signals without an expectation

You can verify that a callback was called. Create a Signaler from the aweXpect.Signaling namespace: using aweXpect.Signaling; // ↓ Counts signals from callbacks without parameters Signaler signaler = new(); Signaler<string> titleSignaler = new(); // ↑ Counts signals from callbacks with a string parameter Call Signal from the callback: class Player { public void Play(string title, Action<string> onCompleted) { // play the track in a background thread and then call the onCompleted callback } } player.Play("Let It Be", title => titleSignaler.Signal(title)); Then verify that the callback was signaled, and limit with Within(…) how long to wait for it: await That(titleSignaler).Signaled().Within(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(5)); You can also verify that the callback was not signaled within the given time: await That(titleSignaler).DidNotSignal().Within(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(1)); Without Within(…), a test can wait 30 seconds Without Within(…), a signaler expectation waits up to the DefaultSignalerTimeout (30 s). DidNotSignal() and a count with an upper bound, such as AtMost(3) or Never(), always wait the full timeout to succeed, and a count that is not reached waits the full timeout before it fails, see waiting for callbacks.

You can verify that a callback was signaled a number of times: await That(signaler).Signaled().AtLeast(3); await That(signaler).Signaled().Exactly(3); await That(signaler).Signaled().AtMost(3); await That(signaler).Signaled().MoreThan(2); await That(signaler).Signaled().LessThan(3); await That(signaler).Signaled().Between(2).And(4); await That(signaler).Signaled().Once(); await That(signaler).Signaled().Twice(); await That(signaler).Signaled().Never(); Signaled(3) is the shorthand for Signaled().AtLeast(3), and DidNotSignal(3) expects the callback to be signaled fewer than three times.

You can filter for signals with specific parameters by providing a predicate: Signaler<string> signaler = new(); signaler.Signal("Yesterday"); signaler.Signal("Let It Be"); signaler.Signal("Yesterday"); await That(signaler).Signaled().AtLeast(2).With(p => p == "Yesterday"); WhoseParameters continues with expectations on the collection of received parameters that match the filter from With: Signaler<string> signaler = new(); signaler.Signal("Yesterday"); signaler.Signal("Let It Be"); await That(signaler).Signaled().AtLeast(2).WhoseParameters.Contains("Let It Be"); A failure message lists the received parameters.

A signaler can also be used directly, e.g. to continue a test only after a callback was signaled. WaitAsync waits without blocking a thread, until the callback was signaled or the timeout expired: Signaler<string> signaler = new(); player.Play("Let It Be", title => signaler.Signal(title)); SignalerResult<string> result = await signaler.WaitAsync(timeout: TimeSpan.FromSeconds(5)); string completed = string.Join(", ", result.Parameters); Fail.Unless(result.IsSuccess, $"only {result.Count} tracks completed: {completed}"); Wait takes the same parameters, but blocks the calling thread while it waits, and IsSignaled returns immediately: Signaler<string> signaler = new(); bool isSignaled = signaler.IsSignaled(2); SignalerResult<string> result = signaler.Wait(2, title => title.StartsWith("Let")); All parameters are optional and have the same meaning for Wait and WaitAsync: Parameter Without it amount waits for one signal; IsSignaled checks for at least one signal predicate counts every signal; only a Signaler<T> has it, to count the signals that match timeout waits for at most the DefaultSignalerTimeout (30 s) cancellationToken only the timeout ends the wait Signals that were received before the wait count as well, so a callback that was already signaled is not missed. Details of waiting A timeout of TimeSpan.Zero does not wait at all, and Timeout.InfiniteTimeSpan waits without a limit. When the timeout expires or the CancellationToken is canceled, the wait returns without throwing an exception. An exception of the predicate ends the wait and is thrown by Wait or WaitAsync, also when the predicate ran on the thread that signaled. The SignalerResult tells how the wait ended: Property Value IsSuccess true when enough signals were received before the timeout expired or the wait was canceled Count the number of signals that were received until the wait ended Parameters the parameters of these signals, also of those that did not match the predicate (Signaler<T> only)

Describes the possible expectations for delegates and the exceptions they throw. Expectation Negated Summary Throws DoesNotThrow throws an exception Throws<T> DoesNotThrow<T> throws a T or a derived exception ThrowsExactly<T> DoesNotThrowExactly<T> throws exactly a T Eventually re-evaluates the delegate until the expectations are met ExecutesIn completes within the expected time Allocates allocates at most or at least the given number of bytes IsCollectedAfter the returned object is garbage collected after the cleanup A delegate can be any of the following. Each of them can also take a CancellationToken parameter (e.g. Func<CancellationToken, Task>), which is canceled when the expectation times out or is canceled: Without return value With return value T Synchronous Action Func<T> Asynchronous Func<Task>, Func<ValueTask> Func<Task<T>>, Func<ValueTask<T>> An asynchronous delegate is awaited, like a task that is passed directly. .NET 8 or later: ValueTask delegates On .NET Framework, .NET Standard 2.0, .NET 6 and .NET 7, a delegate that returns a ValueTask is never awaited. Return .AsTask() instead, as reported by the analyzer rule aweXpect0007. CS0121 with C# 12 or older on .NET 8 An async lambda and a lambda that only throws, as in That(async () => await x.RunAsync()) or That(() => throw new X()), bind to the Task overload through [OverloadResolutionPriority]. The attribute only takes effect with C# 13 or later, which is the default only for .NET 9 and later. With an older language version on .NET 8, such a lambda fits both the Task and the ValueTask overload and fails with CS0121. Set <LangVersion> to 13 or latest, return the task directly (That(() => x.RunAsync())), or declare a local function (void Act() => throw new X();) and pass it.

You can verify that the delegate does not throw any exception: void Act() { } await That(Act).DoesNotThrow(); DoesNotThrow<TException>() only fails when the delegate throws a TException or a derived type, and DoesNotThrowExactly<TException>() only when it throws exactly a TException. Any other exception passes both: void Act() => throw new ArgumentNullException("value"); await That(Act).DoesNotThrow<InvalidOperationException>(); await That(Act).DoesNotThrowExactly<ArgumentException>(); For a delegate with a return value, WhoseResult continues with the returned value as subject, and awaiting DoesNotThrow() returns it: int Act() => 3; await That(Act).DoesNotThrow().WhoseResult.IsEqualTo(3); int result = await That(Act).DoesNotThrow(); Awaiting DoesNotThrow<TException>(), DoesNotThrowExactly<TException>() or their Type overloads returns no value. An expectation must not be applied to the delegate itself That(Act).IsEqualTo(3) compiles, but checks the delegate instead of what it returns, so it silently passes or fails with a message about the delegate. The analyzer rule aweXpect0004 reports it and offers to insert .DoesNotThrow().WhoseResult. A delegate without a return value has nothing to compare at all. Why DoesNotThrow<TException>() returns no value The delegate may have thrown an exception of another type instead, so there may be no value to return. The WhoseResult of DoesNotThrow<TException>() and DoesNotThrowExactly<TException>() requires that no exception was thrown at all.
You can verify that the delegate throws an exception: void Act() => throw new CustomException("Yesterday"); await That(Act).Throws();

You can verify that the delegate throws a specific exception, of the given type or any derived type: void Act() => throw new CustomException("Yesterday"); await That(Act).Throws<CustomException>(); await That(Act).Throws(typeof(CustomException));

You can verify that the delegate throws exactly a specific exception, and not any derived type: void Act() => throw new CustomException("Yesterday"); await That(Act).ThrowsExactly<CustomException>(); await That(Act).ThrowsExactly(typeof(CustomException)); Open generic exception types A Type argument must be an exception type. Like Is(typeof(List<>)) for objects, an open generic type such as typeof(CustomException<>) matches every exception whose type is constructed from it or derives from such a type, while ThrowsExactly only matches the constructed types themselves.

You can verify that the delegate throws an exception only if a predicate is satisfied (otherwise it verifies that no exception is thrown): void Act() => throw new CustomException("Yesterday"); bool expectThrownException = true; await That(Act).Throws<CustomException>().OnlyIf(expectThrownException); This is especially useful with parameterized tests where it depends on a parameter if an exception is thrown or not.

You can verify that the exception is thrown within a given time: using aweXpect.Chronology; // from the aweXpect.Chronology package async Task Act() { await Task.Delay(100); throw new CustomException("Yesterday"); } await That(Act).Throws<CustomException>().Within(1.Seconds()); The duration is applied as timeout, see execution time.

After Throws, the following expectations verify the thrown exception, and their Has… twins verify an exception that is the subject itself: After Throws On an exception subject Verifies WithMessage HasMessage the Message WithParamName HasParamName the ParamName of an ArgumentException WithHResult HasHResult the HResult WithInner, WithoutInner HasInner, DoesNotHaveInner the InnerException WithRecursiveInnerExceptions HasRecursiveInnerExceptions all inner exceptions, recursively Whose Whose any other member Which continues with the exception as subject Directly after Throws, an expectation continues the sentence "throws a CustomException", so it uses the With… vocabulary. For an exception that is the subject itself, the Has… twins start a new sentence. After .Which the thrown exception becomes the subject, so Has… applies again: void Act() => throw new CustomException("Yesterday"); Exception exception = new CustomException("Yesterday"); await That(Act).Throws<CustomException>().WithMessage("Yesterday"); await That(Act).Throws<CustomException>().Which.HasMessage("Yesterday"); await That(exception).HasMessage("Yesterday"); All three verify the same thing, but only the vocabulary that matches its position produces a readable failure message: Has… directly after Throws compiles, but reads "throws a CustomException has message …". The analyzer rule aweXpect0003 flags it and offers to switch to the With… twin or to insert .Which.

You can verify the message of the thrown exception: void Act() => throw new CustomException("Yesterday, all my troubles seemed so far away"); await That(Act).Throws().WithMessage("Yesterday, all my troubles seemed so far away"); await That(Act).Throws().WithMessage().NotEqualTo("Let It Be"); await That(Act).Throws().WithMessage().Containing("troubles"); await That(Act).Throws().WithMessage().NotContaining("Help!"); await That(Act).Throws().WithMessage().StartingWith("Yesterday"); await That(Act).Throws().WithMessage().NotStartingWith("Tomorrow"); await That(Act).Throws().WithMessage().EndingWith("far away"); await That(Act).Throws().WithMessage().NotEndingWith("here to stay"); WithMessage(expected) is the shorthand for WithMessage().EqualTo(expected). The same applies to WithParamName(expected). You can use the same string options and match types as when comparing strings: void Act() => throw new CustomException("Yesterday, all my troubles seemed so far away"); await That(Act).Throws().WithMessage("yesterday*").AsWildcard().IgnoringCase(); Containing counts the occurrences like Contains on a string: without a quantifier the value has to occur at least once, and you can specify how often it has to occur and how it is matched: void Act() => throw new CustomException("Help, I need somebody, help, not just anybody"); await That(Act).Throws().WithMessage().Containing("help").IgnoringCase().Twice(); await That(Act).Throws().WithMessage().Containing("?body").AsWildcard().AtLeast(2); await That(Act).Throws().WithMessage().Containing("yesterday").Never(); Expecting a null message A null argument to WithMessage(expected) or WithParamName(expected) requires the message or parameter name to be null as well.

You can verify the inner exception of the thrown exception: void Act() => throw new CustomException("outer", new CustomException("inner")); await That(Act).Throws().WithInner(); await That(Act).Throws().WithInner<CustomException>(); Pass expectations to continue with the inner exception as subject. They are only checked when the inner exception exists and is of the given type: void Act() => throw new CustomException("outer", new CustomException("inner")); await That(Act).Throws().WithInner(inner => inner.HasMessage("inner")); await That(Act).Throws().WithInner<CustomException>(inner => inner.HasMessage("inner")); You can also verify that the thrown exception has no inner exception, or none of a given type: void Act() => throw new CustomException("outer"); await That(Act).Throws().WithoutInner(); await That(Act).Throws().WithoutInner<ArgumentException>(); WithInner, WithInner(…, expectations) and WithoutInner also take a Type instead of a type argument, e.g. WithInner(typeof(CustomException)).

You can recursively verify the collection of inner exceptions of the thrown exception with the quantifiers of a collection: void Act() => throw new AggregateException("outer", new CustomException("inner")); await That(Act).Throws() .WithRecursiveInnerExceptions(innerExceptions => innerExceptions.AtLeast(1).Are<CustomException>()); The exception must have at least one inner exception.

You can verify additional members of the exception: CustomException exception = new("outer", hResult: 12345); void Act() => throw exception; await That(Act).Throws().WithHResult(12345); // the `HResult` continues with the numeric comparison vocabulary await That(Act).Throws().WithHResult().GreaterThan(12340); // verify arbitrary additional members await That(Act).Throws() .Whose(e => e.HResult, h => h.IsGreaterThan(12340)); // access the thrown exception await That(Act).Throws() .Which.IsSameAs(exception); The ParamName of an ArgumentException continues like the message: void Act() => throw new ArgumentNullException("album"); await That(Act).Throws<ArgumentNullException>().WithParamName("album"); await That(Act).Throws<ArgumentNullException>().WithParamName().NotEqualTo("track"); await That(Act).Throws<ArgumentNullException>().WithParamName().StartingWith("al");

You can verify an exception that is the subject itself, e.g. when a method returns it or a callback receives it, with the Has… twins: Exception exception = new CustomException("Yesterday", new CustomException("Let It Be"), hResult: 12345); ArgumentException argumentException = new ArgumentNullException("album"); await That(exception).HasMessage("Yesterday"); await That(exception).HasHResult().GreaterThan(12340); await That(exception).HasInner<CustomException>(inner => inner.HasMessage("Let It Be")); await That(exception).HasRecursiveInnerExceptions(innerExceptions => innerExceptions.All().Are<CustomException>()); await That(argumentException).HasParamName("album");

You can verify that the value a delegate returns eventually meets the expectations: Eventually() re-evaluates a delegate with a return value until the expectations on the returned value are met, e.g. while a background task is still running: Track track = new(); // Start a background task that plays the track await That(() => track.PlayCount).Eventually().IsGreaterThan(5); See Eventually for how long and how often the delegate is re-evaluated, and how exceptions, timeouts and cancellation are handled.

You can verify the execution time of a delegate: using aweXpect.Chronology; // from the aweXpect.Chronology package async Task PlayIntro() => await Task.Delay(200); await That(PlayIntro).ExecutesIn().AtMost(300.Milliseconds()); await That(PlayIntro).ExecutesIn().AtLeast(100.Milliseconds()); // within 200ms ± 50ms await That(PlayIntro).ExecutesIn(200.Milliseconds()).Within(50.Milliseconds()); await That(PlayIntro).ExecutesIn().Between(100.Milliseconds()).And(300.Milliseconds()); A delegate that throws an exception fails these expectations, however fast it did so: a crash is not a measurement of execution time. The upper bound is applied as timeout, see execution time for how a delegate that runs too long is canceled or abandoned.

When you want to measure how long a delegate ran before it failed, for example a retry that exhausts its attempts, a circuit breaker that trips, or an operation that runs into its own timeout, AllowingExceptions() lets the measured duration decide alone: await That(() => retryPolicy.Execute(alwaysFailing)).ExecutesIn().AllowingExceptions() .AtLeast(300.Milliseconds()) .Because("three attempts with a 100ms backoff must have been made before giving up"); The duration is measured up to the throw, and the exception is still shown in the failure message when the delegate misses the expected time. Timeouts and cancellation with AllowingExceptions() A timeout from WithTimeout or from the upper bound still fails the expectation with "did not finish within …", and a canceled WithCancellation token leaves it inconclusive. An OperationCanceledException that the delegate throws for its own reasons is allowed like any other exception. AllowingExceptions() with AtMost(…) accepts an immediate crash With AtMost(…), a delegate that throws immediately also passes. If the delegate is expected to throw, use Throws<TException>().Within(…) instead.

.NET 8 or later Allocates() is only available on .NET 8 or later. You can verify how many bytes a synchronous delegate allocates: string[] playlist = ["Yesterday", "Let It Be", "Help!"]; int CountLongTitles() { int count = 0; foreach (string title in playlist) { if (title.Length > 5) { count++; } } return count; } string JoinTitles() => string.Join(", ", playlist); await That(CountLongTitles).Allocates().Nothing(); await That(JoinTitles).Allocates().AtMost(1024) .Because("joining the titles should only allocate the joined string"); await That(JoinTitles).Allocates().AtLeast(16); await That(JoinTitles).Allocates().Between(16).And(1024); Nothing() is the shorthand for AtMost(0). There is no expectation on an exact number of bytes, because the size of an object changes between runtime versions and platforms, so prefer bounds with some margin. Only allocations on the current thread are counted; allocations on other threads, e.g. of a started task, are not included. Synchronous delegates only Allocates() supports Action, Func<T> and their variants with a CancellationToken. An asynchronous delegate can continue on another thread after an await, whose allocations would be missed, so Allocates() throws a NotSupportedException for an asynchronous delegate or a task. Like for the execution time, a delegate that throws an exception fails the expectation, unless AllowingExceptions() is specified. The measured bytes then include the exception and the stack trace the runtime captured for it: void Reject() => throw new ArgumentException("The track is unknown."); await That(Reject).Allocates().AllowingExceptions().AtMost(10_000) .Because("rejecting a track should not allocate more than the exception"); The delegate is invoked once for all expectations on it, so it can be combined with other delegate expectations, e.g. That(JoinTitles).Allocates().AtMost(1024).And.ExecutesIn().AtMost(…). How the allocations are measured The bytes are read with GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread() directly before and after a single invocation of the delegate. Allocates() can only be specified once per expectation.

The first invocation of a delegate can include one-time allocations, e.g. of static constructors, lazy caches or pools. AfterWarmUp() invokes the delegate once before the measured invocation, so that they are not counted: Dictionary<int, string> titles = new(); string GetTitle(int track) { if (!titles.TryGetValue(track, out string? title)) { title = $"Track {track}"; titles[track] = title; } return title; } await That(() => GetTitle(7)).Allocates().AfterWarmUp().Nothing() .Because("the title is cached after the first call"); The delegate then runs twice, and the other expectations on it, e.g. on the execution time, see the measured second invocation. Without AfterWarmUp(), the delegate runs exactly once. Exceptions during the warm-up An exception in the warm-up fails the expectation like one in the measured invocation, which is then skipped. With AllowingExceptions(), it is ignored and the second invocation is measured.

You can verify that the object a delegate creates is garbage collected after a cleanup with IsCollectedAfter, e.g. that a view model no longer listens to a long-lived message bus once it is disposed: MessageBus bus = new(); await That(() => new ViewModel(bus)).IsCollectedAfter(vm => vm.Dispose()) .Because("the view model must unsubscribe from the bus when it is disposed"); The expectation fails with "it was still alive" when anything else still references the object, e.g. an event handler or a static collection that the cleanup did not remove. When no cleanup is needed, use IsCollectedAfter(_ => { }). Create the object inside the delegate The delegate must create the object: when it returns an instance that the test also holds, e.g. in a local variable, this reference keeps the object alive. To check an object you only have a WeakReference to, use IsCollected. How the object is collected aweXpect calls the delegate and the cleanup in a separate method that keeps only a weak reference to the object, and then forces full blocking garbage collections. An asynchronous delegate is awaited before the cleanup runs. An exception thrown by the delegate or by the cleanup fails the expectation, as does a delegate that returns null.

Describes the possible expectations for verifying events. Expectation Negated Summary Triggered DidNotTrigger the recording recorded the event TriggeredPropertyChanged DidNotTriggerPropertyChanged PropertyChanged was raised for any property TriggeredPropertyChangedFor DidNotTriggerPropertyChangedFor PropertyChanged was raised for the property The events are recorded first. The samples on this page use the following recording: using aweXpect.Recording; class TrackStartedEventArgs(string title = "") : EventArgs { public string Title { get; } = title; } class Player { public event EventHandler<TrackStartedEventArgs>? TrackStarted; public void Play(string title) => TrackStarted?.Invoke(this, new TrackStartedEventArgs(title)); } Player player = new Player(); IEventRecording<Player> recording = player.Record().Events();

.Record().Events() in the aweXpect.Recording namespace starts a recording of all events of the subject, or of the events with the given names: IEventRecording<Player> recording = player.Record().Events(nameof(Player.TrackStarted)); player.Play("Let It Be"); await That(recording).Triggered(nameof(Player.TrackStarted)); An expectation stops the recording, unless you keep it running with .UntilDisposed(). Events that cannot be recorded Without a registration from the source generator, the handler is bound reflectively. Such a handler must take at most four parameters, must return nothing and must take no parameter by reference. Recording all events skips an event whose handler does not fit, so that the other events of the subject are still recorded, and an expectation on the skipped event throws a NotSupportedException with the reason; recording it by name throws right away.

You can verify that a recording recorded an event: IEventRecording<Player> recording = player.Record().Events(); player.Play("Let It Be"); await That(recording).Triggered(nameof(Player.TrackStarted)); You can also verify that a recording did not record an event: IEventRecording<Player> recording = player.Record().Events(); // Perform an action on the player that must not start a track await That(recording).DidNotTrigger(nameof(Player.TrackStarted)); Triggered expects the event at least once, and DidNotTrigger is equivalent to Triggered(…).Never(). A count negates the expectation, so DidNotTrigger(nameof(Player.TrackStarted)).AtLeast(2) expects the event to be triggered less than twice. Without Within(…), only the events recorded so far count. To wait for events that are triggered in the background, see waiting for events.

You can verify that an event was recorded a specific number of times: IEventRecording<Player> recording = player.Record().Events(); player.Play("Let It Be"); player.Play("Yesterday"); await That(recording).Triggered(nameof(Player.TrackStarted)).Between(1).And(2); The same occurrence constraints as for Contains are available: AtLeast(2), AtMost(3), Between(1).And(4), Exactly(0), MoreThan(1), LessThan(3), Once(), Twice() and Never(). AtLeast, AtMost, MoreThan and LessThan can also be followed by Once() or Twice(), as in AtLeast().Once(), AtMost().Twice(), MoreThan().Once() and LessThan().Twice(): IEventRecording<Player> recording = player.Record().Events(); player.Play("Let It Be"); await That(recording).Triggered(nameof(Player.TrackStarted)).AtMost().Twice();

You can filter the recorded events based on their parameters, and count only the matching ones: IEventRecording<Player> recording = player.Record().Events(); player.Play("Let It Be"); player.Play("Yesterday"); await That(recording).Triggered(nameof(Player.TrackStarted)) .WithParameter<TrackStartedEventArgs>(e => e.Title == "Yesterday"); await That(recording).Triggered(nameof(Player.TrackStarted)) .WithParameter<TrackStartedEventArgs>(e => e.Title == "Yesterday").Once(); This matches an event when any of its parameters is of the given type and satisfies the predicate. To check the parameter at a specific zero-based position instead, pass the position first: IEventRecording<Player> recording = player.Record().Events(); player.Play("Yesterday"); await That(recording).Triggered(nameof(Player.TrackStarted)) .WithParameter<TrackStartedEventArgs>(1, e => e.Title == "Yesterday"); An event whose parameter at that position is missing or of another type does not match. null parameters A parameter that is null is passed to the predicate, unless the given type is a non-nullable value type; without a position, null parameters are ignored. The predicates for the sender and for the EventArgs below also receive a value that is null. When you follow the event best practices, you can also filter the recorded events based on the sender (the first parameter) or on their EventArgs (the second parameter): IEventRecording<Player> recording = player.Record().Events(); player.Play("Let It Be"); await That(recording).Triggered(nameof(Player.TrackStarted)) .WithSender(s => s == player) .Because("the sender is the first parameter"); IEventRecording<Player> recording = player.Record().Events(); player.Play("Let It Be"); await That(recording).Triggered(nameof(Player.TrackStarted)) .With<TrackStartedEventArgs>(e => e.Title.StartsWith("Let")) .Because("the EventArgs are the second parameter");

You can verify that an object triggered the INotifyPropertyChanged.PropertyChanged event, for any property or for a specific one: AlbumViewModel album = // ...implements INotifyPropertyChanged using IDisposableEventRecording<AlbumViewModel> recording = album.Record().Events().UntilDisposed(); album.Rename("Let It Be... Naked"); await That(recording).TriggeredPropertyChanged(); await That(recording).TriggeredPropertyChangedFor(x => x.Title); The expression has to access a property directly on the subject, as in x => x.Title. For any other name, use the overload with the property name, e.g. TriggeredPropertyChangedFor("Title"). The negated expectations verify that the event was not triggered: AlbumViewModel album = // ...implements INotifyPropertyChanged using IDisposableEventRecording<AlbumViewModel> recording = album.Record().Events().UntilDisposed(); // do something that must not change the album await That(recording).DidNotTriggerPropertyChanged(); await That(recording).DidNotTriggerPropertyChangedFor(x => x.Title); An event with a null or empty property name counts as a change of every property. null or empty property names As defined by the INotifyPropertyChanged contract, an event that was triggered with a null or empty property name notifies that all properties changed: it satisfies TriggeredPropertyChangedFor for every property name and lets DidNotTriggerPropertyChangedFor fail for every property name. A whitespace-only name is a name like any other. Expecting the null or the empty property name itself, e.g. TriggeredPropertyChangedFor((string?)null), matches only the events that notify that all properties changed, but no named one, and without distinguishing the two spellings, which the contract allows interchangeably. The expectation then reads "for all properties".

An expectation stops the recording: it detaches the handlers from the subject as soon as it is evaluated. Until then, every constraint of that one expectation sees the recorded events, including the ones that arrive while it waits with Within(…), because .And and .Or combine into a single expectation. A further expectation on the same recording throws an InvalidOperationException, so that it cannot silently answer from the events that were recorded until then: IEventRecording<Player> recording = player.Record().Events(); player.Play("Let It Be"); await That(recording).Triggered(nameof(Player.TrackStarted)).Once(); player.Play("Yesterday"); // ↓ throws, because the previous expectation already stopped the recording await That(recording).Triggered(nameof(Player.TrackStarted)).Twice(); Expect.ThatAll(…) and Expect.ThatAny(…) The expectations within one Expect.ThatAll(…) or Expect.ThatAny(…), including nested ones, share the recording: it is stopped when the whole combination was evaluated. They are evaluated one after the other, so the events that arrive while one of them waits with Within(…) also count for the following ones, as with .And. .UntilDisposed() keeps the recording running across multiple expectations and hands its lifetime to you: using IDisposableEventRecording<Player> recording = player.Record().Events().UntilDisposed(); player.Play("Let It Be"); await That(recording).Triggered(nameof(Player.TrackStarted)).Once(); player.Play("Yesterday"); await That(recording).Triggered(nameof(Player.TrackStarted)).Twice(); Disposing detaches the handlers, so an event that is triggered afterwards is not recorded any more. Stopped or disposed recordings Call .UntilDisposed() before the first expectation: on a recording that an expectation already stopped, it throws an InvalidOperationException. An expectation on a disposed recording throws as well.

Describes the possible expectations for a Task or ValueTask that is passed to Expect.That directly. Expectation Negated Summary Throws, … DoesNotThrow the running Task or ValueTask faults, as for a delegate ExecutesIn the rest of the running task completes within the expected time expectations on T the result of a Task<T> or ValueTask<T> meets them That<Task>(…) expectations on the task object itself

A Task or ValueTask is treated like a delegate: an asynchronous operation without return value that is already running. All expectations for a delegate without return value are available: Task ImportAlbumAsync(string title) => Task.CompletedTask; await That(ImportAlbumAsync("Abbey Road")).DoesNotThrow(); await That(Task.FromException(new CustomException("Yesterday"))).Throws<CustomException>(); The task is already running, so ExecutesIn only measures the remaining time and a timeout only stops waiting for it, see outcome. Pass a delegate (That(() => ImportAlbumAsync("Abbey Road"))) to measure or cancel the whole execution. A ValueTask is consumed by Expect.That, so it must not be awaited anywhere else.

A Task<T> or ValueTask<T> behaves differently: it is awaited and its result becomes the subject, so all expectations for T are available. To check the exception or the execution time of such a task, wrap it in a lambda (() => task), which turns it into a delegate: Task<int> playCount = Task.FromResult(42); await That(playCount).IsEqualTo(42); await That(() => playCount).DoesNotThrow();

An expectation for an object, such as IsNotNull(), does not check what a task passed to That(task) does, so the analyzer rule aweXpect0004 reports it as an error. To make an expectation about the task object rather than about what it does, state the type explicitly: await That<Task>(task).IsNotNull();

A task, like an asynchronous delegate, is awaited, so when it faults with several exceptions (e.g. from Task.WhenAll), only the first one counts as thrown, just as with await. A failure message lists the others under "Other exceptions".
