Describes the possible expectations for collections, e.g. arrays, lists, sets or any other IEnumerable<T>. Page Expectations Equality and containment IsEqualTo, Contains, IsContainedIn, StartsWith, EndsWith Items HasCount, IsEmpty, quantifiers like All() or None(), HasSingle, HasItem Sort order IsInAscendingOrder, IsInDescendingOrder Dictionaries ContainsKey, ContainsValue, Keys, Values and dictionary equality In the overview tables of these pages, "negated comparison" marks a Has… expectation without a negated twin, such as HasCount(): negate the comparison instead, e.g. HasCount().NotEqualTo(3). .NET 8 or later: IAsyncEnumerable<T> On .NET 8 or later, every collection expectation, except the ones for dictionaries, works the same way for an IAsyncEnumerable<T>. The expectation enumerates it asynchronously and passes its cancellation token. CS0121 or an unexpected overload with C# 12 or older Some overloads rely on [OverloadResolutionPriority] to bind as described here, e.g. so that a string is expected as a single item and not as a sequence of characters, or that a params list or a collection expression […] is the expected collection. The attribute only takes effect with C# 13 or later, which is the default only for .NET 9 and later. With an older language version, such a call can bind to a different overload or fail with CS0121, so set <LangVersion> to 13 or latest in a project that targets an older framework.

Several expectations verify that some item matches. They differ in what you can add to them: Expectation Use it when Contains(predicate) a predicate is enough, optionally with how often it matches, e.g. .AtLeast(2) Any().Satisfy(…) the same with a quantifier, which also offers All() and None() Any().ComplyWith(…) the item needs an expectation instead of a predicate, e.g. IsEquivalentTo or a string option HasItem, HasItemThat the position matters (AtIndex(…)); a failure then names the item that was found at the index A failure message shows the predicate as written, while for a nested expectation it describes the expectation, e.g. is greater than 2 for at least one item.

.NET 8 or later Spans can only be passed to Expect.That on .NET 8 or later. On older targets, verify a property of the span, e.g. its Length, synchronously. You can pass a Span<T> or a ReadOnlySpan<T> directly to Expect.That. The items are copied into a SpanWrapper<T>, which implements ICollection<T>, so all collection expectations are available: await That("Help!".AsSpan()).HasCount(5); await That("Help!".AsSpan()).Contains('!'); A span can't be kept across an await, so create it in the statement of the expectation.

.NET 8 or later Before .NET 8, only IsEmpty and IsNotEmpty are available for an ImmutableArray<T>. Call .AsEnumerable() on the array to use the other collection expectations. A default ImmutableArray<T> is treated like a null collection, as the subject and as the expected collection. To tell the two apart, verify its IsDefault property.

Describes the possible expectations for dictionaries. Expectation Negated Summary IsEqualTo IsNotEqualTo has the same entries as the expected dictionary Contains DoesNotContain contains the expected entry ContainsKey DoesNotContainKey contains the expected key ContainsKeys DoesNotContainKeys contains all expected keys (negated: none of them) ContainsValue DoesNotContainValue contains the expected value ContainsValues DoesNotContainValues contains all expected values (negated: none of them) Keys, Values continue with the keys or values as a collection The samples on this page use the following dictionary: Dictionary<string, int> playCounts = new() { { "Let It Be", 42 }, { "Yesterday", 7 } };

You can verify that a dictionary is equal to another one. The entries are compared by key, so the order in which the two dictionaries enumerate them does not matter: Dictionary<string, int> reordered = new() { { "Yesterday", 7 }, { "Let It Be", 42 } }; await That(playCounts).IsEqualTo(reordered); await That(playCounts).IsNotEqualTo(new Dictionary<string, int> { { "Let It Be", 41 } }); The keys are looked up through the dictionary, so its key comparer decides which keys are the same: Dictionary<string, int> ratings = new(StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase) { { "Let It Be", 5 } }; await That(ratings).IsEqualTo(new Dictionary<string, int> { { "LET IT BE", 5 } }); To compare the entries in their enumeration order instead, compare them as a collection of KeyValuePair<TKey, TValue>: SortedDictionary<string, int> sorted = new() { { "Let It Be", 42 }, { "Yesterday", 7 } }; KeyValuePair<string, int>[] expected = [new("Let It Be", 42), new("Yesterday", 7)]; await That(sorted.AsEnumerable()).IsEqualTo(expected); Which key comparers are read The comparer is read from the dictionary types of the framework and from the dictionary that a ReadOnlyDictionary<TKey, TValue> wraps, not from a custom dictionary or a ConcurrentDictionary<TKey, TValue> on .NET Framework. Before .NET 10, the wrapped dictionary is only reached by reflection, so it is not read in a project that enables trimming or Native AOT. For the others, a key of the dictionary that equals no expected key fails the expectation, even when the comparer considers it the same as one.

You can verify that a dictionary contains the expected entry, which is looked up by its key, too: await That(playCounts).Contains("Let It Be", 42); await That(playCounts).Contains(new KeyValuePair<string, int>("Yesterday", 7)); await That(playCounts).DoesNotContain("Let It Be", 7);

You can verify that a dictionary contains the expected key(s) or value(s). Several keys or values can also be given as a collection: await That(playCounts).ContainsKey("Let It Be"); await That(playCounts).ContainsKeys("Let It Be", "Yesterday"); await That(playCounts).DoesNotContainKey("Help!"); await That(playCounts).DoesNotContainKeys("Help!", "Something"); await That(playCounts).ContainsValue(42); await That(playCounts).ContainsValues(42, 7); await That(playCounts).DoesNotContainValue(0); await That(playCounts).DoesNotContainValues(0, 1); await That(playCounts).ContainsKeys(new List<string> { "Let It Be", "Yesterday" }); After ContainsKey or ContainsKeys, you can add expectations on the corresponding value(s). WhoseValues is a collection of the values for the expected keys, so all collection expectations are available: await That(playCounts).ContainsKey("Let It Be").WhoseValue.IsEqualTo(42); await That(playCounts).ContainsKeys("Let It Be", "Yesterday").WhoseValues.IsEqualTo([42, 7]); await That(playCounts).ContainsKeys("Let It Be", "Yesterday") .WhoseValues.All().ComplyWith(v => v.IsPositive()); The values, also the value of an entry, are compared with the same options as the items of a collection, e.g. IgnoringCase() for strings or a tolerance with Within: Dictionary<int, string> titles = new() { { 1, "Let It Be" }, { 2, "Yesterday" } }; Dictionary<string, double> durations = new() { { "Let It Be", 3.85 }, { "Yesterday", 2.07 } }; await That(titles).ContainsValue("let it be").IgnoringCase(); await That(titles).ContainsValues("LET IT BE", "YESTERDAY").IgnoringCase(); await That(titles).Contains(1, "LET IT BE").IgnoringCase(); await That(durations).Contains("Yesterday", 2.0).Within(0.1); DoesNotContainKeys and DoesNotContainValues mean "none of": they fail as soon as the dictionary contains one of them. This is stricter than negating ContainsKeys or ContainsValues with DoesNotComplyWith, which is the exact inverse ("not all") and only fails when the dictionary contains all of them: await That(playCounts).DoesNotComplyWith(d => d.ContainsKeys("Let It Be", "Help!")) .Because("the key \"Help!\" is missing, although \"Let It Be\" is contained"); await That(playCounts).DoesNotContainKeys("Help!", "Something") .Because("none of the keys is contained, while adding \"Let It Be\" would fail");

C# 14 or later Keys and Values are extension properties, which need C# 14 or later, the default only for .NET 10 and later. With an older language version, pass the keys or values themselves, e.g. That(playCounts.Values).All().AreUnique(); the keys then no longer use the key comparer of the dictionary. You can continue with expectations on the keys or on the values of a dictionary: await That(playCounts).Keys.Contains("Let It Be"); await That(playCounts).Values.All().AreUnique(); The keys keep the key comparer of the dictionary, so e.g. Keys.Contains("LET IT BE") succeeds for a key "Let It Be" in a dictionary created with StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase. The keys of a dictionary are unique by design, so its entries are unique as well. To verify that its values are unique, use Values.All().AreUnique(). ConcurrentDictionary on .NET Framework On .NET Framework, the comparer of a ConcurrentDictionary<TKey, TValue> is not read.

Describes how to compare a collection with another collection, and how to verify that it contains, starts with or ends with items. Expectation Negated Summary IsEqualTo IsNotEqualTo has the same items as the expected collection Contains(item) DoesNotContain contains the item, optionally a number of times Contains(predicate) DoesNotContain contains an item that satisfies the predicate Contains(collection) DoesNotContain contains the expected items (a subset) IsContainedIn IsNotContainedIn all its items are contained in the expected collection StartsWith DoesNotStartWith starts with the expected items EndsWith DoesNotEndWith ends with the expected items

You can verify that a collection is equal to another collection: IEnumerable<int> trackNumbers = Enumerable.Range(1, 3); await That(trackNumbers).IsEqualTo([1, 2, 3]); await That(trackNumbers).IsEqualTo([3, 2, 1]).InAnyOrder(); await That(trackNumbers).IsEqualTo([1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3]).IgnoringDuplicates(); await That(trackNumbers).IsEqualTo([3, 3, 2, 2, 1, 1]).InAnyOrder().IgnoringDuplicates(); await That(trackNumbers).IsNotEqualTo([2, 3]); await That(trackNumbers).IsNotEqualTo([4, 3, 2, 1]).InAnyOrder(); Without InAnyOrder() the items are compared in the order in which the collection enumerates them, which is not defined for a set. With IgnoringDuplicates(), only which items occur matters, not how often: every expected item has to be matched by an item of the collection, and every item of the collection has to match an expected item. Multi-dimensional arrays A multi-dimensional array is only equal to an array of the same rank with the same length in every dimension, also with InAnyOrder() or IgnoringDuplicates(), while the other expectations on this page only look at its items. A failed comparison with a collection names an item of such an array by its index in every dimension (e.g. [1,2]). The same holds for equivalency, also when the collection order is ignored.

You can verify that the collection contains a specific item or not: IEnumerable<string> songs = ["Come Together", "Something", "Let It Be"]; await That(songs).Contains("Let It Be"); await That(songs).DoesNotContain("Yesterday"); You can also set occurrence constraints on Contains: IEnumerable<string> playlist = ["Let It Be", "Let It Be", "Let It Be", "Yesterday"]; await That(playlist).Contains("Let It Be").MoreThan(1); await That(playlist).Contains("Let It Be").AtLeast(2); await That(playlist).Contains("Let It Be").Exactly(3); await That(playlist).Contains("Let It Be").AtMost(4); await That(playlist).Contains("Let It Be").LessThan(5); await That(playlist).Contains("Let It Be").Between(1).And(5); await That(playlist).Contains("Yesterday").Once(); await That(playlist).Contains("Let It Be").AtLeast().Twice(); await That(playlist).Contains("Help!").Never(); AtLeast(2.Times()) with the Times() extension from aweXpect.Core reads the same, but the plain number is enough.

You can verify that the collection contains an item that satisfies a condition, with the same occurrence constraints: IEnumerable<int> playCounts = [1, 1, 1, 2]; await That(playCounts).Contains(x => x > 1); await That(playCounts).Contains(x => x == 1).Exactly(3); await That(playCounts).DoesNotContain(x => x >= 42); A quantifier such as Any().Satisfy(…) verifies the same and also accepts a nested expectation, and HasItem verifies the item at an index, see choosing an expectation.

You can verify that a collection contains another collection as a subset: IEnumerable<int> trackNumbers = Enumerable.Range(1, 3); await That(trackNumbers).Contains([1, 2]); await That(trackNumbers).Contains([3, 2]).InAnyOrder(); await That(trackNumbers).Contains([1, 1, 2, 2]).IgnoringDuplicates(); await That(trackNumbers).Contains([3, 3, 1, 1]).InAnyOrder().IgnoringDuplicates(); await That(trackNumbers).Contains([1, 3]).IgnoringInterspersedItems(); Without InAnyOrder the values must appear in the subject in the same order and contiguous, i.e. without other items in between, so [1, 3] is not contained in [1, 2, 3] unless IgnoringInterspersedItems is used. IgnoringDuplicates() works as for equality, except that only the expected items have to be matched. To check for a proper subset, append .Properly() (which would fail for equal collections). InAnyOrder together with IgnoringInterspersedItems InAnyOrder and IgnoringInterspersedItems exclude each other, here and for IsContainedIn: specifying the second one throws an InvalidOperationException.

You can verify that a collection is contained in another collection (the other collection is a superset): IEnumerable<int> trackNumbers = Enumerable.Range(1, 3); await That(trackNumbers).IsContainedIn([1, 2, 3, 4]); await That(trackNumbers).IsContainedIn([4, 3, 2, 1]).InAnyOrder(); await That(trackNumbers).IsContainedIn([1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 4, 4]).IgnoringDuplicates(); await That(trackNumbers).IsContainedIn([1, 4, 2, 3]).IgnoringInterspersedItems(); await That(trackNumbers).IsNotContainedIn([1, 2]); Without InAnyOrder the values must appear in the expected collection in the same order and contiguous, i.e. without other items in between, so [1, 3] is not contained in [1, 2, 3] unless IgnoringInterspersedItems is used. IgnoringDuplicates() works as for equality, except that only the items of the collection have to match. To check for a proper superset, append .Properly() (which would fail for equal collections).

You can verify that a collection starts or ends with other items or not: IEnumerable<string> songs = ["Come Together", "Something", "Let It Be"]; await That(songs).StartsWith("Come Together", "Something"); await That(songs).EndsWith("Let It Be"); await That(songs).DoesNotStartWith("Let It Be"); await That(songs).DoesNotEndWith("Something"); note EndsWith and DoesNotEndWith always enumerate the complete collection.

Instead of the expected items, IsEqualTo, Contains and IsContainedIn (and their negations) also accept one predicate or one expectation per item, with the same options as with expected items: IEnumerable<string> songs = ["Come Together", "Something", "Let It Be"]; await That(songs).IsEqualTo([x => x.Length > 10, x => x == "Something", x => x.EndsWith("Be")]); await That(songs).IsEqualTo([ x => x.IsEqualTo("Let It Be"), x => x.StartsWith("Come"), x => x.IsNotEmpty(), ]).InAnyOrder(); await That(songs).Contains([x => x == "Something", x => x.EndsWith("Be")]); The failure message lists the predicates or expectations as the expected items: using System.Linq.Expressions; IEnumerable<string> songs = ["Two of Us", "Dig a Pony", "Let It Be"]; Expression<Func<string, bool>>[] expected = [x => x == "Two of Us", x => x == "Dig a Pony", x => x == "Let It Be", x => x == "Get Back"]; await That(songs).IsEqualTo(expected); Failure message Expected that songs is equal to collection expected in order, but it lacked 1 of 4 expected items: x => (x == "Get Back") Collection: [ "Two of Us", "Dig a Pony", "Let It Be" ] Expected: [ x => (x == "Two of Us"), x => (x == "Dig a Pony"), x => (x == "Let It Be"), x => (x == "Get Back") ] Predicates with IgnoringDuplicates() Predicates and expectations are never compared with each other. With IgnoringDuplicates(), one item may therefore match several of them, e.g. [5] is equal to [x => x > 0, x => x > 1] in any order ignoring duplicates.

The expectations on this page compare the items with the expected items by their default equality, unless you specify a custom comparer, equivalency, a tolerance or, for strings, one of the string options: IEnumerable<Album> albums = //... Album expected = //... await That(albums).Contains(expected).Equivalent(); await That(albums).StartsWith(expected).Using(new AlbumComparer()); await That(["COME TOGETHER", "SOMETHING"]).EndsWith(["something"]).IgnoringCase(); The rules for sets with a custom comparer apply as well.

A set or a dictionary has no defined order IsEqualTo, Contains with a collection and IsContainedIn compare the items in the order in which the collection enumerates them unless InAnyOrder() is used, so for a HashSet<T>, or for the entries, keys or values of a Dictionary<TKey, TValue>, the result depends on an implementation detail. IsEqualTo on a dictionary itself compares the entries by key instead. The analyzer rule aweXpect0006 warns about it and offers to append .InAnyOrder(). It also warns about StartsWith, EndsWith and IgnoringInterspersedItems(), which have no meaning for such a collection. Sorted sets and dictionaries are not reported. A set that was created with a custom comparer (a HashSet<T>, SortedSet<T>, ImmutableHashSet<T>, ImmutableSortedSet<T> or FrozenSet<T>) compares its items with that comparer. Any other collection, including a set with the default comparer, is compared with the default equality. The comparer of such a set decides in every expectation that compares its items: IsEqualTo, Contains (with an item or a subset), IsContainedIn, HasItem, StartsWith, EndsWith and All().AreEqualTo. Only the comparer of the subject is used, not the one of an expected set. A custom comparer, equivalency, a tolerance or a string option such as IgnoringCase() takes precedence over the comparer of the set, and Using(EqualityComparer<T>.Default) forces the default equality: HashSet<string> albums = new(StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase) { "Help!", "Revolver" }; await That(albums).Contains("HELP!"); await That(albums).IsEqualTo(["REVOLVER", "HELP!"]).InAnyOrder(); await That(albums).IsContainedIn(["REVOLVER", "ABBEY ROAD", "HELP!"]).InAnyOrder(); await That(albums).DoesNotContain("HELP!").Using(StringComparer.Ordinal); await That(albums).IsNotEqualTo(["REVOLVER", "HELP!"]).InAnyOrder().Using(StringComparer.Ordinal); Whenever the comparer of the set decides, the expectation names it, e.g. contains "HELP!" using the subject's StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase at least once. Untyped collections For an untyped IEnumerable, only a set of the expected item type is recognized, e.g. a HashSet<string> for an expected string.

The expectations that compare items with an expected value accept a tolerance for numbers such as int, long, double or decimal, for DateTime, DateTimeOffset and TimeSpan items, and on .NET 8 or later also for DateOnly and TimeOnly: IEnumerable<double> durations = [1.01, 2.02, 3.04]; IEnumerable<int> playCounts = [9, 20, 31]; await That(durations).IsEqualTo([3.0, 2.0, 1.0]).Within(0.1).InAnyOrder(); await That(durations).Contains(2.0).Within(0.1); await That(durations).Contains([2.0, 3.0]).Within(0.1); await That(durations).IsContainedIn([1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0]).Within(0.1); await That(durations).StartsWith(1.0, 2.0).Within(0.1); await That(durations).EndsWith(2.0, 3.0).Within(0.1); await That(durations).HasItem(2.0).Within(0.1).AtIndex(1); await That([2.04, 2.02, 2.01]).All().AreEqualTo(2.0).Within(0.1); await That(playCounts).Contains(10).Within(1); The values of a dictionary accept the same tolerance. For double, float and decimal items, Percent() directly after Within interprets the tolerance as a percentage of each expected item: await That([104.0, 209.0]).IsEqualTo([100.0, 200.0]).Within(5).Percent(); Without Within, the items of the time types use the default tolerance, if one is set. DateOnly and TimeOnly tolerances The tolerance for DateOnly items must be a whole number of days. TimeOnly items are compared on the clock face, so that 23:59 and 00:01 are two minutes apart.

Describes how to verify the number of items, how many items meet an expectation, a single item or the item at an index. Expectation Negated Summary HasCount negated comparison has the expected number of items IsEmpty IsNotEmpty has no items All(), Any(), … use None() the selected number of items meet an expectation HasSingle has exactly one (matching) item HasItem DoesNotHaveItem has the expected item at an index or at any index HasItemThat DoesNotHaveItemThat has an item that meets an expectation at an index or at any index

You can verify the number of items in a collection: IEnumerable<string> songs = ["Come Together", "Something", "Let It Be"]; await That(songs).HasCount(3); await That(songs).HasCount().GreaterThan(2); await That(songs).HasCount().NotBetween(5).And(10); The Has… expectations whose value is a number or a TimeSpan, e.g. HasLength(), HasCount(), HasYear() or HasMajor(), continue with one of the following comparisons, each with a negated counterpart: Comparison Negated Succeeds when the value is EqualTo(x) NotEqualTo(x) equal to x GreaterThan(x) NotGreaterThan(x) greater than x GreaterThanOrEqualTo(x) NotGreaterThanOrEqualTo(x) greater than or equal to x LessThan(x) NotLessThan(x) less than x LessThanOrEqualTo(x) NotLessThanOrEqualTo(x) less than or equal to x Between(min).And(max) NotBetween(min).And(max) between min and max, both bounds included Passing the value directly, e.g. HasCount(3), is a shorthand for EqualTo. Comparing with null The expected value is nullable, e.g. to pass a value mapped from a property. As the actual value is never null, EqualTo(null) fails and NotEqualTo(null) succeeds, while a comparison of order against null, such as GreaterThan(null) or Between(null).And(3), fails even when negated. You can also verify that the collection is empty or not: await That(Array.Empty<Track>()).IsEmpty(); await That(new[] { "Let It Be" }).IsNotEmpty();

You can verify that a certain number of items meet an expectation. A quantifier selects how many: Quantifier Succeeds when the expectation is met by All() every item Any() at least one item (a shorthand for AtLeast(1)) AtLeast(minimum) at least minimum items AtMost(maximum) at most maximum items Between(min).And(max) between min and max items, both bounds included Exactly(expected) exactly expected items LessThan(maximum) fewer than maximum items MoreThan(minimum) more than minimum items None() no item and what the items must meet: Expectation Succeeds for an item that ComplyWith meets the nested expectation Satisfy satisfies the predicate AreEqualTo is equal to the expected value AreEquivalentTo is equivalent to the expected value Are<T> is of type T or a derived type AreExactly<T> is exactly of type T AreUnique occurs exactly once (AreNotUnique: more than once) An empty collection satisfies All(), like it does Enumerable.All, so That(new int[0]).All().Satisfy(x => false) succeeds.

You can verify that items in a collection comply with an expectation on the individual items: IEnumerable<int> playCounts = [1, 2, 3]; await That(playCounts).All().ComplyWith(item => item.IsLessThan(4)); await That(playCounts).Any().ComplyWith(item => item.IsEqualTo(2)); await That(playCounts).AtLeast(2).ComplyWith(item => item.IsGreaterThanOrEqualTo(2)); await That(playCounts).AtMost(1).ComplyWith(item => item.IsNegative()); await That(playCounts).Between(2).And(3).ComplyWith(item => item.IsPositive()); await That(playCounts).Exactly(1).ComplyWith(item => item.IsEqualTo(2)); await That(playCounts).None().ComplyWith(item => item.IsNegative()); Items the nested expectation cannot answer An item for which the nested expectation fails and its negation fails as well decides the result, because the expectation could not answer it: the nested expectation threw (the exception becomes the InnerException), or the item or an inspected member is null. So None().ComplyWith(item => item.StartsWith("Let")) fails for a null item, and so does its negation. The same applies to HasItemThat and to collections compared with item expectations or predicates, where in any order such an item only decides when it matches no other expected item.

You can verify that items in a collection satisfy a condition: Track[] tracks = [new() { Title = "Let It Be", PlayCount = 3 }, new() { Title = "Get Back", PlayCount = 0 }]; await That(tracks).Any().Satisfy(track => track.PlayCount > 0); await That(tracks).None().Satisfy(track => track.Title == null); Contains(predicate) verifies the same as Any().Satisfy(…), and HasItem verifies the item at an index, see choosing an expectation.

You can verify that the items in the collection are equal to the expected value: IEnumerable<string> playlist = ["Let It Be", "Let It Be", "Let It Be"]; await That(playlist).All().AreEqualTo("Let It Be"); The items are compared like in the other collection expectations, so you can specify a custom comparer, equivalency, a tolerance or a string option: IEnumerable<Album> albums = //... Album expected = //... await That(albums).All().AreEqualTo(expected).Equivalent(); await That(albums).All().AreEqualTo(expected).Using(new AlbumComparer()); await That(albums).AtLeast(2).AreEquivalentTo(expected); await That(["let it be", "LET IT BE"]).All().AreEqualTo("Let It Be").IgnoringCase();

You can verify that the items are of a given type, or exactly of that type: IEnumerable<INotification> notifications = //... await That(notifications).All().Are<INotification>(); await That(notifications).AtLeast(1).AreExactly<TrackAddedNotification>(); await That(notifications).None().Are(typeof(TrackRemovedNotification));

You can verify how many items in a collection occur exactly once: await That(["Help!", "Yesterday", "Let It Be"]).All().AreUnique(); await That(["Help!", "Yesterday", "Let It Be", "Help!"]).AtLeast(1).AreNotUnique(); await That(["Help!", "Yesterday", "Help!", "Yesterday"]).None().AreUnique(); await That(["Help!", "Yesterday", "Let It Be", "Get Back", "Michelle", "Michelle"]).AtLeast(4).AreUnique(); For objects, you can also verify the uniqueness of a member, and you can use a custom comparer or ignore the case of strings: Album[] albums = //... await That(albums).All().AreUnique(x => x.Title); await That(albums).All().AreUnique().Using(new AlbumComparer()); await That(["Help!", "Revolver"]).All().AreUnique().IgnoringCase(); For dictionaries, verify the values instead, as the keys are unique by design.

You can verify that the collection contains a single item, and continue with expectations on it with Which: IEnumerable<int> playCounts = [42]; await That(playCounts).HasSingle(); await That(playCounts).HasSingle().Which.IsGreaterThan(41); You can also apply filters for the items: IEnumerable<int> playCounts = [1, 2, 3]; await That(playCounts).HasSingle().Matching(it => it > 2); // Or with generic type: IEnumerable<Artist> artists = //... await That(artists).HasSingle().Matching<Band>(); await That(artists).HasSingle().Matching<Band>(band => band.Members.Count == 4); // Similar to the expectations above, but verify the type exactly: await That(artists).HasSingle().MatchingExactly<Band>(); await That(artists).HasSingle().MatchingExactly<Band>(band => band.Members.Count == 4); The awaited result is the single item: IEnumerable<string> songs = ["Let It Be"]; string song = await That(songs).HasSingle();

You can verify that the collection contains an item that satisfies the expectation on a given index (or any index): IEnumerable<string> songs = ["Two of Us", "Dig a Pony", "Across the Universe", "I Me Mine"]; await That(songs).HasItem("Dig a Pony").AtIndex(1); // at the zero-based index 1 await That(songs).HasItem("Across the Universe").AtIndexFromEnd(1); // zero-based index 1 from the end await That(songs).HasItem(it => it.StartsWith("I Me")); // at any index You can also check that the item matches a specific type: IEnumerable<INotification> values = //... // Verify that the item at index 1 is of type `TrackAddedNotification` await That(values).HasItem().Matching<TrackAddedNotification>().AtIndex(1); // Verify that an item of type `TrackRemovedNotification` for the track with ID 3 exists await That(values).HasItem().Matching<TrackRemovedNotification>(x => x.TrackId == 3); // Similar to the expectations above, but verify the type exactly: await That(values).HasItem().MatchingExactly<TrackAddedNotification>().AtIndex(1); await That(values).HasItem().MatchingExactly<TrackRemovedNotification>(x => x.TrackId == 3); You can also use expectations on the individual items: IEnumerable<string> songs = ["Two of Us", "Dig a Pony", "Across the Universe", "I Me Mine"]; await That(songs).HasItemThat(it => it.IsEqualTo("Dig a Pony")).AtIndex(1); await That(songs).HasItemThat(it => it.StartsWith("Across").And.EndsWith("Universe")); // at any index At any index, HasItem(predicate) and HasItemThat verify the same as Any().Satisfy(…) and Any().ComplyWith(…), see choosing an expectation. Each of these expectations has a negated counterpart. It is satisfied when the index holds a different item, and also when the collection is too short to have an item at that index: IEnumerable<string> songs = ["Two of Us", "Dig a Pony"]; await That(songs).DoesNotHaveItem("I Me Mine").AtIndex(1); await That(songs).DoesNotHaveItem("Two of Us").AtIndex(4); // no item at index 4 await That(songs).DoesNotHaveItem().Matching(it => it.StartsWith("I Me")).AtIndex(1); await That(songs).DoesNotHaveItemThat(it => it.StartsWith("I Me")).AtIndex(1);

Describes how to verify that the items of a collection are sorted. Expectation Negated Summary IsInAscendingOrder IsNotInAscendingOrder the items are sorted ascending IsInDescendingOrder IsNotInDescendingOrder the items are sorted descending

You can verify that a collection is (or is not) sorted in ascending or descending order: IEnumerable<int> trackNumbers = [1, 2, 3]; IEnumerable<int> shuffledTrackNumbers = [1, 3, 2]; await That(trackNumbers).IsInAscendingOrder(); await That(shuffledTrackNumbers).IsNotInAscendingOrder(); await That(["Let It Be", "Help!", "Abbey Road"]).IsInDescendingOrder(); await That(["Help!", "Abbey Road", "Let It Be"]).IsNotInDescendingOrder(); You can also specify a custom comparer: await That(["abbey road", "Help!", "let it be"]).IsInAscendingOrder() .Using(StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase); For objects, you can also verify the sort order on a member: Album[] albums = //... await That(albums).IsInAscendingOrder(x => x.Title); Strings are compared ordinally by default, also in an untyped collection. A SortedSet<T> or ImmutableSortedSet<T>, and the keys of a sorted dictionary, are ordered by their own comparer, unless a comparer or a member is specified. Mixed DateTimeKind values A DateTime sequence that mixes Utc and Local values fails, also when negated, unless a custom comparer is used. The order of Utc and Local values depends on the time zone, so such a sequence fails the check in both forms. This also applies to a DateTime member and to an untyped collection. Values with DateTimeKind.Unspecified are compatible with both kinds.

This library will never be able to cope with all ideas and use cases. Therefore, it is possible to use the aweXpect.Core package and write your own extensions. This package aims to be more stable than the main aweXpect package, to reduce the risk of version conflicts between different extensions. .NET CLI PackageReference Central Package Management dotnet add package aweXpect.Core --prerelease <PackageReference Include="aweXpect.Core" Version="4.0.0-pre.3" /> Directory.Packages.props <PackageVersion Include="aweXpect.Core" Version="4.0.0-pre.3" /> Project file <PackageReference Include="aweXpect.Core" /> Latest version: 4.0.0-pre.3 Namespaces used on this page using System.Text; The samples on this and the following pages verify tracks of the following type, such as "Love Me Do" (2:22) or "Hey Jude" (7:11): public record Track(string Title, TimeSpan Duration);

If you want to verify that a Track is radio friendly, i.e. that it lasts at most three minutes, the simplest way is a method that checks the condition, marked with [GenerateExpectation]: using aweXpect.Core.Extending; public static partial class ThatTrack { [GenerateExpectation("Is{Not}RadioFriendly", "is {not} radio friendly")] private static bool IsRadioFriendly(Track track) => track.Duration <= TimeSpan.FromMinutes(3); } The source generator in aweXpect.Core writes IsRadioFriendly() and IsNotRadioFriendly() with their failure messages, see generated expectations. With [GenerateCollectionExpectation], the same method also verifies the items of a collection, e.g. That(tracks).All().AreRadioFriendly(). When an expectation needs more than a condition, e.g. options, a different result or a nested expectation, write it yourself as described in the rest of this section.

You can extend the expectations for any types, by adding extension methods on IThat<TType>. To write IsRadioFriendly yourself, you specify the following method signature: /// <summary> /// Verifies that the <paramref name="subject"/> is radio friendly, /// i.e. that it lasts at most three minutes. /// </summary> public static AndOrResult<Track, IThat<Track?>> IsRadioFriendly(this IThat<Track?> subject) { // ... } The result type decides how the expectation can continue: AndOrResult allows combining it with further expectations using .And and .Or.

The next step is to extract the ExpectationBuilder. In order to keep the automatic code suggestions for developers clear, IThat<TType> doesn't show it. The Get() extension method in the aweXpect.Core.Extending namespace gives access to it. This namespace holds the helpers for extension authors that extend types every user sees, so they only appear where you import it. You can then use the ExpectationBuilder to add an IsRadioFriendlyConstraint: using aweXpect.Core.Extending; public static partial class ThatTrack { public static AndOrResult<Track, IThat<Track?>> IsRadioFriendly(this IThat<Track?> subject) => new(subject.Get().ExpectationBuilder.AddConstraint((it, grammars) => new IsRadioFriendlyConstraint(it, grammars)), subject); } The factory receives the name of the subject (it) and the grammars of the sentence, which the constraint uses to write its part of the failure message.

The constraint decides whether the subject meets the expectation and writes its part of the failure message. Declare it as a nested class of ThatTrack, next to the expectation, and derive it from the helper class ConstraintResult.WithNotNullValue<Track>, which fails the expectation for a null track: private sealed class IsRadioFriendlyConstraint(string it, ExpectationGrammars grammars) : ConstraintResult.WithNotNullValue<Track>(it, grammars), IValueConstraint<Track?> { public ConstraintResult IsMetBy(Track? actual) { Actual = actual; Outcome = actual?.Duration <= TimeSpan.FromMinutes(3) ? Outcome.Success : Outcome.Failure; return this; } protected override void AppendNormalExpectation(StringBuilder stringBuilder, string? indentation = null) => stringBuilder.Append("is radio friendly"); protected override void AppendNormalResult(StringBuilder stringBuilder, string? indentation = null) { stringBuilder.Append(It).Append(" was "); Formatter.Format(stringBuilder, Actual?.Duration); stringBuilder.Append(" long"); } protected override void AppendNegatedExpectation(StringBuilder stringBuilder, string? indentation = null) => stringBuilder.Append("is not radio friendly"); protected override void AppendNegatedResult(StringBuilder stringBuilder, string? indentation = null) { stringBuilder.Append(It).Append(" was "); Formatter.Format(stringBuilder, Actual?.Duration); stringBuilder.Append(" long"); } } IsMetBy receives the track, keeps it as Actual and decides the Outcome. AppendNormalExpectation writes the expectation text and AppendNormalResult the result text of the failure message. The negated variants write them for the negated expectation, e.g. in DoesNotComplyWith(t => t.IsRadioFriendly()). Constraints and results explains the other kinds of constraints and results, and message conventions how the texts should read.

A test project that references your extension and aweXpect calls the expectation like a built-in one. As ThatTrack is in the namespace aweXpect (see namespace and class names), the test needs no further using: [Test] public async Task Track_ShouldBeRadioFriendly() { Track track = new("Hey Jude", new TimeSpan(0, 7, 11)); await That(track).IsRadioFriendly(); } For "Hey Jude", the test fails with: Failure message Expected that track is radio friendly, but it was 7:11 long
A test project that declares expectations for its own types needs none of this setup: it is for an extension that you publish as a package.

Reference aweXpect.Core in your extension, not aweXpect, and use the lowest version that contains the API you need, so that the extension works together with as many versions of aweXpect as possible. By default, a package marks the analyzers of its dependencies as private (exclude="Analyzers" in its .nuspec). Reference aweXpect.Core with PrivateAssets="contentfiles;build", so that its source generators also run in the projects that use your extension, see Native AOT for extensions: <ItemGroup> <PackageReference Include="aweXpect.Core" Version="…" PrivateAssets="contentfiles;build" /> </ItemGroup>

aweXpect.Core targets netstandard2.0, net8.0 and net10.0, like the extension packages of aweXpect. Include netstandard2.0 in the targets of your extension, so that it also works in test projects on .NET Framework. Keep your extensions trimmable and AOT compatible like aweXpect itself, as described in Native AOT for extensions.

Declare your expectations in the namespace aweXpect, which the users import for Expect.That anyway, so that they need no further using for your extension. Name the class after the subject type, e.g. ThatTrack for the expectations on a Track, and make it partial, so that each expectation can have a file of its own, like ThatJsonElement.HasProperty.cs in aweXpect.Json: namespace aweXpect; public static partial class ThatTrack { // the expectations on a Track }

Some attributes that an extension uses are compiler features that are missing in netstandard2.0 and net48. Declare them as internal types in your own package there: CallerArgumentExpressionAttribute (C# 10) shows the code of the caller in the expectation text, see message conventions. ModuleInitializerAttribute (C# 9) runs code before the first expectation, see module initializers. The source generators of aweXpect.Core also need it, see the source generator. namespace System.Runtime.CompilerServices { [AttributeUsage(AttributeTargets.Parameter)] internal sealed class CallerArgumentExpressionAttribute(string parameterName) : Attribute { public string ParameterName { get; } = parameterName; } [AttributeUsage(AttributeTargets.Method)] internal sealed class ModuleInitializerAttribute : Attribute; }

An expectation on a collection reads the subject only once, also together with other expectations, and can verify its items with the quantifiers of aweXpect, such as All() or AtLeast(2). Namespaces used on this page using System.Text; using aweXpect.Core; using aweXpect.Core.Constraints; using aweXpect.Core.EvaluationContext; using aweXpect.Core.Extending; using aweXpect.Formatting; using aweXpect.Options; using aweXpect.Results; using static aweXpect.Formatting.Format;

A constraint that enumerates a collection subject gets it from the IEvaluationContext with UseMaterializedEnumerable instead of enumerating the subject itself. All expectations on the subject, including the built-in ones, then share one lazily materialized copy, so that a subject which can only be enumerated once, e.g. a query or an iterator with side effects, is enumerated at most once, also when the expectations are combined with .And or .Or. Implement IContextConstraint<T> to receive the context: public static AndOrResult<IEnumerable<Track>, IThat<IEnumerable<Track>?>> HasRadioFriendlyTracks( this IThat<IEnumerable<Track>?> subject, int expected) => new(subject.Get().ExpectationBuilder.AddConstraint((it, grammars) => new HasRadioFriendlyTracksConstraint(it, grammars, expected)), subject); private sealed class HasRadioFriendlyTracksConstraint(string it, ExpectationGrammars grammars, int expected) : ConstraintResult.WithNotNullValue<IEnumerable<Track>>(it, grammars), IContextConstraint<IEnumerable<Track>?> { private int _count; public ConstraintResult IsMetBy(IEnumerable<Track>? actual, IEvaluationContext context) { Actual = actual; if (actual is not null) { _count = context.UseMaterializedEnumerable(actual) .Count(track => track.Duration <= TimeSpan.FromMinutes(3)); Outcome = _count == expected ? Outcome.Success : Outcome.Failure; } return this; } protected override void AppendNormalExpectation(StringBuilder stringBuilder, string? indentation = null) => stringBuilder.Append("has ").Append(expected).Append(" radio friendly tracks"); protected override void AppendNormalResult(StringBuilder stringBuilder, string? indentation = null) => stringBuilder.Append(It).Append(" had ").Append(_count).Append(" radio friendly tracks"); protected override void AppendNegatedExpectation(StringBuilder stringBuilder, string? indentation = null) => stringBuilder.Append("does not have ").Append(expected).Append(" radio friendly tracks"); protected override void AppendNegatedResult(StringBuilder stringBuilder, string? indentation = null) => stringBuilder.Append(It).Append(" did"); } await That(tracks).IsNotEmpty().And.HasRadioFriendlyTracks(3) then enumerates tracks only once. For an IAsyncEnumerable<T>, implement IAsyncContextConstraint<T> and call UseMaterializedAsyncEnumerable with its CancellationToken. How the materialized collection behaves Every call for the same subject in the same evaluation returns the same sequence. It reads the subject only as far as it is enumerated, and a further enumeration replays the items read so far before it continues the subject. Once the expectation and its failure message are complete, the enumerator of the subject is disposed, also when it was not read to its end. A subject that already is a collection is returned unchanged. For any other subject, an exception while it is enumerated fails the expectation like one of the code of the caller. An IAsyncEnumerable<T> stays governed by the token of the first call to UseMaterializedAsyncEnumerable.

An expectation on the items of a collection, i.e. an extension method on IEnumerableItems<TItem>, the items that All(), AtLeast(2) and the other quantifiers select, derives from QuantifiedCollectionConstraint<TCollection, TItem>. IEnumerableItems<TItem> gives access to the quantifier and the subject. The built-in expectations on the items, like Satisfy or AreEqualTo, are such extension methods as well. For a condition on a single item, [GenerateCollectionExpectation] generates such an expectation. public static AndOrResult<IEnumerable<Track>, IThat<IEnumerable<Track>?>> AreRadioFriendly( this IEnumerableItems<Track> items) { return new(items.Subject.Get().ExpectationBuilder.AddConstraint((it, grammars) => new AreRadioFriendlyConstraint(it, grammars, items.Quantifier)), items.Subject); } private sealed class AreRadioFriendlyConstraint( string it, ExpectationGrammars grammars, EnumerableQuantifier quantifier) : QuantifiedCollectionConstraint<IEnumerable<Track>?, Track>(it, grammars, quantifier, g => g.IsPlural() ? "are radio friendly" : "is radio friendly", "were"), IContextConstraint<IEnumerable<Track>?> { public ConstraintResult IsMetBy(IEnumerable<Track>? actual, IEvaluationContext context) { StartEvaluation(); Actual = actual; if (actual is not null) { foreach (Track track in context.UseMaterializedEnumerable(actual)) { Record(track, track.Duration <= TimeSpan.FromMinutes(3)); } Complete(); } return this; } } Track[] tracks = [new("Love Me Do", new TimeSpan(0, 2, 22)), new("She Loves You", new TimeSpan(0, 2, 21))]; await That(tracks).All().AreRadioFriendly(); StartEvaluation forgets the items of an earlier evaluation, as the constraint is evaluated again, e.g. by Eventually() or for each item of an outer collection. Record classifies an item as matching or not matching, and Complete decides the outcome from the quantifier. The expectation text is for a single item and is never negated, as the quantifier carries the negation. The Plural grammar asks for the plural form, e.g. in "whose Tracks are radio friendly for at least 2 items". The verb completes the result, e.g. "but only 1 of 3 were". The other collections have their own interfaces: INonGenericEnumerableItems<TCollection> for a non-generic IEnumerable, IStructEnumerableItems<TCollection, TItem> for an ImmutableArray and IAsyncEnumerableItems<TItem> for an IAsyncEnumerable. Strings have no interface of their own: an expectation only for strings extends IEnumerableItems<string?>. The interfaces are covariant in TItem, so an expectation on the items of Track? also applies to the items of a List<Track> or of a collection of a type derived from Track. Extend IEnumerableItems<Track?> to cover both nullabilities. The base class renders the quantifier like the built-in Satisfy, also when negated or nested, and adds the matching or not matching items as context. DoesNotComplyWith(t => t.AtLeast(2).AreRadioFriendly()) then reads "is radio friendly for fewer than 2 items, but 3 of 3 were", followed by the "Matching items". Unlike the built-in expectations, it does not add the "Collection" context. Early completion, nested item results, the base class and overloads The quantifiers return the derived IQuantifiedEnumerableItems<TItem>, which only adds the type checks Are<TType>() and AreExactly<TType>(), whose type argument cannot be inferred. Overload resolution prefers an expectation on IEnumerableItems<string?> over one on IEnumerableItems<TItem>. Call CompleteEarly() instead of Complete() as soon as IsDetermined, to stop reading the items once they decide the outcome. When the items are verified by nested expectations, record the result of each item with Record(item, itemResult), so that the contexts of the item that explains the failure are shown as well, labeled with its index, e.g. Actual (item [2]):. An item result with Outcome.FailureBothWays is neither matching nor not matching, e.g. because the nested expectations threw. Like the built-in ComplyWith, Record(item, itemResult) stops at such an item and fails with its result and the contexts of the item, also when negated. An item result with Outcome.Undecided, e.g. after a canceled evaluation, leaves the outcome undecided. Neither changes an outcome that the items before already determine: IsDetermined is then true, and the remaining items are not counted. When the item expectation or the verb are only known while the failure message is created, e.g. because they come from nested expectations, derive from QuantifiedCollectionConstraintBase<TCollection, TItem> and implement AppendItemExpectation and Verb instead.

When the caller passes expectations for the items, like the built-in ComplyWith, evaluate them with a ManualExpectationBuilder<TItem> and record the result of each item: public static AndOrResult<IEnumerable<Track>, IThat<IEnumerable<Track>?>> AreTracksThat( this IEnumerableItems<Track> items, Action<IThatSubject<Track>> expectations) => new(items.Subject.Get().ExpectationBuilder.AddConstraint((it, grammars) => new AreTracksThatConstraint(it, grammars, items.Quantifier, expectations)), items.Subject); private sealed class AreTracksThatConstraint : QuantifiedCollectionConstraintBase<IEnumerable<Track>?, Track>, IAsyncContextConstraint<IEnumerable<Track>?>, IExpectationTextConstraint { private readonly ManualExpectationBuilder<Track> _itemExpectations; public AreTracksThatConstraint(string it, ExpectationGrammars grammars, EnumerableQuantifier quantifier, Action<IThatSubject<Track>> expectations) : base(it, grammars, quantifier) { _itemExpectations = new ManualExpectationBuilder<Track>(grammars); expectations(new ThatSubject<Track>(_itemExpectations)); } protected override string Verb => _itemExpectations.GetResultVerb(); public async ValueTask<ConstraintResult> IsMetBy(IEnumerable<Track>? actual, IEvaluationContext context, CancellationToken cancellationToken) { StartEvaluation(); Actual = actual; await _itemExpectations.PrepareExpectation(context, cancellationToken); if (actual is not null) { foreach (Track track in context.UseMaterializedEnumerable(actual)) { Record(track, await _itemExpectations.IsMetBy(track, context, cancellationToken)); } Complete(); } return this; } public async ValueTask<ConstraintResult> GetExpectationResult(IEvaluationContext context, CancellationToken cancellationToken) { await _itemExpectations.PrepareExpectation(context, cancellationToken); return this; } protected override void AppendItemExpectation(StringBuilder stringBuilder, ExpectationGrammars grammars, string? indentation) => _itemExpectations.AppendExpectation(stringBuilder, indentation); protected override void AppendNormalExpectation(StringBuilder stringBuilder, string? indentation = null) { base.AppendNormalExpectation(stringBuilder, indentation); _itemExpectations.AppendReasons(stringBuilder); } protected override void AppendNegatedExpectation(StringBuilder stringBuilder, string? indentation = null) { base.AppendNegatedExpectation(stringBuilder, indentation); _itemExpectations.AppendReasons(stringBuilder); } } Track[] playlist = [new("Love Me Do", new TimeSpan(0, 2, 22)), new("She Loves You", new TimeSpan(0, 2, 21))]; await That(playlist).All().AreTracksThat(track => track.IsRadioFriendly()); PrepareExpectation writes the text of the nested expectations without evaluating them, so that it is complete also when no item is evaluated, e.g. for an empty or a null collection: otherwise a nested DoesNotComplyWith is shown without its negation, and the reasons that must be awaited are missing. Call it at the start of each evaluation and in GetExpectationResult of IExpectationTextConstraint, which is called when only the expectation text is needed. AppendReasons adds the reasons of the nested expectations after the quantifier, e.g. "for all items, because …". The evaluation context of each item Each item is evaluated with its own values in the IEvaluationContext, while the materialized collections are shared with the whole evaluation.

A collection that the caller passes as the expected value, e.g. the titles a playlist must contain, can also be a query that may only be enumerated once. Enumerate it only once per evaluation: copy it at the start of IsMetBy unless it already is a collection, and use only the copy afterwards, also for the failure message: public ConstraintResult IsMetBy(IEnumerable<Track>? actual, IEvaluationContext context) { Actual = actual; ICollection<string> titles = expected as ICollection<string> ?? expected.ToArray(); if (actual is not null) { _missingTitles = titles .Except(context.UseMaterializedEnumerable(actual).Select(track => track.Title)) .ToList(); Outcome = _missingTitles.Count == 0 ? Outcome.Success : Outcome.Failure; } return this; } The subject itself still goes through UseMaterializedEnumerable, so that it is shared with the other expectations on it, while the expected collection belongs to your constraint alone.

To compare items with an expected collection like the collection IsEqualTo does, get a matcher from CollectionMatchOptions and let VerifyItems run it over the items. It returns the outcome together with the failure text of IsEqualTo, e.g. it lacked 1 of 2 expected items: "Outro", so the caller's choice of InAnyOrder(), IgnoringDuplicates() or IgnoringCase() applies to your expectation as well: public static StringCollectionMatchResult<IEnumerable<Track>, IThat<IEnumerable<Track>?>> HasTitles( this IThat<IEnumerable<Track>?> subject, params string[] expected) { OptionsHolder<StringEqualityOptions> options = new(StringEqualityOptions.Default); OptionsHolder<CollectionMatchOptions> matchOptions = new(CollectionMatchOptions.Default); return new(subject.Get().ExpectationBuilder.AddConstraint((it, grammars) => new HasTitlesConstraint(it, grammars, expected, options, matchOptions)), subject, options, matchOptions); } private sealed class HasTitlesConstraint( string it, ExpectationGrammars grammars, string[] expected, IReadOnlyOptionsHolder<StringEqualityOptions> options, IReadOnlyOptionsHolder<CollectionMatchOptions> matchOptions) : ConstraintResult.WithNotNullValue<IEnumerable<Track>>(it, grammars), IAsyncContextConstraint<IEnumerable<Track>?> { private string? _failure; public async ValueTask<ConstraintResult> IsMetBy(IEnumerable<Track>? actual, IEvaluationContext context, CancellationToken cancellationToken) { Actual = actual; _failure = null; foreach (string title in expected) { options.Value.ValidateExpected(title, nameof(expected)); } if (actual is null) { Outcome = Outcome.Failure; return this; } IEnumerable<string?> titles = context.UseMaterializedEnumerable(actual).Select(track => track.Title); (Outcome, _failure) = await matchOptions.Value.GetCollectionMatcher<string?, string?>(expected) .VerifyItems(It, titles, options.Value.ForEvaluation(context, cancellationToken), cancellationToken); return this; } protected override void AppendNormalExpectation(StringBuilder stringBuilder, string? indentation = null) => stringBuilder.Append("has titles that ").Append(matchOptions.Value.GetExpectation( Formatter.Format(expected, FormattingOptions.SingleLine) + options.Value, ExpectationGrammars.Plural)); protected override void AppendNormalResult(StringBuilder stringBuilder, string? indentation = null) => stringBuilder.Append(_failure); protected override void AppendNegatedExpectation(StringBuilder stringBuilder, string? indentation = null) => stringBuilder.Append("has titles that ").Append(matchOptions.Value.GetExpectation( Formatter.Format(expected, FormattingOptions.SingleLine) + options.Value, ExpectationGrammars.Plural | ExpectationGrammars.Negated)); protected override void AppendNegatedResult(StringBuilder stringBuilder, string? indentation = null) => stringBuilder.Append(It).Append(" did"); } await That(tracks).HasTitles("Intro", "Outro").InAnyOrder() then fails with e.g. but it contained item "Bonus" at index 1 that was not expected. Validate every expected item with ValidateExpected(item, nameof(expected)) of the options before you look at the subject, as above, so that an item the options cannot use, e.g. an invalid regex pattern after AsRegex(), throws whichever items the subject has. A custom match type decides which items it rejects. How the items are verified The items are verified one by one until the matcher fails or is determined, e.g. once all expected items of a containment are found, and then completed. While the matcher and the comparison answer synchronously, the result completes synchronously, too. An exception while the items are enumerated fails the expectation like one of the code of the caller. The outcome stays Undecided when the CancellationToken is canceled before all items are read from their source. A collection that is complete in memory, e.g. an array, is verified completely. VerifyItems takes an IEnumerable<T>, so read the items of an IAsyncEnumerable<T> into a list first.

An expectation that compares the subject with an expected value can use the comparisons of aweXpect, so that the caller chooses the comparison with the same options as for the built-in expectations, e.g. Using(comparer), Equivalent() or IgnoringCase(). Namespaces used on this page using aweXpect.Core; using aweXpect.Formatting; using aweXpect.Options; using aweXpect.Results; using static aweXpect.Formatting.Format;

An expectation that compares the subject for equality, e.g. an IsEqualTo for your own type, adds the equality constraint of IsEqualTo with AddEqualityConstraint from aweXpect.Core.Extending. Return an ObjectEqualityResult that shares the OptionsHolder<ObjectMatchType<T>>, so that the caller can choose the comparison, e.g. with Using(comparer) or a custom match type, and the expectation and the failure read like those of IsEqualTo: public static ObjectEqualityResult<Track?, IThat<Track?>, Track?> IsEqualTo( this IThat<Track?> subject, Track? expected) { OptionsHolder<ObjectMatchType<Track?>> options = new(ObjectMatchType<Track?>.Default); return new ObjectEqualityResult<Track?, IThat<Track?>, Track?>( subject.Get().ExpectationBuilder.AddEqualityConstraint(expected, options), subject, options); } For IsNotEqualTo, pass isNegated: true. A null subject is never equal to an expected value that is not null, whatever the comparison. To show the code of the caller instead of the formatted value, e.g. "is equivalent to expected" like IsEquivalentTo, pass the value of a [CallerArgumentExpression] parameter as expectedExpression. How the expected expression is shown Its common leading whitespace is removed, and an expected null is still shown as <null>.

IsEqualTo compares two values with Equals, unless the caller chooses another comparison, e.g. with .Equivalent(). You can offer a comparison of your own: derive from ObjectMatchType<TElement>, pass the name of your option to its base constructor and set it on the options of the result with SetMatchType(matchType), which reads that name. For example, two tracks with the same title can count as equal: public static TSelf ByTitle<TSelf, TElement>(this IObjectEqualityResult<TSelf, TElement> result) where TSelf : IObjectEqualityResult<TSelf, TElement> { result.Options.SetMatchType(new ByTitleMatchType<TElement>()); return (TSelf)result; } private sealed class ByTitleMatchType<TElement>() : ObjectMatchType<TElement>("ByTitle") { private static readonly ByTitleMatcher Matcher = new(); public override MatchPhrase Phrase { get; } = MatchPhrase.Being("titled like").WithName(" by title"); public override ObjectMatcher<TElement> ForEvaluation(MatchEnvironment environment) => Matcher; private sealed class ByTitleMatcher : ObjectMatcher<TElement, Track> { public override ValueTask<MatchResult> Match(TElement actual, Track expected) => new(MatchResult.From(actual is Track track && track.Title == expected.Title)); public override string GetFailure(string it, ExpectationGrammars grammars, TElement? actual, Track expected, MatchResult result, string? indentation) => $"{it}{grammars.SubjectVerb(it, " was", " were")} titled {Formatter.Format((actual as Track)?.Title)}"; } } Track track = new("Hey Jude", new TimeSpan(0, 7, 11)); await That(track).IsEqualTo(new Track("Hey Jude", new TimeSpan(0, 7, 4))).ByTitle(); ForEvaluation returns the matcher for one evaluation. A matcher without state can be shared, as above. Match decides whether two values match, and GetFailure writes the result text of a mismatch. Phrase holds the words of the comparison, from which Core writes the expectation text in every grammar, e.g. "is titled like …", "are not titled like …" or "has item titled like …". When the result text of GetFailure spans several lines, indent the lines after the first by the indentation, e.g. with FormattingOptions.Indented(indentation) for a formatted value, so that it stays aligned inside Expect.ThatAll. Override ValidateExpected(expected, parameterName) to reject an expected value that the match type cannot use, with an ArgumentException for the parameterName it receives, as neither the match type nor the options know the parameter of the expectation. For strings, derive from StringMatchType instead and set it with SetMatchType(matchType, nameof(AsTitle)) on the StringEqualityOptions, which takes the name of your option, as a string match type carries none. Declare the settings that a string match type honors in SupportedSettings: Core rejects every other one, e.g. "IgnoringCase cannot be combined with AsTitle.". The whitespace options are supported unless you leave them out. Matchers, results, phrases and string match types in detail ForEvaluation receives the context and the cancellation of the evaluation in the MatchEnvironment. ObjectMatcher<TElement, TExpected> compares with expected values of a known type, e.g. a Track, and an expected value of another type never matches. Derive from ObjectMatcher<TElement> instead when the type of the expected value varies, e.g. an anonymous object for an equivalency, and implement the generic Match<TExpected>. Match returns MatchResult.Match, MatchResult.NoMatch, or MatchResult.NotComparable(reason) for a subject that it cannot compare at all. The expectation and its negation then both fail, with the reason as the result. Like PredicateResult.FailureBothWays, the reason follows "it". Inside Whose it follows the member name instead, and in a collection "an item", so name the value in the reason as well. A comparison that finds more than the values show, e.g. the differences of two documents, returns MatchResult.NoMatchBecause(explanation) with a MatchExplanation of its own, which the default GetFailure writes. MatchWithExplanation compares for a failure message, while Match only decides, e.g. for each item of a collection; override it when explaining costs more than deciding. MatchPhrase.Being(comparison) reads "is …", MatchPhrase.Verb(singular, plural, participle) has a verb of its own, e.g. "starts with", and MatchPhrase.EqualTo is the equality, which the text of a single item may leave out, e.g. "contains 3". WithName names the match type in a short description of the options, and WithSuffix follows the expected value, e.g. " using TitleComparer". For a string match type, WithPattern(kind, noun) marks the expected value as a pattern, e.g. wildcard "Let*" for an expected item, and WithUnformattedExpected() writes it as it is instead of quoting it, e.g. a JSON document. The matcher can add contexts that explain a failure in AppendContexts, e.g. the options of the comparison. A string matcher only adds them to a failure of the string comparison, also for an item of a collection or a member inside Whose, and not to a failure of another expectation on the same subject. A constraint of your own that compares strings with StringEqualityOptions forwards these contexts from its AppendContexts with options.AppendContexts(contexts), on the options of its evaluation. The ForEvaluation of a StringMatchType also receives the StringMatchSettings, i.e. whether the casing is ignored and the comparer of the caller, and its StringMatcher compares the values after the whitespace options are applied. Core appends these options to the expectation text, e.g. "starts with "Let it" ignoring case". A string match type can also tell Core where its expected value lines up with the subject (Anchors, e.g. a prefix only at the start), count the occurrences of the expected value for a quantified Contains (CountOccurrences of the matcher), and whether a failure lists the differing lines or hints at a different newline style. Through its name, the same option again replaces the earlier match type, and combining it with another comparison throws, e.g. "ByTitle cannot be combined with Equivalent.". Core rejects an unsupported setting of a string match type at the call that specifies the conflict, in either order. The ValidateExpected of a match type is called for every subject, also when nothing is compared with the expected value, e.g. for an empty collection. The items of a collection are compared one after the other with the matcher of the evaluation, so a matcher may keep state across them, e.g. which options matched nothing in any comparison, and report it in AppendContexts. Keep what a single comparison found in its MatchExplanation instead, as a collection compares many items before it explains one. An EquivalencyMatchType<T> compares like IsEquivalentTo. A constraint compares with the matcher that ForEvaluation(new MatchEnvironment(context, cancellationToken)) returns for its evaluation, e.g. with CompareWithExplanation(actual, expected), so that the timeout and the cancellation of the evaluation also end the expectations of an It.Is… in the expected object. It also appends its contexts from this matcher, as only it knows what the comparisons found, e.g. a member to ignore that matched no member.

In the constraint, compare with the options of the evaluation: Compare with the options that ForEvaluation(context, cancellationToken) returns for its evaluation, so that the match type can use the evaluation and keep what its comparisons found. MatchWithExplanation(actual, expected, nameof(expected)) returns a MatchResult, which the constraint keeps for its failure message, as the options keep nothing of a comparison. The string options carry no parameter name: the members that can reject the expected value, e.g. an invalid regex pattern, take the name of the parameter that the ArgumentException reports, e.g. ValidateExpected(expected, nameof(expected)), MatchWithExplanation(…), AreConsideredEqual(actual, expected, nameof(expected)) or CountOccurrences(…). The StringEqualityOptions also write the texts for every match type: GetExpectation(expected, grammars) the expectation and GetExtendedFailure(it, grammars, actual, expected, result) the result, e.g. "it was "Yesterday", which differs …". When the string is a member of the subject, GetExtendedMemberFailure(it, "title", grammars, actual, expected, result) names it like the built-in expectations do, e.g. "it had title "Yesterday", which differs …". For the index options, call MatchesIndex(index, count) on the CollectionIndexOptions for each item, with the number of items or null while it is not known yet. Only true means that the item is at the expected index: null means that a later item could still be, and false that no later item can be, so you can stop there.

An expectation on a property of the subject, e.g. the duration of a track, can return a result that offers the same operators as the built-in property expectations like HasLength(): EqualTo, GreaterThan, Between(…).And(…) and their Not… counterparts, with the same argument checks and texts. Implement the interface for the type of the property: Property type Interface Operators int IIntPropertyResult<TResult> equality, ordering, Between and their negations long ILongPropertyResult<TResult> equality, ordering, Between and their negations double IDoublePropertyResult<TResult, TToleranceResult> equality, ordering, Between and their negations decimal IDecimalPropertyResult<TResult, TToleranceResult> equality, ordering, Between and their negations TimeSpan ITimeSpanPropertyResult<TResult> equality, ordering, Between and their negations an enum IEnumPropertyResult<TResult, TEnum> EqualTo, NotEqualTo string see String properties The operators are extension methods in the aweXpect namespace. They check the arguments with your Validation, which receives the value and the name of its parameter, e.g. minimum, and pass a PropertyComparison<T> to your Compare method. Compare adds the constraint and returns TResult, the result the caller continues with. Implement the interface explicitly, so that its members do not show up next to the operators: public class DurationResult(IThat<Track?> subject) : ITimeSpanPropertyResult<AndOrResult<Track, IThat<Track?>>> { Action<TimeSpan?, string>? ITimeSpanPropertyResult<AndOrResult<Track, IThat<Track?>>>.Validation => null; AndOrResult<Track, IThat<Track?>> ITimeSpanPropertyResult<AndOrResult<Track, IThat<Track?>>>.Compare( PropertyComparison<TimeSpan> comparison) => new(subject.Get().ExpectationBuilder.AddConstraint(comparison, static (c, it, grammars) => new HasDurationConstraint(it, grammars, c)), subject); } An expectation that returns this result, e.g. HasDuration(), then reads That(track).HasDuration().Between(TimeSpan.FromMinutes(2)).And(TimeSpan.FromMinutes(4)). In the constraint, comparison.Evaluate(actual) returns the Outcome, and comparison.AppendExpectation(stringBuilder) writes the comparison, e.g. "between" and both values. IsNegated tells that the operator is a negated one, e.g. NotGreaterThan: the outcome already includes the negation, but the text does not, so that you can place the "not" where your sentence needs it, e.g. "has duration not greater than …" or "does not have duration greater than …". The equality operators of a double or decimal property, EqualTo and NotEqualTo, pass a PropertyEqualityComparison<T> to CompareEquality instead, which returns TToleranceResult. The tolerance is set after the operator returned, e.g. .EqualTo(4.5).Within(0.1) or .Within(1).Percent(), so pass comparison.Options to the result you return, e.g. a NumberToleranceResult<TType, TThat, TNumber>, which offers Within. Its text includes the tolerance, e.g. "equal to 4.5 ± 0.1". null and NaN in property comparisons An ordering against null returns Outcome.FailureBothWays. The equality operators of a double or decimal property compare like IsEqualTo(…).Within(…), e.g. NaN is equal to NaN.

The operators of a string property continue with three kinds of results, so they are split over three interfaces, each with its own Validation and Compare method. Implement those whose operators your property offers: Interface Operators Usual TResult IStringEqualityPropertyResult<TResult> EqualTo, NotEqualTo StringEqualityTypeResult<…> IStringAffixPropertyResult<TResult> StartingWith, EndingWith, their negations, NotContaining StringEqualityResult<…> IStringOccurrencePropertyResult<TResult> Containing, with a quantifier such as AtLeast(2) StringOccurrenceCountResult<…> Compare receives a StringPropertyComparison. The string options are set on your result after the operator returned it, e.g. .IgnoringCase(), so pass comparison.Options, and for Containing also comparison.Quantifier, to the result you return, and evaluate the comparison only in your constraint: public class TitleResult(IThat<Track?> subject) : IStringAffixPropertyResult<StringEqualityResult<Track, IThat<Track?>>> { Action<string?, string>? IStringAffixPropertyResult<StringEqualityResult<Track, IThat<Track?>>>.Validation => null; StringEqualityResult<Track, IThat<Track?>> IStringAffixPropertyResult<StringEqualityResult<Track, IThat<Track?>>>.Compare( StringPropertyComparison comparison) => new(subject.Get().ExpectationBuilder.AddConstraint(comparison, static (c, it, grammars) => new HasTitleConstraint(it, grammars, c)), subject, comparison.Options); } An expectation that returns this result, e.g. HasTitle(), then reads That(track).HasTitle().StartingWith("let").IgnoringCase(). In the constraint, call comparison.ValidateExpected() before you look at the subject, so that an unusable expected value, e.g. an invalid regex pattern, throws whichever value the subject has. Then await comparison.Evaluate(actual, context, cancellationToken) compares the value with the options of the evaluation and returns a StringPropertyOutcome, whose Outcome already includes the negation of an operator like NotStartingWith. comparison.AppendExpectation(stringBuilder, grammars) writes the comparison with its options, e.g. "starting with "let" ignoring case", or "starts with …" with ExpectationGrammars.Active, and outcome.AppendResult(stringBuilder, "title", grammars, indentation) writes the result, e.g. "title was "Yesterday", which differs at index 0: …". Like for the other property types, neither text includes the negation of the operator, so that you can place it where your sentence needs it: for a comparison that IsNegated, add ExpectationGrammars.Negated to the grammars, e.g. grammars.Negate(), which writes "not starting with …" or "does not start with …". outcome.AppendContexts(contexts) adds the contexts of the options. A null string property A null value fails a comparison that looks into the value, e.g. a prefix or an occurrence, both ways.

An operator of your own for any of these property types, except string, passes the comparison that PropertyComparison<T>.Satisfying(predicate, expectation) creates to Compare, like the built-in operators do. It works on every result that implements the interface, also on those of aweXpect.Core and of other packages. For example, the day of the week on which an album was released can be on a weekend: public static TResult OnWeekend<TResult>(this IEnumPropertyResult<TResult, DayOfWeek> result) => result.Compare(PropertyComparison<DayOfWeek>.Satisfying( static day => day is DayOfWeek.Saturday or DayOfWeek.Sunday, "on a weekend")); public static TResult NotOnWeekend<TResult>(this IEnumPropertyResult<TResult, DayOfWeek> result) => result.Compare(PropertyComparison<DayOfWeek>.Satisfying( static day => day is DayOfWeek.Saturday or DayOfWeek.Sunday, "on a weekend", isNegated: true)); The predicate receives the value of the property, which is null when the property is. The expectation is the text of the comparison without its negation and follows the name of the property, e.g. "has release day on a weekend" or "whose release day is on a weekend". For a negated operator pass isNegated: true with the same predicate and text: the comparison is then met when the predicate does not hold, and the result places the "not", e.g. "does not have release day on a weekend" or "whose release day is not on a weekend". Create a comparison that does not depend on an argument once and reuse it, as it is immutable.

A constraint decides whether the subject meets the expectation, and its result writes the failure message. This page shows the kinds of constraints and results, and the rules they follow for negation, null subjects and side effects. Namespaces used on this page using System.Text; using System.Threading; using System.Threading.Tasks; using aweXpect.Core; using aweXpect.Core.Constraints; using aweXpect.Core.EvaluationContext; using aweXpect.Formatting; using aweXpect.Results; using static aweXpect.Formatting.Format;

The basis for expectations are constraints. You can add different constraints to the ExpectationBuilder that is available for the IThat<T>. They differ in the input and output parameters for the IsMetBy method: Constraint IsMetBy receives Use it IValueConstraint<T> the actual value for a synchronous check IAsyncConstraint<T> the actual value and a CancellationToken for asynchronous work or to observe the timeout IContextConstraint<T>, IAsyncContextConstraint<T> additionally an IEvaluationContext to share data, to read a collection once or for side effects IsMetBy returns a ConstraintResult, which decides the outcome and writes the expectation and the result texts of the failure message. The evaluation context The IEvaluationContext allows storing and receiving data between expectations. This mechanism is used for example to avoid enumerating an IEnumerable multiple times across multiple constraints. A value stored while an item of a collection or a member after Whose or Which is evaluated is only received by the expectations on that item or member, so a value cached for one item is not handed to the next one. Its Cancellation describes the cancellation of the evaluation: the Token (the same token that an asynchronous constraint receives), the effective Timeout, and the Reason of a cancellation: None, the Timeout, or the Caller. With OnCompleted, a constraint registers a callback that runs when the whole expectation is decided, see side effects.

An IAsyncConstraint<T> receives the CancellationToken of the expectation, which is canceled when the timeout (WithTimeout) elapses or the caller cancels (WithCancellation). Pass it on to the asynchronous work: public async ValueTask<ConstraintResult> IsMetBy(Track? actual, CancellationToken cancellationToken) { Actual = actual; if (actual is not null) { Outcome = await IsInCatalogAsync(actual, cancellationToken) ? Outcome.Success : Outcome.Failure; } return this; } An OperationCanceledException from that token needs no handling: a timeout fails the expectation with "did not finish within …", and a cancellation by the caller leaves it inconclusive. Stopping without an exception A constraint that stops at the cancellation without throwing leaves its Outcome undecided. A timeout then fails the expectation in the same way. After a cancellation, the helper classes write the result text with AppendUndecidedResult, which you can override. By default it writes "it could not be verified, because the evaluation was already canceled". Leave the Outcome undecided only for a cancellation. An expectation whose outcome stays undecided although nothing was canceled, e.g. because one branch of IsMetBy does not set it or a collection constraint does not call Complete(), fails with "it could not be verified, because the expectation did not decide its outcome". A timeout of your own An expectation that waits for something outside aweXpect with a timeout of its own, e.g. Within(timeout), cancels its wait with CancelAfter of the IEvaluationContext and measures it with GetTimestamp() and GetElapsedTime(…). They all use the clock of the evaluation, which is the real one unless the caller sets another with WithTimeProvider(…), so that the timeout and the measured time agree, also on a virtual clock: using CancellationTokenSource waitCts = CancellationTokenSource.CreateLinkedTokenSource(cancellationToken); context.CancelAfter(waitCts, timeout); long startTimestamp = context.GetTimestamp(); try { await WaitForTrackAsync(actual, waitCts.Token); Outcome = Outcome.Success; } catch (OperationCanceledException) { Outcome = context.Cancellation.HasWaitElapsed(timeout, context.GetElapsedTime(startTimestamp)) ? Outcome.Failure : Outcome.Undecided; } HasWaitElapsed tells a wait that reached its timeout, which fails the expectation, apart from a cancellation by the caller or a shorter timeout of the evaluation, which leave it undecided.

All constraints should also provide the expectations and results for the negated case, so that they are compatible with DoesNotComplyWith. The recommended practice is to use the same class for the constraint and its ConstraintResult, derived from one of the following helper classes: Helper class null subject Use it when the expectation ConstraintResult.WithNotNullValue<T> fails the expectation and its negation inspects the subject ConstraintResult.WithEqualToValue<T> is an ordinary value, compared with the expected compares for equality or identity ConstraintResult.WithValue<T> is not handled handles null itself or has a non-nullable subject All three take the name of the subject (it) and the grammars in their constructor and expose the name as the inherited It property. You set the Actual property in the IsMetBy method and override AppendNormalExpectation, AppendNegatedExpectation and AppendNormalResult. By default, the negated result is described like the normal one; override AppendNegatedResult when it differs, e.g. "it was" for a negated "it was not". WithEqualToValue<T> additionally takes a flag indicating if the expected value is null. The IsRadioFriendlyConstraint of your first expectation derives from ConstraintResult.WithNotNullValue<Track>, as it inspects the subject. The helper classes let .And combine the result texts like the built-in expectations, e.g. "it was 2 and was not even" instead of "it was 2 and it was not even". Pass it to the base class and use the inherited It property. Deriving from ConstraintResult directly A constraint can also derive from ConstraintResult directly. It then writes the texts in AppendExpectation and AppendResult, returns the value in TryGetStoredValue and implements NegateInPlace() itself. This example does not support the negated case: private sealed class IsRadioFriendlyConstraint(string it, ExpectationGrammars grammars) : ConstraintResult(grammars), IValueConstraint<Track?> { private Track? _actual; public ConstraintResult IsMetBy(Track? actual) { _actual = actual; Outcome = actual?.Duration <= TimeSpan.FromMinutes(3) ?
