Outcome.Success : Outcome.Failure; } return this; } protected override void AppendNormalExpectation(StringBuilder stringBuilder, string? indentation = null) => stringBuilder.Append("has title ").Append(options.Value.GetExpectation(expected, ExpectationGrammars.None)); protected override void AppendNormalResult(StringBuilder stringBuilder, string? indentation = null) { stringBuilder.Append(It).Append(" had title "); Formatter.Format(stringBuilder, Actual?.Title); } protected override void AppendNegatedExpectation(StringBuilder stringBuilder, string? indentation = null) => stringBuilder.Append("does not have title ") .Append(options.Value.GetExpectation(expected, ExpectationGrammars.None)); } Track track = new("Let It Be", new TimeSpan(0, 4, 3)); await That(track).HasTitle("let it be").IgnoringCase(); IgnoringCase() is called after the constraint was added, so the constraint reads options.Value only in IsMetBy and in its texts. The string options write the expectation text with the options, e.g. "has title equal to "let it be" ignoring case". The constraint compares with the options of its evaluation, see comparing with the options.

The options of an expectation are an immutable value, e.g. a Quantifier or StringEqualityOptions, in an OptionsHolder<TOptions>. The holder is a plain reference to the current value: an option replaces the value in the holder, and the value itself never changes, so a value can be shared and stored. Each options type starts from its Default, e.g. Quantifier.Default ("at least once") or StringEqualityOptions.Default. Create the holder in your expectation, e.g. new OptionsHolder<Quantifier>(Quantifier.Default), and pass it to your constraint and to your result. A result declares which options it offers by implementing IOptionsProvider<TOptions>, which returns this holder. The constraint reads holder.Value when it evaluates, never when it is built, as the options are set on the result after the constraint was added; a constraint that only reads the options can take the holder as a covariant IReadOnlyOptionsHolder<TOptions>. Pass your result as TSelf to AndOrResult<TType, TThat, TSelf>, so that Because(…), WithTimeout(…) and WithCancellation(…) also return your result and the options can still follow them: public class TrackCountResult<TThat>( ExpectationBuilder expectationBuilder, TThat returnValue, OptionsHolder<Quantifier> quantifier, OptionsHolder<StringEqualityOptions> options) : AndOrResult<IEnumerable<Track>, TThat, TrackCountResult<TThat>>(expectationBuilder, returnValue), IOptionsProvider<Quantifier>, IOptionsProvider<StringEqualityOptions> { OptionsHolder<Quantifier> IOptionsProvider<Quantifier>.Options => quantifier; OptionsHolder<StringEqualityOptions> IOptionsProvider<StringEqualityOptions>.Options => options; } An expectation that returns this result then offers the count and the string options, e.g. .ContainsTitle("let it be").IgnoringCase().AtLeast(2). Options Offered by implementing AtLeast, Between, Once, … IOptionsProvider<Quantifier> IgnoringCase, Using, … IOptionsProvider<StringEqualityOptions> AsRegex, AsWildcard additionally IStringPatternMatchTypeOptions AsPrefix, AsSuffix additionally IStringMatchTypeOptions, which includes the pattern marker InAnyOrder, IgnoringDuplicates IOptionsProvider<CollectionMatchOptions> IgnoringInterspersedItems, Properly additionally ICollectionContainmentOptions, IProperContainmentOptions AtIndex, AtIndexFromEnd IOptionsProvider<CollectionIndexOptions> Using, Equivalent IObjectEqualityResult<TSelf, TElement> Within on items IObjectEqualityWithToleranceResult<TSelf, TElement, TTolerance> Within on numbers INumberToleranceResult<TSelf, TNumber> Within on times IOptionsProvider<TimeTolerance> The interfaces with TSelf let the compiler infer the element type from your result, so pass your result type as TSelf. An expectation that already sets an option itself, e.g. StartsWith the match type, returns a result that does not offer it again. Creating the holder only when an option is set Most callers set no option, so the holder is often created for nothing. When only your constraint and your result share the holder, the constraint can create it on demand: it implements IOptionsHolderSource<TOptions>, compares with the default options until the result asks for its Holder, and you pass the constraint to the result instead of a holder. AddConstraint(state, constraintBuilder, out constraint) returns the added constraint for this. The results take an IOptionsHolderSource<TOptions>, which a holder implements as well, so both ways work with the same results: public static StringEqualityResult<Track, IThat<Track?>> IsTitled(this IThat<Track?> subject, string expected) => new(subject.Get().ExpectationBuilder.AddConstraint(expected, static (expected, it, grammars) => new IsTitledConstraint(it, grammars, expected), out IsTitledConstraint constraint), subject, constraint); private sealed class IsTitledConstraint(string it, ExpectationGrammars grammars, string expected) : ConstraintResult.WithNotNullValue<Track>(it, grammars), IAsyncContextConstraint<Track?>, IOptionsHolderSource<StringEqualityOptions> { private OptionsHolder<StringEqualityOptions>? _holder; OptionsHolder<StringEqualityOptions> IOptionsHolderSource<StringEqualityOptions>.Holder => _holder ??= new OptionsHolder<StringEqualityOptions>(StringEqualityOptions.Default); private StringEqualityOptions Options => _holder?.Value ?? StringEqualityOptions.Default; public async ValueTask<ConstraintResult> IsMetBy(Track? actual, IEvaluationContext context, CancellationToken cancellationToken) { Actual = actual; if (actual is not null) { bool isEqual = await Options.ForEvaluation(context, cancellationToken) .AreConsideredEqual(actual.Title, expected, nameof(expected)); Outcome = isEqual ? Outcome.Success : Outcome.Failure; } return this; } protected override void AppendNormalExpectation(StringBuilder stringBuilder, string? indentation = null) => stringBuilder.Append("is titled ").Append(Options.GetExpectation(expected, ExpectationGrammars.None)); protected override void AppendNormalResult(StringBuilder stringBuilder, string? indentation = null) { stringBuilder.Append(It).Append(" had title "); Formatter.Format(stringBuilder, Actual?.Title); } protected override void AppendNegatedExpectation(StringBuilder stringBuilder, string? indentation = null) => stringBuilder.Append("is not titled ").Append(Options.GetExpectation(expected, ExpectationGrammars.None)); } Keep creating the holder in the expectation when something else that is built with the expectation reads it as well, e.g. the item matcher of a collection expectation: it would not see a holder that the constraint creates later.

You can also set the options of aweXpect.Core in your own code, e.g. in an option of your own. Each method of an options value that sets an option returns a new value with the option set, e.g. Quantifier.Default.AtLeast(2), and the same methods are extension methods on the holder in the aweXpect.Options namespace, which replace the value in the holder and return the holder, so that calls chain, e.g. result.Options.IgnoringCase().AsPrefix(). The members that only read the options are on result.Options.Value. warning Import aweXpect.Options where you call an option on a holder. Without it, the compiler only finds the user-facing option of the same name in aweXpect, which extends the result and not the holder, and reports CS0311. warning Use the value that an option method returns. Most options types are readonly structs, so a call whose result is discarded, e.g. options.AtLeast(2);, compiles and changes nothing. The analyzer rule aweXpect0009 reports it in a project that references aweXpect. The general rules for options apply to the options of aweXpect.Core as well as to those of your own. For an extension, these details matter as well: Options that set the same thing in different ways throw an InvalidOperationException at the call, with a message like AtMost cannot be combined with AtLeast. or AsSuffix cannot be combined with AsPrefix. The hooks for a strategy of your own are named Set… and take the name of your option, e.g. SetMatchType(matchType, nameof(AsTitle)) on the StringEqualityOptions or SetMatch(match, nameof(AtTrackNumber)) on the CollectionIndexOptions, so that a competing option throws with that name, while the same name again replaces the earlier strategy. An object match type carries its name itself, and SetComparer on the CollectionOrderOptions takes no name, as no other option sets the order. A hook that combines with the earlier calls instead of replacing them, like the predicates of a signal or event filter, is named Add…, e.g. AddPredicate.
documents.s: Setting options in your own code

documents.t: Follow the same rules for an options type of your own: an immutable value with a Default, whose option methods return a new value, and an extension method on its holder per option. For example, a playlist expectation can ignore the bonus tracks and compare in album order or shuffled, but not both: [ImmutableOptions] public readonly struct PlaylistOptions { private readonly string? _orderOption; private PlaylistOptions(string? orderOption, bool ignoresBonusTracks) { _orderOption = orderOption; IgnoresBonusTracks = ignoresBonusTracks; } public static PlaylistOptions Default => default; public bool IgnoresBonusTracks { get; } public bool IsShuffled => _orderOption == nameof(Shuffled); public PlaylistOptions IgnoringBonusTracks(bool ignoreBonusTracks = true) => new(_orderOption, ignoreBonusTracks); public PlaylistOptions InAlbumOrder() => WithOrder(nameof(InAlbumOrder)); public PlaylistOptions Shuffled() => WithOrder(nameof(Shuffled)); private PlaylistOptions WithOrder(string option) { if (_orderOption is not null && _orderOption != option) { throw Tracing.WriteException(new InvalidOperationException( $"{option} cannot be combined with {_orderOption}.")); } return new PlaylistOptions(option, IgnoresBonusTracks); } } public static class PlaylistOptionsHolderExtensions { public static OptionsHolder<PlaylistOptions> IgnoringBonusTracks( this OptionsHolder<PlaylistOptions> holder, bool ignoreBonusTracks = true) { holder.Value = holder.Value.IgnoringBonusTracks(ignoreBonusTracks); return holder; } } The user-facing option extends every result that provides the options and returns it, so that the caller can go on with the result, e.g. .HasTracks(12).IgnoringBonusTracks(): public static TSelf IgnoringBonusTracks<TSelf>(this TSelf result, bool ignoreBonusTracks = true) where TSelf : IOptionsProvider<PlaylistOptions> { result.Options.IgnoringBonusTracks(ignoreBonusTracks); return result; } Mark the options type with [ImmutableOptions], so that the analyzer rule aweXpect0009 reports a call whose returned options are discarded, also for an option method that is an extension method on the type. Default is the value of default(PlaylistOptions), so that an options field that was never set is valid. Throw with Tracing.WriteException, so that it is written to the trace writer of Customize.aweXpect.EnableTracing(…) like the built-in exceptions, and word the message like the built-in ones. When the expectation text names the options, write that text in ToString(): an OptionsHolder<TOptions> returns the same text, so that the expectation can append the holder itself.

A result that can be stored and continued more than once, e.g. a filter of aweXpect.Reflection, must not change when a continuation sets an option. Such a result implements ICopyOnOption<StringEqualityOptions, TSelf> in addition to IOptionsProvider<StringEqualityOptions>: the string options then pass its options with the new option to WithOptions(options), which returns a new result with them in a new holder, while the result they were called on stays unchanged. The quantifiers, e.g. Once(), and the index options AtIndex(…) and AtIndexFromEnd(…) do the same for a result that implements ICopyOnOption<Quantifier, TSelf> or ICopyOnOption<CollectionIndexOptions, TSelf>. A string option of your own, e.g. a preset of several options, passes the new options to OptionsProvider.WithOptions(result, options), so that it keeps a stored result unchanged as well: it returns the copy of a result that implements ICopyOnOption<…> and sets the options in the holder of any other result. public static TSelf IgnoringCaseAndIndentation<TSelf>(this TSelf result) where TSelf : IOptionsProvider<StringEqualityOptions> => OptionsProvider.WithOptions(result, result.Options.Value.IgnoringCase().IgnoringIndentation()); Options on a stored result The new options carry every option set so far, so a repeated option replaces the earlier one and a competing option still throws. Like every constraint, such a result reads its holder when it evaluates: an option that sets the holder directly, without WithOptions, still applies, but it changes the result it was called on.

A TimeToleranceResult<TType, TThat> adds .Within(…) and stores the tolerance in the holder of the TimeTolerance options you pass to it and to your constraint; start the holder with TimeTolerance.Default. For a date without a time of day, such as the release date of an album as a DateOnly, start it with TimeTolerance.Days instead, as the built-in expectations do. public static TimeToleranceResult<DateOnly, IThat<DateOnly>> IsOnSameDayAs( this IThat<DateOnly> subject, DateOnly expected) { OptionsHolder<TimeTolerance> tolerance = new(TimeTolerance.Days); return new(subject.Get().ExpectationBuilder.AddConstraint((it, grammars) => new IsOnSameDayAsConstraint(it, grammars, expected, tolerance)), subject, tolerance); } The caller then allows a difference of whole days, e.g. for the release date of Abbey Road: DateOnly releaseDate = new(1969, 9, 26); await That(releaseDate).IsOnSameDayAs(new DateOnly(1969, 9, 27)).Within(TimeSpan.FromDays(1)); In the constraint, compare with tolerance.Value.GetToleranceOrDefault(). Without .Within(…), it returns the DefaultTimeComparisonTolerance from Customize.aweXpect.Settings(), and for TimeTolerance.Days only its whole days, like the built-in expectations do. Append the tolerance to the expectation text like any other option, e.g. with stringBuilder.Append(tolerance): TimeTolerance.Days writes the whole days that apply, e.g. " ± 1 day", and nothing when there are none.

The basics of asynchronous constraints, the CancellationToken and an undecided outcome, are described in constraints and results. This page shows how an expectation waits for a condition, and how code that has to answer synchronously calls asynchronous code. Namespaces used on this page using System.Text; using aweXpect.Core; using aweXpect.Core.Constraints; using aweXpect.Core.EvaluationContext; using aweXpect.Options; using aweXpect.Results;

An expectation that returns a RepeatedCheckResult<TType, TThat> lets the caller wait for a condition with .Within(timeout) and .CheckEvery(interval), like Satisfies does. Pass the same holder of RepeatedCheckOptions to the result and to the constraint, and make the check with CheckRepeatedly of its value, which honors the options. For a player that starts playing asynchronously: public class Player { public bool IsPlaying { get; private set; } public void Play(string title) => IsPlaying = true; } public static RepeatedCheckResult<Player, IThat<Player?>> IsPlaying(this IThat<Player?> subject) { OptionsHolder<RepeatedCheckOptions> options = new(RepeatedCheckOptions.Default); return new RepeatedCheckResult<Player, IThat<Player?>>(subject.Get().ExpectationBuilder .AddConstraint((it, grammars) => new IsPlayingConstraint(it, grammars, options)), subject, options); } private sealed class IsPlayingConstraint( string it, ExpectationGrammars grammars, OptionsHolder<RepeatedCheckOptions> options) : ConstraintResult.WithNotNullValue<Player>(it, grammars), IAsyncContextConstraint<Player?> { public async ValueTask<ConstraintResult> IsMetBy(Player? actual, IEvaluationContext context, CancellationToken cancellationToken) { Actual = actual; if (actual is not null) { Outcome outcome = await options.Value.CheckRepeatedly(_ => { bool isPlaying = actual.IsPlaying; Outcome = isPlaying ? Outcome.Success : Outcome.Failure; return new ValueTask<bool>(isPlaying != IsNegated); }, context); if (outcome == Outcome.Undecided) { Outcome = Outcome.Undecided; } } return this; } protected override void AppendNormalExpectation(StringBuilder stringBuilder, string? indentation = null) => stringBuilder.Append("is playing").Append(options); protected override void AppendNormalResult(StringBuilder stringBuilder, string? indentation = null) => stringBuilder.Append(It).Append(" was not playing"); protected override void AppendNegatedExpectation(StringBuilder stringBuilder, string? indentation = null) => stringBuilder.Append("is not playing").Append(options); protected override void AppendNegatedResult(StringBuilder stringBuilder, string? indentation = null) => stringBuilder.Append(It).Append(" was playing"); } Player player = new(); _ = Task.Delay(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(1)).ContinueWith(_ => player.Play("Let It Be")); await That(player).IsPlaying() .Within(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(5)).CheckEvery(TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(100)); The check returns whether the expectation is met, so for a negated variant created with .Invert() it returns true when the player is not playing. The helper class inverts the stored Outcome itself. When CheckRepeatedly returns Undecided, because the evaluation was canceled, set the Outcome of the constraint to Undecided as well, as the sample does. Appending the options writes " within …" to the expectation text when Within was specified. Timing, contexts, exceptions and cancellation CheckRepeatedly makes the first check immediately. When IsRepeated is true, because Within set a positive or an infinite timeout, it repeats the check in the interval until it succeeds, and makes the last check at the timeout. The check receives the IEvaluationContext to use. The first check gets the context of the evaluation, every further check a new one, so that a collection taken with UseMaterializedEnumerable is read again instead of replaying the items that a previous check read. An exception of code of the caller called through UserCode.Invoke counts as not met while the check is repeated. When the last check still throws, the expectation fails with that exception. CheckRepeatedly returns the Outcome: Success when a check succeeded, Failure when the last check failed, and Undecided when the evaluation was canceled before the timeout. The cancellation is only observed while waiting for the next check, so the first check is made even when the evaluation is already canceled. A cancellation at the timeout, or by an effective timeout of the evaluation (WithTimeout or TestCancellation.FromTimeout) that is not shorter than Within when the checks started with the evaluation, lets the last check decide. For Undecided, the constraint sets its Outcome to Undecided: the helper class then reports that the expectation could not be verified, and a shorter effective timeout is reported as "did not finish within …".

Some code has to answer synchronously although it calls asynchronous code, e.g. an IEnumerable<T> that filters its items with an asynchronous predicate. Wait there with SynchronousBoundary.Wait from aweXpect.Core.Extending instead of .GetAwaiter().GetResult(): public IEnumerator<Track> GetEnumerator() => _tracks.Where(track => SynchronousBoundary.Wait(() => IsInCatalogAsync(track))).GetEnumerator(); The expectations of aweXpect run on the synchronization context of the caller, e.g. on the UI thread of a WPF or WinForms test. Blocking that thread would deadlock as soon as the asynchronous code continues on it, so Wait starts the operation without the synchronization context and the task scheduler of the caller.

Expectations for types outside the base class library are provided by separate packages. Each package adds extension methods on IThat<T> for its types, so once it is referenced, its expectations appear on That(…) next to the built-in ones. Core extensions live in the aweXpect repository and are released together with aweXpect, always with the same version. Separate extensions have their own repository and release cycle. Package Release Expectations aweXpect.Json core JSON strings, JsonElement, JsonNode and the JSON serialization of objects: IsEqualTo(…).AsJson(), IsValidJson, Matches, HasProperty, IsObject, IsArray, IsJsonSerializable, IsJsonSerializedAs aweXpect.Xml core XML strings, XElement and XDocument: IsEqualTo(…).AsXml(), IsValidXml, Matches, HasAttribute, HasElement aweXpect.Web core HttpRequestMessage, HttpResponseMessage, Uri and IPAddress: HasMethod, HasRequestUri, HasStatusCode, HasHeader, HasContent, HasHost, HasQueryParameter aweXpect.Reflection core assemblies, types and members, for architecture and convention tests aweXpect.Snapshots core strings, objects and public APIs compared with a reviewed snapshot stored next to the test: MatchesSnapshot, MatchesPublicApiSnapshot aweXpect.Logging separate the records of a FakeLogger or FakeLogCollector: Logged, LoggedWarning, DidNotLog, WithMessage, Within, Then aweXpect.Testably separate the file and time systems of Testably.Abstractions: HasFile, HasDirectory, timers, watcher events aweXpect.Mockolate separate interactions with Mockolate mocks: Once, Never, AtLeast, Then, AllInteractionsAreVerified aweXpect.Chronology adds no expectations, but readable TimeSpan and DateTime values like 5.Seconds() or 24.December(2024). It does not depend on aweXpect, and many samples in this documentation use it.

If no package covers your types, you can add expectations yourself with the same API these packages use. Extending aweXpect walks you through your first expectation and the conventions for its failure messages.

aweXpect.Chronology contains extension methods that create TimeSpan, DateTime, DateTimeOffset, DateOnly and TimeOnly values in a readable way, e.g. 5.Seconds() or 24.December(2024). It belongs to the aweXpect family, but does not depend on aweXpect, so you can use it in any code.

.NET CLI PackageReference Central Package Management dotnet add package aweXpect.Chronology <PackageReference Include="aweXpect.Chronology" Version="1.1.0" /> Directory.Packages.props <PackageVersion Include="aweXpect.Chronology" Version="1.1.0" /> Project file <PackageReference Include="aweXpect.Chronology" /> Latest version: 1.1.0 The extension methods are in the aweXpect.Chronology namespace: using aweXpect.Chronology; Target frameworks The package supports .NET Standard 2.0, .NET 8 and .NET 10. The DateOnly and TimeOnly conversions require .NET 8 or later.

Category Methods Example Result TimeSpan units Milliseconds, Seconds, Minutes, Hours, Days 5.Minutes() TimeSpan TimeSpan operators +, -, * (by double), / (by double), unary - 5.Minutes() * 2 TimeSpan Date January … December 24.December(2024) DateTime Time of day At(hours, minutes, [seconds], [milliseconds]), At(TimeSpan) 24.December(2024).At(18, 30) DateTime Kind AsUtc, AsLocal 24.December(2024).AsUtc() DateTime Offset WithOffset(TimeSpan) 24.December(2024).WithOffset(2.Hours()) DateTimeOffset Relative Before, After 3.Hours().Before(25.December(2024)) DateTime .NET 8+ conversions implicit casts to DateOnly / TimeOnly DateOnly d = 24.December(2024); DateOnly / TimeOnly

Add the following extension methods on int and double that allow creating a TimeSpan: .Milliseconds() .Seconds() .Minutes() .Hours() .Days() Traditional: TimeSpan timeout = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(10); With aweXpect.Chronology: TimeSpan timeout = 10.Seconds(); It is also possible to combine multiple extension methods: TimeSpan timeout = 1.Minutes(30.Seconds()); The builder also supports arithmetic operators +, -, * (by double), / (by double) and unary negation: TimeSpan doubled = 5.Minutes() * 2; TimeSpan combined = 1.Minutes() + 30.Seconds(); TimeSpan negative = -10.Seconds();

Add extension methods on int for each month that allow creating a DateTime: Traditional: DateTime time = new DateTime(2024, 12, 24); With aweXpect.Chronology: DateTime time = 24.December(2024); A time of day can be specified with explicit components or a TimeSpan: DateTime time = 24.December(2024).At(18, 30); DateTime preciseTime = 24.December(2024).At(18, 30, 45, 500); DateTime fromTimeSpan = 24.December(2024).At(18.Hours(30.Minutes())); Set the DateTimeKind with AsUtc() or AsLocal(): DateTime utc = 24.December(2024).At(18, 30).AsUtc(); DateTime local = 24.December(2024).At(18, 30).AsLocal(); Combine with TimeSpan extensions to express relative dates with Before or After: DateTime earlier = 3.Hours().Before(25.December(2024)); DateTime later = 3.Hours().After(25.December(2024));
Use WithOffset to attach a UTC offset to a date or date-and-time: DateTimeOffset time = 24.December(2024).At(14, 30).WithOffset(2.Hours());
On .NET 8 and later, the builders implicitly convert to DateOnly and TimeOnly: DateOnly date = 24.December(2024); TimeOnly time = 18.Hours(30.Minutes());
aweXpect.Json extends aweXpect with expectations for JSON strings, JsonElement, JsonNode and the JSON serialization of objects with System.Text.Json.

.NET CLI PackageReference Central Package Management dotnet add package aweXpect.Json --prerelease <PackageReference Include="aweXpect.Json" Version="4.0.0-pre.3" /> Directory.Packages.props <PackageVersion Include="aweXpect.Json" Version="4.0.0-pre.3" /> Project file <PackageReference Include="aweXpect.Json" /> Latest version: 4.0.0-pre.3 The package brings Expect.That with it, but not the expectations for strings, numbers or collections, so reference aweXpect as well, e.g. for the IsEqualTo of IsEqualTo(…).AsJson(). The expectations live in the namespace aweXpect, so using aweXpect; is all you need; only the customization lives in aweXpect.Json. The examples write That(...) instead of Expect.That(...), which needs using static aweXpect.Expect; (see Getting started).

string json = """{"title": "Let It Be", "artist": "The Beatles", "durationSeconds": 243}"""; // compare JSON strings by their structure instead of their formatting string expected = """{ "artist": "The Beatles", "title": "Let It Be", "durationSeconds": 243 }"""; await That(json).IsEqualTo(expected).AsJson(); // verify that a string is valid JSON that matches an expected value await That(json).IsValidJsonMatching(new { title = "Let It Be" }); // verify single values of a JsonElement or JsonNode JsonElement track = JsonDocument.Parse(json).RootElement; await That(track) .HasProperty("title", t => t.IsString("Let It Be")).And .HasProperty("durationSeconds", d => d.IsNumber<int>()).And .DoesNotHaveProperty("password"); // verify the JSON contract of a type, e.g. `record Track(string Title, string Artist)` await That(new Track("Let It Be", "The Beatles")).IsJsonSerializedAs( """{"Title": "Let It Be", "Artist": "The Beatles"}"""); A failing comparison names every difference by its JSON path. If the title was "Yesterday", IsValidJsonMatching would fail with: Failure message Expected that json is valid JSON which matches new { title = "Let It Be" }, but it differed as $.title was "Yesterday" instead of "Let It Be" JSON options: - ignore additional properties

Expectations for string: Expectation Negated Summary IsEqualTo(…).AsJson() IsNotEqualTo(…).AsJson() equal to the expected JSON, compared by structure IsValidJson IsNotValidJson can be parsed as JSON, optionally with expectations on its root IsValidJsonMatching valid JSON that matches the expected value IsValidJsonMatchingExactly valid JSON that matches the expected value exactly Expectations for JsonElement and JsonNode: Expectation Negated Summary Matches matches the expected value, additional properties allowed MatchesExactly matches the expected value exactly HasProperty DoesNotHaveProperty a JSON object with the property, optionally with expectations HasValueAt DoesNotHaveValueAt a value at a path, optionally with expectations HasElementAt a JSON array with an element at the index, optionally with expectations IsObject a JSON object IsObject().WhoseProperties collection expectations on the properties of a JSON object IsArray a JSON array IsArray().WhoseElements collection expectations on the elements of a JSON array IsString a JSON string, optionally equal to a value or with expectations IsNumber a JSON number, optionally with expectations on its value IsString().StartingWith(…), … a JSON string compared with a string operator, e.g. EqualTo, EndingWith or Containing(…).AtLeast(2) IsNumber().GreaterThan(…), … a JSON number compared as double with a number operator, e.g. Between(…).And(…) or EqualTo(…).Within(…) IsNumber<TNumber> a JSON number that fits into the number type, e.g. an int, optionally equal to a value IsBoolean a JSON boolean, i.e. true or false, optionally equal to a value or with expectations IsNull the JSON value null, only for a JsonElement Expectations for any object, serialized with System.Text.Json: Expectation Negated Summary IsJsonSerializable survives a round trip through the JSON serializer IsJsonSerializedAs serialized by the JSON serializer as the expected JSON The comparisons can be relaxed with options like TreatingNullAsAbsent(), IgnoringArrayOrder(), IgnoringMember(name) or ComparingNumbersWithin(tolerance), see Matching JSON.

These benchmarks compare the happy-path overhead of aweXpect.Json (passing assertions, the dominant case in a healthy test suite) against the equivalent FluentAssertions calls. Methodology Suite: HappyCaseBenchmarks driven by BenchmarkDotNet. Job: MediumRun with the in-process toolchain. Runner: ubuntu-latest GitHub Actions agent, refreshed on every push to main. FluentAssertions has expectations on JsonNode, but not on JSON strings or JsonElement. Where it lacks an expectation, its benchmark does what a FluentAssertions user writes instead, e.g. parse the string into a JsonNode. Each tab shows the latest measured time and allocated memory; bars are scaled within the row so length corresponds to magnitude. Lower is better. Set a value under Customize.aweXpect.Json() for the current async flow, or under Customize.aweXpect.Global.Json() for all tests. Value Default Summary DefaultJsonDocumentOptions AllowTrailingCommas = true the options to parse JSON strings DefaultJsonSerializerOptions AllowTrailingCommas = true the options to format JSON values, serialize the subject of IsJsonSerializable and IsJsonSerializedAs and, once set, expected values You can change the default JsonDocumentOptions and the default JsonSerializerOptions. Each value is set on its own: using (Customize.aweXpect.Json().DefaultJsonDocumentOptions.Set(new JsonDocumentOptions { AllowTrailingCommas = false, })) { // parses JSON strings without allowing trailing commas } To use other JsonDocumentOptions for a single expectation, pass them with WithDocumentOptions(…) wherever JsonOptions are accepted, also in IsValidJson(o => …): string track = """{"title": "Let It Be", /* 1970 */ "artist": "The Beatles"}"""; await That(track).IsValidJsonMatching(new { title = "Let It Be" }, o => o.WithDocumentOptions(d => d with { CommentHandling = JsonCommentHandling.Skip }));

A JsonNode and its subtypes JsonObject, JsonArray and JsonValue, nullable or not, have the same expectations as a JsonElement: Matches, MatchesExactly, HasProperty, DoesNotHaveProperty, HasValueAt, DoesNotHaveValueAt, HasElementAt, IsObject (with WhoseProperties), IsArray (with WhoseElements), IsString, IsNumber and IsBoolean, with the same options and failure messages: JsonNode? track = JsonNode.Parse("""{"title": "Let It Be", "artist": "The Beatles"}"""); await That(track).Matches(new { title = "Let It Be" }); await That(track).HasProperty("artist", a => a.IsString("The Beatles")); JsonArray titles = new("Let It Be", "Yesterday"); await That(titles).IsArray().WhoseElements.HasCount(2); MatchesExactly(new { title = "Let It Be" }) on the track would fail with: Failure message Expected that track matches new { title = "Let It Be" } exactly, but it differed as $.artist had unexpected "The Beatles" The expectations keep the type of the subject for chaining with .And. A call that names the number type, like IsNumber<int>() or IsNumber<double>(243), continues on a JsonNode, as C# cannot infer the node type then, except on a JsonValue, which has IsNumber<TNumber> overloads of its own. note The node is verified in the state it has when the expectation is awaited, so changes made after That(…) are included. A null node is the JSON value null, as JsonNode.Parse("null") returns it. Use the general IsNull() expectation of aweXpect to verify that a node is the JSON value null, e.g. HasProperty("label", l => l.IsNull()), so there is no JSON-specific IsNull() for a JsonNode. Nested nodes and null nodes The expectations on a property, a value at a path or an element receive the node itself, e.g. for IsSameAs(…). Likewise, WhoseElements provides the nodes of an array as JsonNode? items and WhoseProperties the properties of an object as KeyValuePair<string, JsonNode?> items with the name and the node of the value, instead of JsonElement and JsonProperty items: JsonArray playlist = new(new JsonObject { ["title"] = "Let It Be" }); JsonNode first = playlist[0]!; await That(playlist).HasElementAt(0, e => e.IsSameAs(first)); await That(playlist).IsArray().WhoseElements.Contains(first); await That(first).IsObject().WhoseProperties.All().Satisfy(p => p.Value is JsonValue); Matches(null) succeeds for a null node, while IsObject() would fail with: Failure message Expected that node is an object, but it was null

Describes the possible expectations for matching a JsonElement or a JsonNode with an expected value, and the options to relax the comparison. Expectation Negated Summary Matches matches the expected value, additional properties allowed MatchesExactly matches the expected value exactly

You can verify that a JsonElement matches an expected object. Matches ignores additional properties, while MatchesExactly also fails for them: JsonElement track = JsonDocument.Parse("""{"title": "Let It Be", "artist": "The Beatles"}""").RootElement; await That(track).Matches(new { title = "Let It Be" }); await That(track).MatchesExactly(new { title = "Let It Be", artist = "The Beatles" }); Matches accepts the same values as MatchesExactly with the option IgnoringAdditionalProperties(). MatchesExactly(new { title = "Let It Be" }) would fail because of the additional artist property: Failure message Expected that track matches new { title = "Let It Be" } exactly, but it differed as $.artist had unexpected "The Beatles"

You can verify that a JsonElement matches an expected array: JsonElement titles = JsonDocument.Parse("""["Let It Be", "Yesterday", "Hey Jude"]""").RootElement; await That(titles).Matches(["Let It Be", "Yesterday", "Hey Jude"]); await That(titles).MatchesExactly(["Let It Be", "Yesterday", "Hey Jude"]); Unlike additional properties, additional array elements are not ignored by Matches. Matches(["Let It Be", "Yesterday"]) would fail with: Failure message Expected that titles matches ["Let It Be", "Yesterday"], but it differed as $[2] had unexpected "Hey Jude" JSON options: - ignore additional properties

You can also verify that a JsonElement matches a primitive value: await That(JsonDocument.Parse("4.05").RootElement).Matches(4.05); await That(JsonDocument.Parse("true").RootElement).Matches(true); await That(JsonDocument.Parse("null").RootElement).Matches(null); An expected string is JSON text, so Matches("42") expects the number 42. To match a JSON string, write it with quotes or as an It.Is<string>() expectation: JsonElement title = JsonDocument.Parse("\"Let It Be\"").RootElement; await That(title).Matches("\"Let It Be\""); await That(title).Matches(It.Is<string>().That.IsEqualTo("Let It Be")); A string inside an expected object or array, e.g. new { title = "Let It Be" }, and a string typed as object, e.g. (object)"Let It Be", stay JSON strings. Any expected value, also a nested one, can be an It.Is<T>() expectation instead, e.g. Matches(new { duration = It.Is<long>().That.IsGreaterThan(200) }). Numbers in It.Is<T>() A JSON number meets It.Is<T>() as a T when System.Text.Json can read it as that numeric type, so It.Is<long>(), It.Is<double>() and It.Is<decimal>() all accept 243, while an integer type does not accept a number with a fraction or an exponent, e.g. 2.5 or 1e3.

An expected string is parsed as JSON text: JsonElement track = JsonDocument.Parse("""{"title": "Let It Be", "artist": "The Beatles"}""").RootElement; await That(track).Matches("""{"title": "Let It Be"}"""); MatchesExactly("""{"title": "Let It Be"}""") would fail because of the additional artist property: Failure message Expected that track matches """{"title": "Let It Be"}""" exactly, but it differed as $.artist had unexpected "The Beatles" The JSON text is parsed with the JsonDocumentOptions of WithDocumentOptions(…), and WithSerializerOptions(…) does not apply to it. Invalid JSON throws an ArgumentException when the expectation is written, so that also a negated expectation, e.g. within DoesNotComplyWith(…), cannot pass. The expected value can also be a JsonElement, a JsonDocument or a JsonNode, whose JSON is used as it is.

The options are available wherever JsonOptions are accepted, e.g. Matches, MatchesExactly, IsEqualTo(expected).AsJson(o => …), IsValidJsonMatching and IsJsonSerializedAs. They work like the options of aweXpect: Option Configures IgnoringAdditionalProperties() ignores additional properties of objects TreatingNullAsAbsent() a property with the value null counts as absent IgnoringAdditionalArrayElements() ignores additional elements of arrays IgnoringArrayOrder() the elements of arrays can be in any order IgnoringMember(name), IgnoringMembers(path => …) leaves values out of the comparison ComparingNumbersWithin(tolerance) numbers match within an absolute or relative tolerance WithDocumentOptions(…) the JsonDocumentOptions used to parse JSON strings WithSerializerOptions(…) the JsonSerializerOptions for the expected value

By default, a property with the value null differs from a missing property. With TreatingNullAsAbsent(), a property with the value null counts as absent, in both directions: JsonElement track = JsonDocument.Parse("""{"title": "Let It Be", "album": null}""").RootElement; await That(track).MatchesExactly(new { title = "Let It Be" }, o => o.TreatingNullAsAbsent()); await That(track).MatchesExactly(new { title = "Let It Be", artist = (string?)null }, o => o.TreatingNullAsAbsent()); Without the option, MatchesExactly(new { title = "Let It Be" }) would fail with: Failure message Expected that track matches new { title = "Let It Be" } exactly, but it differed as $.album had unexpected <null> Elements of an array with the value null are not affected.

With IgnoringAdditionalArrayElements(), the additional elements of all compared arrays, also nested ones, are ignored: JsonElement titles = JsonDocument.Parse("""["Let It Be", "Yesterday", "Hey Jude"]""").RootElement; await That(titles).Matches(["Let It Be", "Yesterday"], o => o.IgnoringAdditionalArrayElements());

By default, arrays are compared by index. With IgnoringArrayOrder(), the elements of all compared arrays, also nested ones, can be in any order: JsonElement titles = JsonDocument.Parse("""["Let It Be", "Yesterday", "Hey Jude"]""").RootElement; await That(titles).MatchesExactly(["Hey Jude", "Let It Be", "Yesterday"], o => o.IgnoringArrayOrder()); Combined with IgnoringAdditionalArrayElements(), the expected elements only have to be contained in the subject in any order. MatchesExactly(["Hey Jude", "Something", "Help!"], o => o.IgnoringArrayOrder()) would fail with: Failure message Expected that titles matches ["Hey Jude", "Something", "Help!"] exactly, but it differed as $ had missing "Something" and $ had missing "Help!" and $[0] had unexpected "Let It Be" and $[1] had unexpected "Yesterday" JSON options: - ignore array order How the elements are paired Each expected element is paired with the first matching element of the subject that is not paired yet. The expected elements that could not be paired are reported as missing on the array, the remaining elements of the subject as unexpected at their index. When exactly one element remains unpaired on each side, they are compared with each other instead, e.g. $[1] was "Yesterday" instead of "Something". HasElementAt still verifies the element at its index. The pairing is greedy, so overlapping It.Is… expectations can fail, although another pairing would succeed.

Generated values, e.g. ids, timestamps or ETags, can be left out of the comparison with IgnoringMember(name) or IgnoringMembers(path => …). An ignored value and everything below it is neither compared nor reported as missing or unexpected: JsonElement track = JsonDocument.Parse( """{"id": 42, "title": "Let It Be", "meta": {"createdAt": "2026-10-16", "etag": "abc"}}""").RootElement; await That(track).MatchesExactly( new { id = 1, title = "Let It Be", meta = new { createdAt = "2026-01-01" } }, o => o.IgnoringMember("id").IgnoringMember("createdAt").IgnoringMembers(path => path.EndsWith(".etag"))); The name is matched against the JSON path, as it is shown in failure messages, and must cover whole trailing segments of it, with the same casing, as JSON property names are case-sensitive: "id" ignores $.id and $.items[0].id, but not $.parentId or $.ID, "meta.createdAt" only ignores createdAt within meta, and "$.id" only ignores the property of the root. "[0]" ignores the first element of every array. The members to ignore are listed in the "JSON options" context. When the comparison fails, each name that matched no member is named below them, together with the member it most likely meant, e.g. one that differs only in casing, as a misspelled name otherwise silently ignores nothing. For a track {"title": "Let It Be", "createdAt": "2026-10-16"}, MatchesExactly(new { title = "Yesterday", createdAt = "2026-01-01" }, o => o.IgnoringMember("craetedAt")) would fail with: Failure message Expected that track matches new { title = "Yesterday", createdAt = "2026-01-01" } exactly, but it differed as $.title was "Let It Be" instead of "Yesterday" and $.createdAt was "2026-10-16" instead of "2026-01-01" JSON options: - ignore members: ["craetedAt"] "craetedAt" matched no member (did you mean "createdAt"?) Ignored indices and explicit expectations With IgnoringArrayOrder(), an index refers to the element of the subject, which is then left out of the pairing. Explicit expectations like HasProperty("id"), DoesNotHaveProperty("id") or HasElementAt(0, …) still verify an ignored value.

Calculated numbers rarely match an expected literal exactly. With ComparingNumbersWithin(tolerance), a number matches when it differs from the expected number by at most the tolerance, and with ComparingNumbersWithin(tolerance).Percent() by at most the percentage of the expected number. The option can be combined with the other options: JsonElement album = JsonDocument.Parse( """{"durationMinutes": 47.050000000000004, "rating": 4.6005}""").RootElement; await That(album).MatchesExactly(new { durationMinutes = 47.05, rating = 4.6m }, o => o.ComparingNumbersWithin(0.001)); await That(album).MatchesExactly(new { rating = 4.6m }, o => o.ComparingNumbersWithin(1).Percent().IgnoringAdditionalProperties()); The tolerance applies to every number in the compared JSON, also to integers such as ids or counts. For a track {"title": "Hey Jude", "durationSeconds": 431}, MatchesExactly(new { title = "Hey Jude", durationSeconds = 400 }, o => o.ComparingNumbersWithin(5).Percent()) would fail with: Failure message Expected that track matches new { title = "Hey Jude", durationSeconds = 400 } exactly, but it differed as $.durationSeconds was 431 instead of 400 ± 5% JSON options: - compare numbers within ± 5% Zero and very large numbers Like the tolerance in aweXpect, a relative tolerance only matches an equal number when the expected number is 0. The numbers are compared as double, so numbers outside its range are compared by their text.

The expected value is serialized to JSON before the comparison. By default, the property names of an anonymous object are kept as they are, so a subject with camelCase names needs new { title = "Let It Be" }. With WithSerializerOptions(…), the expected value is serialized with the given JsonSerializerOptions instead, e.g. with a naming policy: JsonElement track = JsonDocument.Parse("""{"title": "Let It Be", "artist": "The Beatles"}""").RootElement; JsonSerializerOptions camelCase = new() { PropertyNamingPolicy = JsonNamingPolicy.CamelCase }; await That(track).MatchesExactly(new { Title = "Let It Be", Artist = "The Beatles" }, o => o.WithSerializerOptions(camelCase)); The comparison itself stays strict: only the JSON of the expected value changes. Without the option, the expected value is serialized with the DefaultJsonSerializerOptions of the customization when they are customized, except in IsJsonSerializedAs. It.Is… expectations keep working with any options. Pass the options of a source-generated JsonSerializerContext to use it with trimming or Native AOT. Source-generated serializer contexts Options with a TypeInfoResolver, e.g. those of a source-generated JsonSerializerContext, serialize the expected value without reflection. Each type of the expected value, also the runtime type of a value in an object property, must then be registered in the context; otherwise a NotSupportedException names the missing [JsonSerializable(typeof(…))] attribute.

The failure message lists the active options in a "JSON options" context, like in the examples above, and omits it when no option is active. The options of WithDocumentOptions(…) and WithSerializerOptions(…) are not listed. As Matches and IsValidJsonMatching ignore additional properties by default, their failures list ignore additional properties.

Describes the possible expectations for the kind and the content of a JsonElement or a JsonNode. Expectation Negated Summary HasProperty DoesNotHaveProperty a JSON object with the property, optionally with expectations HasValueAt DoesNotHaveValueAt a value at a path, optionally with expectations HasElementAt a JSON array with an element at the index, optionally with expectations IsObject a JSON object IsObject().WhoseProperties collection expectations on the properties of a JSON object IsArray a JSON array IsArray().WhoseElements collection expectations on the elements of a JSON array IsString a JSON string, optionally equal to a value, compared with an operator or with expectations IsNumber a JSON number, optionally compared with an operator or with expectations on its value IsNumber<TNumber> a JSON number that fits into the number type, optionally equal to a value IsBoolean a JSON boolean, i.e. true or false, optionally equal to a value or with expectations IsNull the JSON value null, only for a JsonElement

You can verify that a JsonElement is a JSON object with or without a property. The expectations on the value of a property are the ones of a JsonElement, so all expectations on this page are available for it, and the typed values give access to all expectations of aweXpect: JsonElement track = JsonDocument.Parse( """{"title": "Let It Be", "artist": "The Beatles", "durationSeconds": 243}""").RootElement; await That(track) .HasProperty("title", t => t.IsString("Let It Be")).And .HasProperty("durationSeconds", d => d.IsNumber<int>(n => n.IsBetween(120).And(600))).And .DoesNotHaveProperty("password"); The failure names the value by its JSON path. If the title was "Yesterday", the expectation would fail with: Failure message Expected that track has property "title" which is a string equal to "Let It Be" and has property "durationSeconds" which is an int which is between 120 and 600 and does not have property "password", but $.title was "Yesterday", which differs at index 0: ↓ (actual) "Yesterday" "Let It Be" ↑ (expected) Actual ($.title): "Yesterday" A failed lookup or value adds the complete JSON that it verified, indented, as Actual context, as the failure itself shows a value only in a single line and shortened. A nested expectation adds the value it verified, labeled with its JSON path, e.g. Actual ($.title):, instead of the whole document. Every failing part of a combined expectation is reported. The expectations on a property are only verified when the property exists, otherwise the failure says that it did not exist, e.g. but property $.title did not exist. With .DoesNotHaveProperty("artist"), the track would fail with: Failure message Expected that track has property "title" and does not have property "artist", but it had property "artist" with "The Beatles" Actual: { "title": "Let It Be", "artist": "The Beatles", "durationSeconds": 243 } The name is taken literally, so that names like "@odata.context" or "user.name" can be addressed. The expectations can be nested, and the JSON path in the failure continues with each level: JsonElement album = JsonDocument.Parse( """{"artist": {"name": "The Beatles", "origin": {"city": "Liverpool"}}}""").RootElement; await That(album).HasProperty("artist", a => a .HasProperty("origin", o => o.Matches(new { city = "Liverpool" }))); If the city was "London" instead, the expectation would fail with: Failure message Expected that album has property "artist" which has property "origin" which matches new { city = "Liverpool" }, but $.artist.origin differed as $.artist.origin.city was "London" instead of "Liverpool" JSON options ($.artist.origin): - ignore additional properties Paths, other kinds and negation The paths of a nested Matches continue the path in the same way, also for the members to ignore, e.g. IgnoringMembers(path => path == "$.artist.origin.city"). In the JSON path of a failure, a name that is no plain identifier is written in brackets, e.g. $['@odata.context'], so that it cannot be read as several segments. A subject that is no JSON object fails HasProperty and DoesNotHaveProperty alike, e.g. with but it was an array. Negated, e.g. within DoesNotComplyWith(…), the expectations on a property are an alternative: the negation is met when the property does not exist or its value does not satisfy them. Negating HasProperty("title", t => t.IsString("Let It Be")) would fail for the track with: Failure message Expected that track does not have property "title" or $.title is not a string equal to "Let It Be", but $.title was "Let It Be" Actual ($.title): "Let It Be" The same applies to HasValueAt and HasElementAt.

A property with the value null exists, so HasProperty accepts it and DoesNotHaveProperty fails for it. Verify the value with IsNull(): JsonElement track = JsonDocument.Parse("""{"title": "Let It Be", "label": null}""").RootElement; await That(track).HasProperty("label", l => l.IsNull()).And.DoesNotHaveProperty("legacyId"); With TreatingNullAsAbsent(), a property with the value null counts as absent, so DoesNotHaveProperty accepts it and HasProperty fails for it, also on the way to a value at a path: JsonElement track = JsonDocument.Parse("""{"title": "Let It Be", "label": null}""").RootElement; await That(track).DoesNotHaveProperty("label").TreatingNullAsAbsent(); Without the option, the expectation would fail with: Failure message Expected that track does not have property "label", but it had property "label" with <null> Actual: { "title": "Let It Be", "label": null }

You can verify a nested value with a path relative to the subject, instead of nesting HasProperty and HasElementAt. The path is a property name, followed by any number of .name or zero-based [index] segments, and is written without a leading $. Wildcards, filters and recursive descent are not supported, and property names that contain ., [ or ] can only be addressed with HasProperty: JsonElement album = JsonDocument.Parse( """{"artist": {"origin": {"city": "Liverpool"}}, "tracks": [{"title": "Come Together"}]}""").RootElement; await That(album) .HasValueAt("artist.origin.city", c => c.IsString("Liverpool")).And .HasValueAt("tracks[0].title", t => t.IsString()); If the artist had no origin, the expectation would fail with the first segment that could not be reached: Failure message Expected that album has value at "artist.origin.city" which is a string equal to "Liverpool" and has value at "tracks[0].title" which is a string, but property $.artist.origin did not exist Actual: { "artist": {}, "tracks": [ { "title": "Come Together" } ] } TreatingNullAsAbsent() is available like for HasProperty. Without expectations, HasValueAt only verifies that the value exists, and DoesNotHaveValueAt that it does not: JsonElement album = JsonDocument.Parse( """{"artist": {"origin": {"city": "Liverpool"}}, "tracks": [{"title": "Come Together"}]}""").RootElement; await That(album) .HasValueAt("tracks[0].title").And .DoesNotHaveValueAt("artist.origin.country").And .DoesNotHaveValueAt("tracks[1].title"); Values of another kind on the way A value on the way that has another kind than the next segment requires fails with e.g. but $.artist was a string instead of an object. A missing property or index on the way satisfies DoesNotHaveValueAt, while a value of another kind on the way fails it like HasValueAt, as the path cannot be looked up in it.

You can verify the element at a zero-based index of a JSON array: JsonElement tracks = JsonDocument.Parse("""[{"title": "Let It Be"}, {"title": "Yesterday"}]""").RootElement; await That(tracks).HasElementAt(0, t => t.HasProperty("title", p => p.IsString("Let").AsPrefix())); If the first track was "Yesterday", the expectation would fail with: Failure message Expected that tracks has element at index 0 which has property "title" which is a string starting with "Let", but $[0].title was "Yesterday", which differs at index 0: ↓ (actual) "Yesterday" "Let" ↑ (expected prefix) Actual ($[0].title): "Yesterday" An index beyond the end fails with e.g. but index $[2] did not exist, without verifying the expectations. HasElementAt(2) without expectations only verifies that the element exists. To verify the number of elements or the elements regardless of their position, use WhoseElements, and to match the elements directly, use Matches with an expected array, e.g. Matches(new[] { "Let It Be", "Yesterday" }).

You can verify that a JsonElement is a JSON object: JsonElement track = JsonDocument.Parse("""{"title": "Let It Be", "artist": "The Beatles"}""").RootElement; await That(track).IsObject(); You can verify the properties of an object regardless of their name with WhoseProperties. Like WhoseElements for arrays, it provides all collection expectations of aweXpect, here on the JsonProperty items in the order of the document, e.g. HasCount(2) for the number of properties: JsonElement track = JsonDocument.Parse( """{"title": "Let It Be", "artist": "The Beatles", "album": "Let It Be"}""").RootElement; await That(track).IsObject().WhoseProperties.HasCount(3); await That(track).IsObject().WhoseProperties .All().Satisfy(p => p.Value.ValueKind == JsonValueKind.String); await That(track).IsObject().WhoseProperties .All().ComplyWith(p => p.Whose(x => x.Value, v => v.IsString())); await That(track).IsObject().WhoseProperties .None().Satisfy(p => p.Name.StartsWith("_")); If the track also had "durationSeconds": 243, the second expectation would fail with: Failure message Expected that track is an object whose properties satisfy p => p.Value.ValueKind == JsonValueKind.String for all items, but only 3 of 4 did Not matching items (properties): [ "durationSeconds":243 ] Collection (properties): [ "title":"Let It Be", "artist":"The Beatles", "album":"Let It Be", "durationSeconds":243 ] warning A JsonProperty has no value equality, so verify the properties with predicates on their Name and Value, like Satisfy(p => …) or Contains(p => …), or with expectations on their value, like ComplyWith(p => p.Whose(x => x.Value, v => …)). Duplicate property names A name that occurs more than once in the object is kept in WhoseProperties as often as it occurs.

You can verify that a JsonElement is a JSON array: JsonElement titles = JsonDocument.Parse("""["Let It Be", "Yesterday"]""").RootElement; await That(titles).IsArray(); You can verify the elements of an array regardless of their position with WhoseElements. It provides all collection expectations of aweXpect, e.g. the quantifiers All(), AtLeast(…), AtMost(…), Exactly(…), Between(…).And(…) and None() with ComplyWith(…) or Satisfy(…), as well as Contains(…), HasCount(…) and IsEmpty(): JsonElement tracks = JsonDocument.Parse( """ [ {"title": "Let It Be", "artist": "The Beatles", "durationSeconds": 243}, {"title": "Yesterday", "artist": "The Beatles", "durationSeconds": 125}, {"title": "Hey Jude", "artist": "The Beatles", "durationSeconds": 431} ] """).RootElement; await That(tracks).IsArray().WhoseElements .All().ComplyWith(t => t.Matches(new { artist = "The Beatles" })); await That(tracks).IsArray().WhoseElements .AtLeast(2).ComplyWith(t => t.HasProperty("durationSeconds", d => d.IsNumber())); await That(tracks).IsArray().WhoseElements .Contains([t => t.Matches(new { title = "Hey Jude" })]); await That(tracks).IsArray().WhoseElements .Contains(t => t.GetProperty("durationSeconds").GetInt32() > 400); await That(tracks).IsArray().WhoseElements.HasCount(3); If "Yesterday" was by "Paul McCartney" instead, the first expectation would fail with: Failure message Expected that tracks is an array whose elements match new { artist = "The Beatles" } for all items, but only 2 of 3 did Not matching items (elements): [ {"title":"Yesterday","artist":"Paul McCartney","durationSeconds":125} ] Collection (elements): [ {"title":"Let It Be","artist":"The Beatles","durationSeconds":243}, {"title":"Yesterday","artist":"Paul McCartney","durationSeconds":125}, {"title":"Hey Jude","artist":"The Beatles","durationSeconds":431} ] JSON options (elements[1]): - ignore additional properties warning A JsonElement has no value equality, so value-based expectations on the elements, like Contains(someElement) or AreEqualTo(…), are not useful. Use expectations like ComplyWith(e => e.Matches(…)), Contains([e => e.Matches(…)]) or predicates like Contains(e => …) instead. A single lambda in Contains(e => …) is such a predicate on the JsonElement, so pass expectations on an element as a collection.

You can verify that a JsonElement is a JSON string, number, boolean (true or false) or null: JsonElement title = JsonDocument.Parse("\"Let It Be\"").RootElement; await That(title).IsString(); await That(JsonDocument.Parse("243").RootElement).IsNumber(); await That(JsonDocument.Parse("false").RootElement).IsBoolean(); await That(JsonDocument.Parse("null").RootElement).IsNull(); IsNumber() on the title would fail with: Failure message Expected that title is a number, but it was a string IsString, IsNumber and IsBoolean also accept an expected value. IsString(…) compares the string exactly and takes the string options of aweXpect, e.g. AsPrefix(), AsWildcard(), AsRegex() or IgnoringCase(), and IsNumber(…) takes a tolerance of the type of the expected value with Within(…), also relative to the expected value with Within(…).Percent(): JsonElement track = JsonDocument.Parse( """{"title": "Let It Be", "rating": 4.5, "explicit": false}""").RootElement; await That(track) .HasProperty("title", t => t.IsString("let").AsPrefix().IgnoringCase()).And .HasProperty("rating", r => r.IsNumber(4.5).Within(0.1)).And .HasProperty("explicit", e => e.IsBoolean(false)); If the rating was 4.7, the expectation would fail with: Failure message Expected that track has property "title" which is a string starting with "let" ignoring case and has property "rating" which is a double equal to 4.5 ± 0.1 and has property "explicit" which is a boolean equal to False, but $.rating was 4.7 Actual ($.rating): 4.7 Like IsString(), a value of another kind fails the expectation, e.g. IsString("4.5") on the rating fails with but $.rating was a number. IsString() and IsNumber() also offer operators on their result, which compare the value in the same sentence. A string offers EqualTo, StartingWith, EndingWith and Containing, their negations and NotContaining, with the string options of aweXpect, e.g. IgnoringCase() or AsWildcard(), and with a quantifier for Containing, e.g. Containing("e").AtLeast(2). A number is compared as double with EqualTo, GreaterThan, GreaterThanOrEqualTo, LessThan, LessThanOrEqualTo, Between(…).And(…) and their negations, and EqualTo and NotEqualTo take a tolerance with Within(…), also relative with Within(…).Percent(): JsonElement track = JsonDocument.Parse( """{"title": "Let It Be", "rating": 4.5}""").RootElement; await That(track) .HasProperty("title", t => t.IsString().StartingWith("let").IgnoringCase()).And .HasProperty("rating", r => r.IsNumber().Between(1).And(5)); If the rating was 6, the expectation would fail with: Failure message Expected that track has property "title" which is a string starting with "let" ignoring case and has property "rating" which is a number between 1.0 and 5.0, but $.rating was 6 Actual ($.rating): 6 Only one operator can follow IsString() or IsNumber(); chain further checks with .And, e.g. IsString().StartingWith("Let").And.IsString().EndingWith("Be"). For richer checks, IsString, IsNumber and IsBoolean accept expectations on the value as a string, a double or a bool, so that all expectations of aweXpect apply to it: JsonElement track = JsonDocument.Parse( """{"title": "Let It Be", "rating": 4.5, "explicit": false}""").RootElement; await That(track) .HasProperty("title", t => t.IsString(s => s.StartsWith("Let").And.HasLength(9))).And .HasProperty("rating", r => r.IsNumber(n => n.IsBetween(1).And(5))).And .HasProperty("explicit", e => e.IsBoolean(b => b.IsFalse())); note For a nullable JsonElement?, IsNull() is the general expectation of aweXpect that verifies that the subject itself is null, so IsString(), IsNumber() and IsBoolean() are available, but not a JSON-specific IsNull(). Negation, operators and very large numbers A value of another kind satisfies the negation of IsString, IsNumber and IsBoolean, so it succeeds within DoesNotComplyWith(…). A second operator on the same result of IsString() or IsNumber() throws an InvalidOperationException. A number that does not fit into a double, which IsNumber() alone accepts, fails both an operator and its negation, as whether it is e.g. greater than 3 cannot be answered; the same holds for IsNumber(n => …). An invalid pattern, e.g. of AsRegex(), throws whichever value the subject has.

IsNumber<TNumber>() verifies that a number fits into the number type, e.g. that it is an integer within the range of an int, and IsNumber<TNumber>(n => …) verifies the value as this type. The supported types are byte, sbyte, short, ushort, int, uint, long, ulong, BigInteger, float, double and decimal, and on .NET 8 or later also nint, nuint, Int128, UInt128 and Half. IsNumber(n => …) without a type argument verifies the number as double: JsonElement track = JsonDocument.Parse("""{"durationSeconds": 243, "price": 9.99}""").RootElement; await That(track) .HasProperty("durationSeconds", d => d.IsNumber<long>(n => n.IsBetween(120).And(600))).And .HasProperty("price", p => p.IsNumber<decimal>(n => n.IsEqualTo(9.99m))); If the duration was 243.5, HasProperty("durationSeconds", d => d.IsNumber<int>()) would fail with: Failure message Expected that track has property "durationSeconds" which is an int, but $.durationSeconds was 243.5, which is not an int Actual ($.durationSeconds): 243.5 IsNumber(expected) compares the number as the type of the expected value, so IsNumber(243) reads it as int, IsNumber(9.99m) as decimal and IsNumber(4.5) as double. A long or a decimal is thereby compared exactly, without the rounding of a double: JsonElement track = JsonDocument.Parse("""{"durationSeconds": 243, "price": 9.99}""").RootElement; await That(track) .HasProperty("durationSeconds", d => d.IsNumber(243)).And .HasProperty("price", p => p.IsNumber(9.99m)); warning A number that does not fit into the type of the expected value fails the expectation, like for IsNumber<TNumber>(). If the duration was 243.0, the expectation above would fail with: Failure message Expected that track has property "durationSeconds" which is an int equal to 243 and has property "price" which is a decimal equal to 9.99, but $.durationSeconds was 243.0, which is not an int Actual ($.durationSeconds): 243.0 Compare such a number as double with IsNumber(243.0) or IsNumber<double>(243).

Describes the possible expectations for the JSON serialization of objects with System.Text.Json. Expectation Negated Summary IsJsonSerializable survives a round trip through the JSON serializer IsJsonSerializedAs serialized by the JSON serializer as the expected JSON

You can verify that an object is JSON serializable: public record Track(string Title, string Artist); Track track = new("Let It Be", "The Beatles"); await That(track).IsJsonSerializable(); This verifies that the object can be serialized to JSON and deserialized again, and that the result is equivalent to the original object. For example, a property with a private setter loses its value: public class PlayCounter { public string Title { get; set; } = ""; public int PlayCount { get; private set; } public void Play() => PlayCount++; } PlayCounter counter = new() { Title = "Let It Be" }; counter.Play(); await That(counter).IsJsonSerializable(); Failure message Expected that counter is serializable as JSON, but it was not: Property PlayCount differed: Actual: 0 Expected: 1 Equivalency options: - include public fields and properties As with IsEquivalentTo, the failure lists the equivalency options, and a member to ignore that matched no member, e.g. a misspelled IgnoringMember("PlayCont"), gets a hint with the closest member. You can specify both the JsonSerializerOptions and the equivalency options: await That(track).IsJsonSerializable( new JsonSerializerOptions { IncludeFields = true }, e => e.IgnoringMember(nameof(Track.Artist))); Without JsonSerializerOptions, the subject is serialized with the default options of the customization. Runtime type and null subjects The subject is serialized and deserialized as its runtime type, so that the members of a derived type survive the round trip as well, and keeps its declared type for further expectations after .And. A null subject fails the expectation.

You can verify the JSON that an object is serialized to by System.Text.Json, e.g. to test the contract of a public API: public enum Genre { Pop = 1, Rock = 2 } public record Track(string Title, Genre Genre, string? Album = null); Track track = new("Let It Be", Genre.Rock); JsonSerializerOptions serializerOptions = new(JsonSerializerDefaults.Web) { DefaultIgnoreCondition = JsonIgnoreCondition.WhenWritingNull, Converters = { new JsonStringEnumConverter(JsonNamingPolicy.CamelCase) }, }; await That(track).IsJsonSerializedAs("""{"title": "Let It Be", "genre": "rock"}""", serializerOptions); await That(track).IsJsonSerializedAs(new { title = "Let It Be", genre = "rock" }, serializerOptions); With new JsonSerializerOptions(JsonSerializerDefaults.Web) instead, the first expectation would fail with: Failure message Expected that track is serialized as JSON {"title": "Let It Be", "genre": "rock"}, but it differed as $.genre was number 2 instead of "rock" and $.album had unexpected <null> Serialized: {"title":"Let It Be","genre":2,"album":null} Unlike IsJsonSerializable, which verifies that an object survives a round trip through the serializer, IsJsonSerializedAs verifies the JSON itself: the property names and their casing, the representation of enums, omitted null values and the effect of converters. The expected value is either JSON text or an object that is compared like in Matches, including It.Is… expectations. Without JsonSerializerOptions, the subject is serialized with the default options of the customization. A null subject is serialized as null, and a subject that cannot be serialized, e.g. because of a reference cycle, fails the expectation with the message of the exception. The subject and an expected object are serialized on two separate paths: Value Serialized with Without them the subject the JsonSerializerOptions or JsonTypeInfo<T> parameter the default options of the customization an expected object o => o.WithSerializerOptions(…) the default options of System.Text.Json So the JsonSerializerOptions parameter only serializes the subject, and an expected object is serialized neither with this parameter nor with the customized default options, so that a naming policy cannot hide how the subject is actually serialized. To serialize the expected object with other options, pass them with WithSerializerOptions(…): JsonSerializerOptions camelCase = new() { PropertyNamingPolicy = JsonNamingPolicy.CamelCase }; await That(track).IsJsonSerializedAs(new { Title = "Let It Be", Genre = 2, Album = (string?)null }, camelCase, o => o.WithSerializerOptions(camelCase)); The serialized JSON is compared exactly, like in MatchesExactly, so additional properties fail the expectation. All JsonOptions are available to relax the comparison, e.g. IgnoringAdditionalProperties(), IgnoringArrayOrder(), TreatingNullAsAbsent() or IgnoringMember(name): await That(track).IsJsonSerializedAs(new { title = "Let It Be" }, serializerOptions, o => o.IgnoringAdditionalProperties()); Trimming and Native AOT Unless a JsonTypeInfo<T> is passed, the subject is serialized by reflection, which is switched off when publishing with trimming or Native AOT. In such an application, pass the source-generated JsonTypeInfo<T> of the subject together with the expected value as a JSON string: [JsonSerializable(typeof(Track))] internal partial class TrackContext : JsonSerializerContext; await That(track).IsJsonSerializedAs("""{"Title": "Let It Be", "Genre": 2}""", TrackContext.Default.Track, o => o.TreatingNullAsAbsent()); More on trimming and Native AOT IsJsonSerializable takes the JsonTypeInfo<T> as well, and then serializes and deserializes the subject as T. It also compares the deserialized object with the subject by equivalency, which needs the members of the subject type registered. The source generator of aweXpect registers them at the call site, but it cannot see the properties that the System.Text.Json source generator adds to the context. Pass the type info from a variable of type JsonTypeInfo<T> instead, or name the type in [assembly: GenerateMetadata(typeof(Track))]: JsonTypeInfo<Track> typeInfo = TrackContext.Default.Track; await That(track).IsJsonSerializable(typeInfo); Expected values in any expectation, e.g. in Matches or IsValidJsonMatching, are serialized by reflection as well, so an anonymous object always needs it. Only values that consist of null, strings, characters, booleans, numbers, JsonElement, JsonDocument, JsonNode (unless a JsonValue wraps another type), It.Is… expectations and collections of them are written without reflection and work in such an application, e.g. Matches(2) or Matches(new[] { 1, 2 }). The expectations on properties and values, like HasProperty("count", c => c.IsNumber<int>()), need no serialization at all. A named type works when it is registered in a source-generated context, whose options are passed with WithSerializerOptions(…): await That(element).Matches(new Track("Let It Be", Genre.Rock), o => o.WithSerializerOptions(TrackContext.Default.Options));

Describes the possible expectations for strings that contain JSON. Expectation Negated Summary IsEqualTo(…).AsJson() IsNotEqualTo(…).AsJson() equal to the expected JSON, compared by structure IsValidJson IsNotValidJson can be parsed as JSON, optionally with expectations on its root IsValidJsonMatching valid JSON that matches the expected value IsValidJsonMatchingExactly valid JSON that matches the expected value exactly

You can verify that a string is equal to the expected JSON, compared by its structure instead of its formatting: string track = """{"title":"Let It Be","artist":"The Beatles","durationSeconds":243}"""; string expected = """ { "title": "Let It Be", "artist": "The Beatles", "durationSeconds": 243 } """; await That(track).IsEqualTo(expected).AsJson(); If the track had a duration of 241 seconds instead, the expectation would fail with: Failure message Expected that track is JSON equivalent to { "title": "Let It Be", "artist": "The Beatles", "durationSeconds": 243 }, but it differed as $.durationSeconds was 241 instead of 243 Actual: {"title":"Let It Be","artist":"The Beatles","durationSeconds":241} Expected: { "title": "Let It Be", "artist": "The Beatles", "durationSeconds": 243 } As JSON is compared by its structure, AsJson() cannot be combined with the string options IgnoringCase() or Using(comparer). Instead, AsJson(o => …) accepts the JSON options to relax the comparison. note AsJson() is not available on Contains or DoesNotContain for a string subject, as parts of a JSON string are usually not valid JSON. Use IsEqualTo(expected).AsJson() or IsValidJsonMatching(expected) instead. On a collection of strings, Contains(expected).AsJson() compares each item as JSON.

You can verify that a string is valid JSON: string track = """{"title": "Let It Be"}"""; await That(track).IsValidJson(); If the closing brace was missing, the expectation would fail with: Failure message Expected that track is valid JSON, but it could not be parsed: Expected depth to be zero at the end of the JSON payload. There is an open JSON object or array that should be closed. LineNumber: 0 | BytePositionInLine: 21. This verifies that the string can be parsed by JsonDocument.Parse without exceptions. You can also specify the JsonDocumentOptions with WithDocumentOptions(…); the other JSON options are ignored, as there is nothing to compare: string track = """{"title": "Let It Be"}"""; await That(track).IsValidJson( o => o.WithDocumentOptions(d => d with { CommentHandling = JsonCommentHandling.Disallow })); You can also verify that a string is not valid JSON: string track = "Let It Be"; await That(track).IsNotValidJson(); The JsonDocumentOptions are available here as well, e.g. to reject a trailing comma, which is allowed by default: string track = """{"title": "Let It Be",}"""; await That(track).IsNotValidJson( o => o.WithDocumentOptions(d => d with { AllowTrailingCommas = false })); If the string is valid JSON, e.g. "[1, 2]", the expectation fails with: Failure message Expected that track is not valid JSON, but it was "[1, 2]" You can add further expectations on the root JsonElement parsed from the subject, optionally followed by the document options: string track = """{"title": "Let It Be"}"""; await That(track).IsValidJson(j => j.Matches(new { title = "Let It Be" })); await That(track).IsValidJson(j => j.IsObject(), o => o.WithDocumentOptions(d => d with { AllowTrailingCommas = true })); Or you can verify that the string is valid JSON and matches an expected value in one step: string track = """{"title": "Let It Be", "artist": "The Beatles"}"""; await That(track).IsValidJsonMatching(new { title = "Let It Be" }); await That(track).IsValidJsonMatchingExactly(new { title = "Let It Be", artist = "The Beatles" }); await That(track).IsValidJsonMatching("""{"title": "Let It Be"}"""); An expected string is JSON text, like in Matches. IsValidJsonMatching(new { title = "Yesterday" }) would fail with: Failure message Expected that track is valid JSON which matches new { title = "Yesterday" }, but it differed as $.title was "Let It Be" instead of "Yesterday" JSON options: - ignore additional properties null subjects and negation A null subject fails IsValidJson and IsNotValidJson alike. With expectations on the root element and with IsValidJsonMatching or IsValidJsonMatchingExactly, a string that is not valid JSON fails also when the expectation is negated, e.g. within DoesNotComplyWith(…), as there is no root element to verify. Only the negation of IsValidJson() without expectations is met by a string that is not valid JSON.
aweXpect.Logging contains expectations for the log records that are written with Microsoft.Extensions.Logging. It is an extension for aweXpect.

.NET CLI PackageReference Central Package Management dotnet add package aweXpect.Logging <PackageReference Include="aweXpect.Logging" Version="0.2.0" /> Directory.Packages.props <PackageVersion Include="aweXpect.Logging" Version="0.2.0" /> Project file <PackageReference Include="aweXpect.Logging" /> Latest version: 0.2.0 It does not include aweXpect itself.

// collect the log records with a FakeLogger from Microsoft.Extensions.Diagnostics.Testing FakeLogCollector collector = new(); ILogger logger = new FakeLogger(collector); logger.LogWarning("Retry limit reached"); // verify that a record with the log level was logged await That(collector).LoggedWarning(); A failing expectation lists the collected records. If only an error was logged, LoggedWarning() would fail with: Failure message Expected that collector logged a record with level Warning at least once, but it did not log any such record Records: [ [Error] "Retry limit reached" ]

Expectation Subject Summary Logged FakeLogCollector, FakeLogger logged at least one record with the log level, e.g. LoggedWarning() DidNotLog FakeLogCollector, FakeLogger logged no record with the log level, e.g. DidNotLogError() Then FakeLogCollector, FakeLogger logged further records after a matching record, in the given order Within FakeLogCollector, FakeLogger reads the records repeatedly until the timeout, e.g. for a background service

The expectations verify the records of a FakeLogCollector from the Microsoft.Extensions.Diagnostics.Testing package, which collects everything that is logged to a FakeLogger: FakeLogCollector collector = new(); ILogger logger = new FakeLogger(collector); All expectations are also available on a FakeLogger itself, which verifies the records of its Collector, so also the records of other loggers that write to the same collector: FakeLogger<OrderService> logger = new(); logger.LogWarning("Retry limit reached"); await That(logger).LoggedWarning().And.DidNotLogError(); And and Or then continue with further expectations on these records, e.g. Logged or DidNotLog.

You can verify that at least one record with the log level was logged: logger.LogWarning("Retry limit reached"); await That(collector).LoggedWarning(); There is a method for each log level: LoggedTrace(), LoggedDebug(), LoggedInformation(), LoggedWarning(), LoggedError() and LoggedCritical(). When the level is a parameter, e.g. in a theory, you can pass it instead: await That(collector).Logged(level); The log level must match exactly, so a record with the level Error does not satisfy LoggedWarning(). If only an error was logged, the expectation would fail with: Failure message Expected that collector logged a record with level Warning at least once, but it did not log any such record Records: [ [Error] "Retry limit reached" ] The failure message lists the level and the message of the first records. When nothing was logged at all, it says so instead: Failure message Expected that collector logged a record with level Warning at least once, but it did not log any record The records are read once, when the expectation is evaluated, so a record that is logged afterwards is neither considered nor listed, unless you specify a timeout. With OrHigher(), a record with a more severe level also counts, e.g. to verify that no warning or error was logged: await That(collector).LoggedWarning().OrHigher().Never(); Without a log level, a record of any level is enough: await That(collector).Logged();
