You can additionally verify the message of the record: logger.LogWarning("Retry limit 3 reached"); await That(collector).LoggedWarning().WithMessage("Retry limit 3 reached"); await That(collector).Logged().WithMessage("Retry limit * reached").AsWildcard(); The message must be equal by default. As for other strings, you can change the match type with AsWildcard(), AsRegex(), AsPrefix() or AsSuffix(), and the comparison e.g. with IgnoringCase(). If the message differs, the expectation would fail with: Failure message Expected that collector logged a record with level Warning and message matching "Retry limit * reached" at least once, but it did not log any such record Records: [ [Warning] "Connection lost" ] If WithMessage is specified more than once, the message of a record must match all of them.

You can additionally verify the type of the exception of the record, which includes derived types: logger.LogError(new FileNotFoundException(), "Configuration missing"); await That(collector).LoggedError().WithException<IOException>(); The failure message lists the type of the exception after the message of a record, e.g. if the exception had another type: Failure message Expected that collector logged a record with level Error and exception of type IOException at least once, but it did not log any such record Records: [ [Error] "Configuration missing" (InvalidOperationException) ]

When several loggers write to the same collector, e.g. with AddFakeLogging() in a service collection, you can verify the category of the logger and the event ID of the record: await That(collector).LoggedWarning().WithCategory<OrderService>(); await That(collector).Logged().WithCategory("MyApp.Orders").WithEventId(1001); await That(collector).Logged().WithCategory("MyApp.Orders.").AsPrefix(); WithCategory<T>() expects the category of an ILogger<T>, i.e. the full name of the type, where nested types are separated by a dot and generic types are named without their type arguments, and compares it exactly. The category of WithCategory(string) must be equal by default, but as for the message, you can change the match type, e.g. with AsPrefix() or AsWildcard(), and the comparison, e.g. with IgnoringCase(). The event ID is compared exactly, and the failure message lists the category and the event ID for each record when they are compared: Failure message Expected that collector logged a record with category "MyApp.Orders" and event ID 1001 at least once, but it did not log any such record Records: [ [Warning] "Retry limit reached" (category "MyApp.Orders", event ID 1002) ]

With structured logging, a record stores its message template and the values of its placeholders as properties: logger.LogWarning("Retry {Attempt} of {MaxAttempts}", 3, 5); await That(collector).LoggedWarning().WithProperty("Attempt"); await That(collector).LoggedWarning().WithProperty("Attempt").WithValue("3"); await That(collector).Logged().WithMessageTemplate("Retry {Attempt} of {MaxAttempts}").Twice(); WithProperty alone only requires the property, while WithValue also verifies its value. The FakeLogger stores the values of the properties as strings in the invariant culture, e.g. "1.5" for the double 1.5, so the expected value is a string, too. It must be equal by default, and as for the message, you can change the match type of the value, e.g. with AsWildcard(), and the comparison, e.g. with IgnoringCase(): await That(collector).Logged().WithProperty("OrderId").WithValue("ORD-*").AsWildcard(); The template does not depend on the logged values, so it identifies the statement that logged a record. It must be equal by default, and as for the message, you can change the match type, e.g. with AsPrefix() or AsWildcard(), and the comparison, e.g. with IgnoringCase(): await That(collector).Logged().WithMessageTemplate("Retry {Attempt} of {MaxAttempts}*").AsWildcard(); The failure message lists the compared template and properties for each record: Failure message Expected that collector logged a record with level Warning and property Attempt with value equal to "3" at least once, but it did not log any such record Records: [ [Warning] "Retry 2 of 5" (property Attempt "2") ] A record that was logged with a custom state object instead of a message template has no properties, which the failure message shows as (no structured state).

By default, a single matching record is enough. You can specify how many matching records are expected instead: await That(collector).LoggedWarning().Once(); await That(collector).LoggedWarning().Twice(); await That(collector).LoggedWarning().Exactly(3.Times()); await That(collector).LoggedWarning().AtLeast(2.Times()); await That(collector).LoggedWarning().AtMost().Once(); await That(collector).LoggedWarning().Between(1).And(3.Times()); await That(collector).LoggedWarning().LessThan(3.Times()); await That(collector).LoggedWarning().MoreThan().Once(); await That(collector).LoggedError().Never(); If two warnings were logged, LoggedWarning().Once() would fail with: Failure message Expected that collector logged a record with level Warning exactly once, but it logged 2 such records Records: [ [Warning] "Retry 1", [Warning] "Retry 2" ] As for quantified collection expectations in aweXpect, the failure message additionally lists the records that explain the failure, when the quantifier fails in only one direction: with only an upper bound, e.g. AtMost(…) or Never(), the matching records: Failure message Expected that collector did not log a record with level Warning, but it logged 1 such record Matching records: [ [Warning] "Retry 1" ] Records: [ [Information] "Starting", [Warning] "Retry 1" ] with only a lower bound above one, e.g. AtLeast(2.Times()), the not matching records. When the expectation is negated, this depends on its negation instead, e.g. AtLeast(2.Times()) lists the matching records when negated. Only one quantifier can be specified for each Logged, after the message: await That(collector).LoggedWarning().WithMessage("Retry *").AsWildcard().Twice();

You can verify that no matching record was logged: await That(collector).DidNotLogError(); await That(collector).DidNotLogWarning().OrHigher(); await That(collector).DidNotLog().WithMessage("*password*").AsWildcard(); As for Logged, there is a method for each log level, e.g. DidNotLogError(), and DidNotLog(LogLevel) for a level that is a parameter. DidNotLog takes the same filters as Logged, but no quantifier, as it is the same as Logged(…).Never(). If an error was logged, DidNotLogWarning().OrHigher() would fail with: Failure message Expected that collector did not log a record with level Warning or higher, but it logged 1 such record Matching records: [ [Error] "Retry limit reached" ] Records: [ [Information] "Starting", [Error] "Retry limit reached" ]

With Then, you can verify that further records were logged after a matching record, in the given order: await That(collector).LoggedInformation().WithMessage("Starting") .Then( r => r.LoggedWarning().WithMessage("Retry *").AsWildcard(), r => r.LoggedError().OrHigher().WithException<TimeoutException>()); Each step takes the same filters as Logged and must match a record that was logged after the one of the previous step, so a record cannot match two steps, while other records may be logged in between. As the order implies that each record was logged at least once, it cannot be combined with a quantifier. If a record was logged too early or not at all, the expectation would fail with: Failure message Expected that collector logged a record with level Information and message equal to "Starting", then a record with level Warning and message matching "Retry *", then a record with level Error or higher and exception of type TimeoutException in order, but it logged a record with level Warning and message matching "Retry *" too early Records: [ [Warning] "Retry 1", [Information] "Starting" ]

Records of a background service, e.g. a hosted service or a timer, can be logged after the expectation is evaluated. With Within, the records are read repeatedly until the timeout: await That(collector).LoggedInformation().WithMessage("Started").Within(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(5)); await That(collector).LoggedWarning().Once().Within(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(5)); await That(collector).DidNotLogError().OrHigher().Within(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(5)); The records are read until their amount decides the outcome, so the expectation only waits as long as necessary: An expectation that further records can meet, e.g. Logged or AtLeast(…), succeeds as soon as it is met. An expectation that further records can violate, e.g. DidNotLog, Never(), AtMost(…) or Once(), waits for the full timeout and fails as soon as it is violated. The records are read every 100 milliseconds by default (Customize.aweXpect.Settings().DefaultCheckInterval). You can change the interval with CheckEvery directly after Within: await That(collector).LoggedWarning() .Within(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(5)).CheckEvery(TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(10)); The failure message then lists the records that were logged until the expectation failed: Failure message Expected that collector did not log a record with level Error or higher within 0:05, but it logged 1 such record Matching records: [ [Error] "Retry limit reached" ] Records: [ [Information] "Started", [Error] "Retry limit reached" ] When the evaluation is canceled before the outcome is decided, e.g. via WithCancellation, the expectation is inconclusive.
aweXpect.Mockolate contains expectations to verify interactions with mocks from Mockolate. It is an extension for aweXpect.

.NET CLI PackageReference Central Package Management dotnet add package aweXpect.Mockolate <PackageReference Include="aweXpect.Mockolate" Version="3.4.0" /> Directory.Packages.props <PackageVersion Include="aweXpect.Mockolate" Version="3.4.0" /> Project file <PackageReference Include="aweXpect.Mockolate" /> Latest version: 3.4.0 It does not include aweXpect itself. The expectations live in the namespace aweXpect, the HTTP content matchers in Mockolate.Web.

IPlayer player = IPlayer.CreateMock(); player.Play("Let It Be"); player.Stop(); // verify how often a method was invoked await That(player.Mock.Verify.Play("Let It Be")).Once(); // verify the order of the interactions await That(player.Mock.Verify.Play("Let It Be")).Then(m => m.Stop()); // verify that no interaction was forgotten await That(player.Mock.Verify).AllInteractionsAreVerified(); A failing verification lists the matching and all interactions with the mock. If the track was played twice, Once() would fail with: Failure message Expected that the MusicStore.IPlayer mock invoked method Play(Let It Be) exactly once, but it was found twice Matching Interactions: [ invoke method Play(Let It Be), invoke method Play(Let It Be) ] All Interactions: [ invoke method Play(Let It Be), invoke method Play(Let It Be) ]

Expectation Summary Once, Twice, Never the interaction happened exactly once, twice or never AtLeastOnce, AtLeastTwice, AtLeast the interaction happened at least the given number of times AtMostOnce, AtMostTwice, AtMost the interaction happened at most the given number of times Exactly, Between the interaction happened exactly or in a range of times Times the number of interactions satisfies a predicate Then the interactions happened in the given order AllInteractionsAreVerified every interaction with the mock was verified AllSetupsAreUsed every setup of the mock was used Verifications of a minimum number of interactions and of their order can wait for interactions that happen in the background with Within(timeout), see Waiting for interactions and Interaction order. The HTTP content matchers add JSON matchers for It.IsHttpContent() in setups and verifications of a mocked HttpClient.

Describes the JSON matchers that this package adds to Mockolate's It.IsHttpContent(). Matcher Summary WithJsonMatching the JSON body matches the expected object WithJson the JSON body is equivalent to the expected JSON string IgnoringAdditionalProperties whether additional properties in the JSON body are ignored IgnoringAdditionalArrayElements whether additional array elements in the JSON body are ignored .NET 8 or later The HTTP content matchers require .NET 8 or later. The matchers are in the namespace Mockolate.Web. They are argument matchers, not expectations: use them in setups or verifications of a mocked HttpClient to match the JSON body of a request.

WithJsonMatching compares the body with an object, and WithJson with a JSON string, ignoring differences in formatting and property order: HttpClient httpClient = HttpClient.CreateMock(); httpClient.Mock.Setup .PostAsync(It.IsAny<Uri>(), It.IsHttpContent().WithJsonMatching(new { title = "Let It Be", year = 1970 })) .ReturnsAsync(new HttpResponseMessage(HttpStatusCode.Created)); httpClient.Mock.Setup .PostAsync(It.IsAny<Uri>(), It.IsHttpContent().WithJson("{\"year\": 1965, \"title\": \"Yesterday\"}")) .ReturnsAsync(new HttpResponseMessage(HttpStatusCode.Created)); Trimming and Native AOT WithJsonMatching serializes the expected value by reflection, which is switched off when publishing with trimming or Native AOT enabled, so use WithJson with the expected JSON as a string there.

WithJson requires the body to be equivalent to the expected JSON: additional properties of objects and additional elements at the end of arrays do not match. WithJsonMatching ignores both by default. Change this on either matcher with IgnoringAdditionalProperties and IgnoringAdditionalArrayElements: httpClient.Mock.Setup .PostAsync(It.IsAny<Uri>(), It.IsHttpContent() .WithJson("{\"title\": \"Let It Be\", \"tracks\": [\"Two of Us\"]}") .IgnoringAdditionalProperties() .IgnoringAdditionalArrayElements()) .ReturnsAsync(new HttpResponseMessage(HttpStatusCode.Created)); httpClient.Mock.Setup .PostAsync(It.IsAny<Uri>(), It.IsHttpContent() .WithJsonMatching(new { title = "Let It Be", year = 1970 }) .IgnoringAdditionalProperties(false)) .ReturnsAsync(new HttpResponseMessage(HttpStatusCode.Created)); No match returns the default response When the body does not match, the setup is not used and the mocked HttpClient returns its default response instead of failing. Earlier versions of WithJson ignored additional properties and array elements: to keep that behavior, add .IgnoringAdditionalProperties().IgnoringAdditionalArrayElements() or pass the expected object to WithJsonMatching.

Describes the possible expectations for verifying how often an interaction with a mock happened. Expectation Negated Summary Once the interaction happened exactly once Twice the interaction happened exactly twice Never the interaction never happened AtLeastOnce the interaction happened at least once AtLeastTwice the interaction happened at least twice AtLeast the interaction happened at least the given number of times AtMostOnce the interaction happened at most once AtMostTwice the interaction happened at most twice AtMost the interaction happened at most the given number of times Exactly the interaction happened exactly the given number of times Between the number of interactions is in the given range Times the number of interactions satisfies a predicate The samples use the following interface: public interface IPlayer { bool Play(string title); void Pause(); void Stop(); }

You can verify how often a method was invoked: using aweXpect.Core; // for Times() using static aweXpect.Expect; IPlayer player = IPlayer.CreateMock(); player.Play("Let It Be"); await That(player.Mock.Verify.Play("Let It Be")).Once(); await That(player.Mock.Verify.Play("Yesterday")).Never(); await That(player.Mock.Verify.Play(It.IsAny<string>())).AtLeastOnce(); await That(player.Mock.Verify.Play(It.IsAny<string>())).AtMost(3.Times()); await That(player.Mock.Verify.Play(It.IsAny<string>())).Between(1).And(3.Times()); await That(player.Mock.Verify.Play(It.IsAny<string>())).Times(n => n % 2 == 1); When the track was played twice, Once() fails with: Failure message Expected that the MusicStore.IPlayer mock invoked method Play(Let It Be) exactly once, but it was found twice Matching Interactions: [ invoke method Play(Let It Be), invoke method Play(Let It Be) ] All Interactions: [ invoke method Play(Let It Be), invoke method Play(Let It Be) ]

With Within(TimeSpan timeout), you can verify that the expected number of interactions happens within the given time. This is useful for interactions that happen asynchronously in the background. Within is available on AtLeast…, Once, Twice, Exactly, Between and Times. It is not available on Never or AtMost…, since an upper bound cannot be confirmed by waiting longer. For the order of interactions, see Then. IPlayer player = IPlayer.CreateMock(); _ = Task.Run(async () => { await Task.Delay(500); player.Play("Hey Jude"); }); await That(player.Mock.Verify.Play("Hey Jude")).AtLeastOnce().Within(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(1)); When the interaction does not happen in time, e.g. a Stop() expected within 100 ms, the expectation fails: Failure message Expected that the MusicStore.IPlayer mock invoked method Stop() at least once within 0:00.100, but it was never found Matching Interactions: [] All Interactions: [ invoke method Play(Hey Jude) ] Instead of a fixed time span, you can also provide a CancellationToken to wait for the expected interactions until it is canceled. Like for all aweXpect expectations, a cancellation leaves the expectation inconclusive instead of failing it, so use Within to limit how long the verification waits: await That(player.Mock.Verify.Play("Hey Jude")).AtLeastOnce().WithCancellation(token); Waiting without Within Unlike other aweXpect expectations, these verifications also wait for the interaction when only WithTimeout or WithCancellation is given: the timeout or the token bounds how long they wait, and the verification fails when the timeout elapses. Within sets an explicit wait, which is shown in the expectation; a shorter WithTimeout still ends it early with "it did not finish within …". note A Times predicate that throws counts as not met while waiting, so the verification waits for further interactions, and only fails with the exception when the predicate still throws at the end. A selector of Then that throws fails the verification immediately.

DoesNotComplyWith evaluates the verification inside it non-negated, so put Within on the verification inside it to verify that an interaction does not happen within the given time. It waits the whole time and fails as soon as the interaction happens: await That(player.Mock.Verify.Stop()).DoesNotComplyWith(it => it.AtLeastOnce().Within(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(1))); warning Within on DoesNotComplyWith itself does not help here: it only checks again until the interaction is not found, so it succeeds immediately when the interaction did not happen yet.
documents.s: Waiting for an interaction not to happen

documents.t: Describes the possible expectations for verifying the order of interactions with a mock. Expectation Negated Summary Then the interactions happened in the given order The samples use the IPlayer interface from Interaction count.

You can verify that methods were invoked in a specific order: IPlayer player = IPlayer.CreateMock(); player.Play("Let It Be"); player.Pause(); player.Stop(); await That(player.Mock.Verify.Play("Let It Be")).Then( m => m.Pause(), m => m.Stop()); Other interactions may happen in between. When the player was stopped before it was paused, the expectation fails: Failure message Expected that the MusicStore.IPlayer mock invoked method Play(Let It Be), then invoked method Pause(), then invoked method Stop() in order, but it invoked method Stop() too early All Interactions: [ invoke method Play(Let It Be), invoke method Stop(), invoke method Pause() ]

With Within(TimeSpan timeout), the verification waits until the whole sequence happened, e.g. when the interactions happen asynchronously in the background. Interactions that are recorded while waiting count for every step, so a Stop() after the Pause() also satisfies a sequence whose first Stop() came too early. IPlayer player = IPlayer.CreateMock(); _ = Task.Run(async () => { player.Play("Let It Be"); await Task.Delay(50); player.Pause(); player.Stop(); }); await That(player.Mock.Verify.Play("Let It Be")) .Then(m => m.Pause(), m => m.Stop()) .Within(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(1)); When the sequence is not complete in time, the expectation fails: Failure message Expected that the MusicStore.IPlayer mock invoked method Play(Let It Be), then invoked method Pause(), then invoked method Stop() in order within 0:01, but it invoked method Stop() not at all All Interactions: [ invoke method Play(Let It Be), invoke method Pause() ] The timeout is a budget for the whole sequence, counted from the start of the verification: A step with a timeout of its own, e.g. m => m.Stop().Within(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(5)), waits up to that timeout, regardless of the budget. Every other step only waits for what is left of the budget. When nothing is left, e.g. because a step with its own timeout took longer, it is checked once without waiting. Without any timeout, the sequence is checked once. Like for the interaction count, WithTimeout without Within also sets the budget, and WithCancellation waits until the token is canceled, which leaves the expectation inconclusive.

Describes the possible expectations for verifying that all interactions with a mock were verified and all its setups were used. Expectation Negated Summary AllInteractionsAreVerified every interaction with the mock was verified AllSetupsAreUsed every setup of the mock was used The samples use the IPlayer interface from Interaction count.

You can verify that all interactions with the mock were verified. This detects unintended or forgotten interactions: IPlayer player = IPlayer.CreateMock(); player.Play("Let It Be"); player.Play("Yesterday"); player.Stop(); await That(player.Mock.Verify.Play(It.IsAny<string>())).Twice(); await That(player.Mock.Verify).AllInteractionsAreVerified(); The verification of Play covers both tracks, but Stop() was never verified: Failure message Expected that the MusicStore.IPlayer mock has all interactions verified, but it had 1 unverified interaction Unverified Interactions: [ invoke method Stop() ]

You can verify that all setups of the mock were used. This detects setups that are no longer needed: IPlayer player = IPlayer.CreateMock(); player.Mock.Setup.Play("Let It Be").Returns(true); player.Mock.Setup.Play("Yesterday").Returns(true); player.Play("Let It Be"); await That(player.Mock.Verify).AllSetupsAreUsed(); Failure message Expected that the MusicStore.IPlayer mock has used all setups, but it had 1 unused setup Unused Setups: [ bool Play("Yesterday") ]
aweXpect.Reflection extends aweXpect with expectations for reflection types, so you can write architecture and convention tests for assemblies, types and members.

.NET CLI PackageReference Central Package Management dotnet add package aweXpect.Reflection --prerelease <PackageReference Include="aweXpect.Reflection" Version="4.0.0-pre.3" /> Directory.Packages.props <PackageVersion Include="aweXpect.Reflection" Version="4.0.0-pre.3" /> Project file <PackageReference Include="aweXpect.Reflection" /> Latest version: 4.0.0-pre.3 The package brings Expect.That with it, but not the expectations for strings, numbers or collections, so reference aweXpect as well. The expectations live in the namespace aweXpect; the sources In and Types, their filters and the customization need using aweXpect.Reflection;, and a stored selection like Filtered.Types needs using aweXpect.Reflection.Collections;. The examples write That(...) instead of Expect.That(...), which needs using static aweXpect.Expect; (see Getting started).

Write architecture and convention tests as plain, readable expectations: select the assemblies, types or members you care about with In or Types, then expect a rule on them with Expect.That. // "Every async method must end in 'Async'" await That(In.AssemblyContaining<PlaylistService>() // ① pick a source .Methods() // ② navigate to a member kind .WhichAreAsync()) // ③ filter it down .HaveName("Async").AsSuffix(); // ④ expect Every expectation follows the same four-part shape: Step What it does Examples ① Source choose where to look In.AllLoadedAssemblies(), In.AssemblyContaining<T>(), In.Type<T>() ② Navigate move to a member kind .Types(), .Methods(), .Properties(), .Fields(), .Events(), .Constructors() ③ Filter (optional) narrow the set .WhichArePublic(), .With<T>(), .WithName(…), .Which(…) ④ Expect state the rule That(…).HaveName(…), .AreClasses(), .Return<Task>() Steps ② and ③ are optional. You can verify a single Type, MethodInfo, … or a whole Assembly directly, and every expectation works the same whether the subject is one item or a collection (Assembly[], IEnumerable<Type?>, …). The supported reflection subjects are Assembly, Type, ConstructorInfo, EventInfo, FieldInfo, MethodInfo and PropertyInfo.

// Verify all test classes (those containing a [Fact] or [Theory] method) follow the naming convention await That(In.AllLoadedAssemblies() .Public.Classes() .WhichContainMethods(m => m.With<FactAttribute>().OrWith<TheoryAttribute>())) .HaveName("Tests").AsSuffix(); // Verify all async methods have an "Async" suffix await That(In.AssemblyContaining<PlaylistService>() .Methods().WhichAreAsync()) .HaveName("Async").AsSuffix(); // Verify all methods with an "Async" suffix return Task or ValueTask await That(In.AssemblyContaining<PlaylistService>() .Methods().WithName("Async").AsSuffix()) .Return<Task>().OrReturn<ValueTask>(); // Verify controllers follow the naming convention await That(In.AllLoadedAssemblies() .Types().WhichInheritFrom<ControllerBase>()) .HaveName("Controller").AsSuffix(); // Verify each event handler is named after the event it handles (e.g. "OnTrackAdded") await That(In.AssemblyContaining<Playlist>() .Methods().Which(m => m.GetParameters().Length == 1)) .HaveName(method => "On" + method.GetParameters()[0].ParameterType.Name); // Verify each serializable type has exactly one parameterless constructor await That(In.AllLoadedAssemblies() .Types().With<SerializableAttribute>()) .ContainConstructors(c => c.WithNoParameters()).Exactly(1);

There is no separate rule engine: a "layer" is just a reusable type selection, and an architecture rule is just an expectation on it. Combine several rules into a single verification with Expect.ThatAll: Filtered.Types domainTypes = Types.InNamespace("MusicStore.Domain"); Filtered.Types infrastructureTypes = Types.InNamespace("MusicStore.Infrastructure"); await Expect.ThatAll( That(domainTypes).DoNotDependOn(infrastructureTypes), That(domainTypes).AreSealed()); A failing rule reports all violations, numbered per expectation: Failure message Expected all of the following to succeed: [01] Expected that types within namespace "MusicStore.Domain" in all loaded assemblies all do not depend on types within namespace "MusicStore.Infrastructure" in all loaded assemblies [02] Expected that types within namespace "MusicStore.Domain" in all loaded assemblies all are sealed but [01] it contained types with the dependency [02] only 1 of 3 were [01] Not matching items: [ PlaylistService ] [02] Not matching items: [ Album, Track ] [02] Collection: [ Album, PlaylistService, Track ] The dependency rules (DependOn / DependOnlyOn / HaveDependenciesOutside), dependency cycle detection (HaveNoDependencyCycles) and exemptions (Except) are documented in Architecture rules.

Each filter narrows a selection and its expectation counterpart verifies it, e.g. .WhichArePublic() and .IsPublic() (.ArePublic() for collections): Page Covers Examples Common filters access modifiers, attributes, the obsolete marker, names and namespaces of types and members WhichArePublic / IsPublic, With<TAttribute> / Has<TAttribute> Assemblies name, target framework, version, strong name and dependencies WhichTarget / Targets, WhichDependOn / DependsOn Types and inheritance kinds of types, base classes, interfaces and contained members, and how inherited members count WhichAreClasses / IsAClass, WhichInheritFrom<T> / InheritsFrom<T> Methods, operators and constructors return types and parameters WhichAreAsync / IsAsync, WhichReturn<T> / Returns<T>, WithParameter<T> / HasParameter<T> Properties, fields and events member types, nullability and accessors WhichAreOfType<T> / IsOfType<T>, WhichAreRequired / IsRequired Architecture rules type dependencies, dependency cycles and layers as type selections DependOn / DependOnlyOn / HaveDependenciesOutside, HaveNoDependencyCycles The overview lists all topics, including combined filters, custom predicates (Which / Satisfies, Except) and quantifiers. Each filter and expectation has its negation where it makes sense, e.g. WithoutName / DoesNotHaveName, WithoutNamespace / DoesNotHaveNamespace, WhichAreNotOfType<T> / IsNotOfType<T>, WhichDoNotReturn<T> / DoesNotReturn<T>, WithoutParameter<T> / DoesNotHaveParameter<T> or WhichDoNotTarget / DoesNotTarget. On a collection, a negated expectation (DoNotReturn<T>, AreNotOfType<T>, …) verifies that none of the items match. The tables in Filters and expectations list every negation in a Negated column. The name filters and expectations accept the string matching options like AsPrefix(), AsSuffix() or AsWildcard(). Filters and expectations documents the complete vocabulary.

Set a value under Customize.aweXpect.Reflection() for the current async flow, or under Customize.aweXpect.Global.Reflection() for all tests. Value Default Summary Settings().ExcludedAssemblyPrefixes System, Microsoft, … assemblies excluded from In.AllLoadedAssemblies() and from DependOnlyOn IncludedCompilerGeneratedMembers CompilerGeneratedMembers.None the compiler-generated types and members included in the navigations IncludedSpecialNameMembers SpecialNameMembers.None the operators and accessors included in .Methods() DependencyResolver built-in signature-level resolver how the type-level dependency expectations determine the dependencies of a type ExcludedAttributeTypes none additional compiler-emitted attributes that never count as dependencies

Selecting types and members: the In and Types sources and navigating between assemblies, types and members Filters and expectations: the complete reference for all subject kinds, string matching options and quantifiers Architecture rules: type dependencies, dependency cycles and layers as type selections Customization: assembly exclusions, compiler-generated members and the dependency resolver Comparisons: feature maps against FluentAssertions and against NetArchTest and ArchUnitNET

An architecture rule restricts which other types a type may reference: its dependencies. Type dependencies introduces the dependency filters and expectations (including dependency cycles), and Layers as type selections shows how to combine them into a full architecture test suite. The examples use a music store application with the layers MusicStore.Api, MusicStore.Application, MusicStore.Domain, MusicStore.Data and MusicStore.Infrastructure.

The dependency filters and expectations follow the familiar filter/expect pairing: Filter Expect (single) Expect (many) depends on namespace .WhichDependOn("x", …) .DependsOn("x", …) .DependOn("x", …) does not depend on .WhichDoNotDependOn("x", …) .DoesNotDependOn("x", …) .DoNotDependOn("x", …) depends on type .WhichDependOn<T>() .DependsOn<T>() .DependOn<T>() does not depend on type .WhichDoNotDependOn<T>() .DoesNotDependOn<T>() .DoNotDependOn<T>() depends only on set .WhichDependOnlyOn("x", …) .DependsOnlyOn("x", …) .DependOnlyOn("x", …) has dependencies outside set .WhichHaveDependenciesOutside("x", …) .HasDependenciesOutside("x", …) .HaveDependenciesOutside("x", …) // The API layer must not reference the data layer await That(Types.InNamespace("MusicStore.Api")) .DoNotDependOn("MusicStore.Data"); // The API layer may only reference the application and domain layers await That(Types.InNamespace("MusicStore.Api")) .DependOnlyOn("MusicStore.Application", "MusicStore.Domain"); // Filter for the types that depend on a namespace In.AllLoadedAssemblies().Types().WhichDependOn("System.Data") A type depends on every type referenced in its declared signature: the base type and directly implemented interfaces, generic arguments and parameter constraints, field/property/event types, indexer parameters, method return/parameter/generic-argument types, constructor parameters and the types of attributes applied to the type, its members, their parameters and return values (including typeof(…) and enum attribute arguments). Purely synthetic references that you never wrote, like the compiler's own plumbing, are ignored. Types you write in authored signatures always do count, including primitives and void return types (namespace System); in practice, almost every type with members does depend on System. Signature-level only Dependencies are computed from reflection metadata, so body-level references such as new Data.AlbumRepository(), static calls and local variables are not detected. Nested types are separate types with their own dependency surface: verifying typeof(Outer) does not include what Outer.Inner references. The collection-based expectations (e.g. over Types.InNamespace(…)) enumerate nested types as their own items and therefore cover them. For IL/body-level accuracy, plug in your own resolver via Customize.aweXpect.Reflection().DependencyResolver (see Customization). Namespace matching is ordinal and case-sensitive and, like WhichAreWithinNamespace, includes sub-namespaces by default (so MusicStore.Data matches MusicStore.Data.Sql but not MusicStore.DataImport). A dependency in the global namespace can be targeted or allowed with an empty string (""). Each result is chainable: // Widen the set with .OrOn(…) await That(Types.InNamespace("MusicStore.Api")) .DependOnlyOn("MusicStore.Application").OrOn("MusicStore.Domain"); // Opt out of sub-namespace matching for the whole expression await That(types).DoNotDependOn("MusicStore.Data").ExcludingSubNamespaces(); For DependsOnlyOn a type's own namespace is always allowed, and by default so are its sub-namespaces. Use .ExcludingOwnSubNamespaces() to also forbid references into a type's own sub-namespaces: await That(Types.InNamespace("MusicStore.Domain")) .DependOnlyOn("MusicStore.Domain").ExcludingSubNamespaces().ExcludingOwnSubNamespaces(); HasDependenciesOutside is the positive counterpart of DependsOnlyOn for finding the violators of an allowed set, without a double-negated "does not depend only on". The allowed set follows the same rules (sub-namespaces included, the own namespace and framework assemblies never count as outside, the same chainable refinements): // Select the current violators of an architecture rule (e.g. for a baseline) In.AllLoadedAssemblies().Types().WhichHaveDependenciesOutside("MusicStore.Application", "MusicStore.Domain") // Verify that a known legacy type still has its external dependency await That(typeof(LegacyImportService)) .HasDependenciesOutside("MusicStore.Application", "MusicStore.Domain"); DependsOn and DoesNotDependOn also accept a specific type via <T>() or (Type), with .OrOn<T>() / .OrOn(Type) to widen. For collections of types, DependOn and DoNotDependOn accept the same forms and verify that every type, or none of them, depends on the specific type. The WhichDependOn / WhichDoNotDependOn filters accept the same forms, including .OrOn<T>() / .OrOn(Type): await That(typeof(Album)).DoesNotDependOn<DbContext>().OrOn<SqlConnection>(); // No controller may reference the DbContext directly await That(Types.InNamespace("MusicStore.Api.Controllers")) .DoNotDependOn<DbContext>(); // The same with a type only known at runtime Type dbContextType = typeof(DbContext); await That(Types.InNamespace("MusicStore.Api.Controllers")) .DoNotDependOn(dbContextType); // Filter for the types that reference the DbContext In.AllLoadedAssemblies().Types().WhichDependOn(dbContextType) All dependency families additionally accept a reusable Filtered.Types selection as target; see Layers as type selections. On collections of types, DependOn, DependOnlyOn and HaveDependenciesOutside also follow aweXpect's quantifiers and keep their options, like .OrOn(…) or .ExcludingSubNamespaces(). DoNotDependOn means that no type depends on the target (none depend on namespace "MusicStore.Data"), the same as None().DependOn(…): await That(Types.InNamespace("MusicStore.Api.Controllers")) .AtMost(1).DependOn<DbContext>(); await That(Types.InNamespace("MusicStore.Domain")) .AtLeast(2).DependOnlyOn("MusicStore.Domain").ExcludingOwnSubNamespaces(); Framework dependencies are ignored unless you name one explicitly DependOnlyOn ignores dependencies whose assembly name matches one of the ExcludedAssemblyPrefixes (e.g. System covers System and System.Text.Json), so you never have to whitelist System.*, while a type's own namespace is always allowed. DependsOn / DoesNotDependOn / WhichDependOn still match a framework namespace when you name it explicitly (e.g. DoesNotDependOn("System.Data")). The default prefixes include Microsoft, so DependOnlyOn also ignores dependencies on e.g. Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore, Microsoft.AspNetCore and Microsoft.Extensions.*; a domain entity inheriting DbContext does not fail DependOnlyOn("MusicStore.Domain"). To forbid such dependencies, name them explicitly (DoesNotDependOn<DbContext>() or DoNotDependOn("Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore")) or customize the ExcludedAssemblyPrefixes. Note that the customization also affects assembly scanning and assembly-level dependency expectations. What counts as a dependency in detail Element types of arrays/pointers/by-ref and generic type arguments are unwrapped (List<Data.Album> depends on List<Data.Album>, which also matches a List<> target, and on Data.Album; a closed-generic target like List<Data.Track> only matches that exact construction). Function-pointer signatures (delegate*<…>) are not decomposed; the types inside them are invisible to dependency expectations. The ignored synthetic references are compiler-generated members, the implicit object/ValueType/Enum base type, interfaces inherited from the base type, records' synthesized IEquatable<T>, delegates' runtime infrastructure (only the Invoke signature counts), enums' underlying-value plumbing and the attributes the compiler emits onto authored code (nullability metadata, required members, async/iterator state machines, …). Should a future compiler version emit a marker attribute this library does not know about yet, exclude it yourself via Customize.aweXpect.Reflection().ExcludedAttributeTypes (full attribute type names; extends the built-in set).

The "slices should be free of cycles" architecture rule: verify that the namespaces of a set of types do not (transitively) depend on each other. // No dependency cycles among the namespaces under MusicStore await That(Types.InNamespace("MusicStore")) .HaveNoDependencyCycles(); A namespace A depends on a namespace B when some type in A references a type in B (in its signature). Each cycle is reported, e.g. MusicStore.Billing -> MusicStore.Catalog -> MusicStore.Billing. By default a namespace and its sub-namespaces count as a single namespace, consistent with how the other dependency expectations treat a type's own sub-namespaces. So a reference between a namespace and its ancestor/descendant (e.g. MusicStore.Catalog ↔ MusicStore.Catalog.Domain) cannot by itself form a cycle. Use ExcludingSubNamespaces() to treat every namespace on its own, so that such a parent/child reference can form a cycle: // Treat every namespace as its own node (MusicStore.Catalog ↔ MusicStore.Catalog.Domain can now form a cycle) await That(Types.InNamespace("MusicStore")) .HaveNoDependencyCycles().ExcludingSubNamespaces(); Pass a slice root to group all namespaces below it into one slice each (by the namespace segment immediately following the root), so that, for example, MusicStore.Catalog, MusicStore.Catalog.Domain and MusicStore.Catalog.Api collapse into the single slice MusicStore.Catalog: // Group MusicStore.Catalog.* / MusicStore.Billing.* / … into one slice each before looking for cycles await That(Types.InNamespace("MusicStore")) .HaveNoDependencyCycles("MusicStore"); Failure message Expected that Types.InNamespace("MusicStore") have no dependency cycles when grouped into slices under "MusicStore", but it had a dependency cycle Dependency cycles: MusicStore.Billing -> MusicStore.Catalog -> MusicStore.Billing How cycles are detected The dependencies are read through the same resolver as the other dependency expectations. The namespaces of the analyzed types form the nodes of a directed graph, and each strongly-connected component with more than one node is reported as a cycle. Only namespaces present in the analyzed set form nodes, so dependencies on framework or otherwise out-of-set namespaces never create an edge, and a namespace referencing itself is not a cycle. By default a namespace and its sub-namespaces collapse into a single node (a family). Because the family is one node (not just a suppressed pair of edges), a cycle that leaves the family and returns through a different member of it (e.g. MusicStore.Catalog -> MusicStore.Billing -> MusicStore.Catalog.Domain) is still detected. Configuring a custom dependency resolver (e.g. an IL-level one) also sharpens cycle detection: body-level references it surfaces can complete a cycle that the signature-level default cannot see.

There is no separate rule engine: a "layer" is just a reusable Filtered.Types selection (with the full filter vocabulary at your disposal), and an architecture rule is just an expectation on it. Filtered.Types domainTypes = Types.InNamespace("MusicStore.Domain"); Filtered.Types infrastructureTypes = Types.InNamespace("MusicStore.Infrastructure"); Filtered.Types repositoryTypes = Types.InNamespace("MusicStore.Data").WithName("Repository").AsSuffix(); The dependency expectations and filters accept such a selection as a target, alongside the namespace and specific-type forms: DependsOn / DoesNotDependOn / DependsOnlyOn / HasDependenciesOutside (and the plural DependOn / DoNotDependOn / DependOnlyOn / HaveDependenciesOutside and the WhichDependOn / WhichDoNotDependOn / WhichDependOnlyOn / WhichHaveDependenciesOutside filters) take one or more Filtered.Types arguments. Multiple targets and .OrOn(…) mean any of; for the only-on and outside families the union is the allowed set, while the own-namespace and framework rules apply unchanged, including the .ExcludingOwnSubNamespaces() opt-out. // Outgoing rule with a selection as target: await That(domainTypes).DoNotDependOn(infrastructureTypes); // Incoming rules are written explicitly from the other side: await That(infrastructureTypes).DoNotDependOn(domainTypes); // Allowed set as union of selections (own namespace + framework stay allowed): await That(repositoryTypes).DependOnlyOn(domainTypes).OrOn(infrastructureTypes); Combine several rules into a single verification with aweXpect's Expect.ThatAll(…) (see combining expectations): every rule is evaluated and all failures are reported together. Any expectation works on a selection, not just the dependency ones, so naming conventions or sealing rules live in the same check: await Expect.ThatAll( That(domainTypes).DoNotDependOn(infrastructureTypes), That(repositoryTypes).DependOnlyOn(domainTypes).OrOn(infrastructureTypes), That(domainTypes).AreSealed()); A failing rule reports all violations, numbered per expectation. Here PlaylistService references the infrastructure layer, and Album and Track are not sealed: Failure message Expected all of the following to succeed: [01] Expected that types within namespace "MusicStore.Domain" in all loaded assemblies all do not depend on types within namespace "MusicStore.Infrastructure" in all loaded assemblies [02] Expected that types within namespace "MusicStore.Data" with name ending with "Repository" in all loaded assemblies all depend only on types within namespace "MusicStore.Domain" in all loaded assemblies or types within namespace "MusicStore.Infrastructure" in all loaded assemblies [03] Expected that types within namespace "MusicStore.Domain" in all loaded assemblies all are sealed but [01] it contained types with the dependency [03] only 1 of 3 were [01] Not matching items: [ PlaylistService ] [03] Not matching items: [ Album, Track ] [03] Collection: [ Album, PlaylistService, Track ] Exemptions to a rule use the Except filter on the subject selection: await That(domainTypes.Except<LegacyImportService>()).DoNotDependOn(infrastructureTypes); await That(domainTypes.Except(type => type.Name.StartsWith("Generated"))).AreSealed(); A layer spanning several namespaces is built by widening a dependency target with additional selections (or .OrOn(…)); for a subject spanning several namespaces, verify each namespace selection as its own rule inside the same Expect.ThatAll(…). How a selection is matched as a target Each target selection is resolved once per expectation; a dependency matches when it is a member of the union of the resolved selections. Matching is by type identity, where a generic type definition in the selection (e.g. a scanned Repository<>) matches any of its constructions. For the only-on and outside families, an empty selection allows only the own namespace and framework dependencies. A selection is an explicit target, so framework types contained in it are matched normally by DependsOn / DoesNotDependOn.
